﴿Ṭā Sīn Mīm﴾ The discussion of its counterpart has already been given at the opening of Surat ash-Shu'ara'.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 28, verses 2–3:**

﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ ﴿We recite to you, [O Muhammad], some of the news of Moses and Pharaoh in truth, for a people who believe.﴾ The demonstrative in His saying ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ is of the same kind as the demonstrative in its counterpart in Surat al-Shu'ara'. Thus, what is referred to is what was being recited of the Qur'an on the day this verse was revealed, as a way of drawing attention to the Qur'an and affirming that its matter is a great one.

The clause ﴿We recite to you, [O Muhammad], some of the news of Moses﴾ is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i).

The narrative of Moses and Pharaoh is prefaced with His saying "We recite to you" in order to arouse eagerness for this news, because of the many lessons it contains regarding the magnificent way in which God manages His creation.

Al-tilawa (recitation) means reading a text that is either written or memorized, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And to recite the Qur'an﴾ [al-Naml: 92]. It takes the preposition (ʿala) when it reaches the one to whom it is recited, and this was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾ [al-Baqara: 102] in Surat al-Baqara, and at His saying "﴿And when His verses are recited to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 2]" in Surat al-Anfal.

Attributing the recitation to God is a metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi), because He is the One who commands the recitation of what is revealed to Him of speech, while the one who literally recites is Jibril, by command from God. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are the verses of God which We recite to you in truth﴾ [al-Baqara: 252] in Surat al-Baqara.

The recitation was directed to the Prophet ﷺ because he is the one who receives that which is recited. This report is expressed as "news" (naba') to indicate that it is a report of great importance and significance.

The lam in ﴿for a people who believe﴾ is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil): that is, "We recite to you for the sake of a people who believe." Thus the purpose of reciting this news to the Prophet ﷺ is that a people who believe may benefit from it, and the Prophet conveys it to the believers. If a group of the believers asked, or yearned, for a detailed account of what came of the story of Moses and Pharaoh in Surat al-Shu'ara' and Surat al-Naml, and this is the apparent meaning, then specifying them for the causation is clear, and the Prophet's own benefit from it along with them is more fitting and stronger. For this reason it did not mention him explicitly, relying on the indication of the implicit meaning (dalalat al-fahwa), because the context is to inform the one who asked, and others are not considered in this context.

If the revelation of this story was not in response to a yearning among the Muslims, then specifying the believers for the recitation on their account is an honouring of them as the ones who benefit from lessons and admonitions, since by their faith they have become seekers of knowledge and wisdom, yearning for such beneficial narratives in order to increase their certainty. The increase in knowledge for the Prophet ﷺ through this is evident from the fact that he is the recipient and the conveyor, so that he may recall from it what he already knew and increase in knowledge of what perhaps he did not know; and in this is the strengthening of his heart, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And all [of] the news of the messengers We relate to you by which We strengthen your heart. And there has come to you in these the truth and an admonition and a reminder for the believers﴾ [Hud: 120].

Thus the meaning of "for a people who believe" is a people for whom faith is their character and disposition. To indicate the meaning of faith having taken firm root in their souls, the description of faith was applied to the word "people" so as to convey that their being believers is among the constituents of their peoplehood, as we have mentioned more than once. Therefore the meaning is: those who are characterized by faith. The present tense form was used to indicate that their faith exists in the present and is continuous and renewed.

In this there is a turning away from concern with the polytheists in the telling of this story, with what is intended in it of lesson and admonition, for they did not benefit from it; rather, benefit from it was gained by those who believed and those who will believe after hearing it.

The ba' in His saying "bi-al-haqq" is for accompaniment (mula'aba), and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "natlu," or an adjective of the recitation implied by "natlu."

Al-haqq means truth (al-sidq), because truth is a thing that is established (haqq), since al-haqq is what is fitting to be established among people of sound intellects and upright religions.

The object of "natlu" is omitted, indicated by its qualifier, which is "min naba' Musa wa Fir'awn." The estimated meaning is: "We recite to you a discourse of the news of Moses and Pharaoh."

The "min" is partitive (tab'idiyya), since what is recited in this surah is in reality a part of the story of Moses and Pharaoh. Do you not see that things from the story of Moses have been mentioned in the Qur'an which are not mentioned here, such as the mention of the sign of the flood and the locusts?

Al-Zamakhshari made "min" a noun with the meaning of "part" (ba'd), making it the object of "natlu." Al-Akhfash made "min" superfluous (zaʼida), because he holds that "min" may be added in affirmative speech, and so he made "naba'" of Musa the object, governed by the superfluous preposition.

Al-naba' is an important, great report.

[Page 66]

﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a group among them: slaughtering their sons and sparing their women. Indeed, he was among the corrupters.﴾

This sentence and what is conjoined to it are an elucidation (bayan) of the clause "natlu" (We recite), or an elucidation of "﴿the story of Moses and Pharaoh﴾ [al-Qasas: 3]". The summary is presented first to indicate that this is a narrative of great importance and weight, containing diverse lessons. It is opened with the emphatic particle (inna) to give attention to the report.

The story begins by mentioning its causes so that it serves as a lesson for the believers, who take from it patterns (sunan) by which they come to know the causes of things and their effects, and by whose methods they conduct their affairs. Had it not been for Pharaoh's tyranny, which is among the most ugly of traits, total destruction would not have befallen him and his people, and the Children of Israel would not have emerged from the humiliation of servitude. This is the fulfilment of the proverb: "The misfortunes of one people are the benefits of another." Also relevant is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿It may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216].

Pharaoh's greatness in this world is depicted by his words "exalted himself in the land," so that the lesson of his destruction after that exaltation becomes the greatest of lessons.

The meaning of "exalting" (ʿulluw) here is arrogance (kibr), which is the blameworthy form of non-physical exaltation, like that in His saying: ﴿We assign that abode of the Hereafter to those who do not desire haughtiness in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 83]. Its meaning is that one perceives oneself as elevated above the position of others, such that no one is his equal. Thus "exaltation" is used metaphorically for the sense of superiority over others, without any right of religion, law, or the observance of the rights of created beings. When one perceives this in oneself, he does not heed, in his conduct, the pursuit of righteousness or the avoidance of corruption and harm; rather, he follows whatever his desire drives him toward and the satisfaction of his whims. It suffices you that Pharaoh made himself a god and claimed to be the son of the sun.

Therefore, the superiority of one person over another in some matter is not from the blameworthy exaltation, since he is deserving of that superiority in it, in accordance with a rational cause, such as the superiority of the knowledgeable over the ignorant, the righteous over the wicked, and the intelligent over the dull; or with a customary cause, which includes the legal (qanuni), that is, every superiority without which the order of communities cannot be sustained, such as the superiority of a commander over his soldiers and of a judge over the litigants.

The most just superiority is that which arises from religion and the Law, such as the superiority of the believer over the

[Page 67]

disbeliever, and of the pious over the wicked. The Exalted said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest; they are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. And to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [al-Hadid: 10]. Superiority in every work belongs to those who have expertise in it and excel in it; beyond that, the default is equality.

This Pharaoh is (Ramesses) II, who was the third king of the nineteenth dynasty in the terminology of historians of the Pharaohs, and he was a great conqueror of formidable power. It was in his time that Moses, peace be upon him, was born, according to verification.

"The land" (al-ard) refers to the land of Egypt, and the definite article in it is for familiarity (ʿahd), since the mention of Pharaoh makes it known to the hearer, because "Pharaoh" is the name of the king of Egypt. It is also permissible to take "the land" to mean the whole earth, that is, the widely known and famous part of it. The use of "the land" is then like the customary generalization, for the kingdom of Pharaoh (Ramesses) II extended from the lands of India, from the borders of the river (Kanak) in India, to the river Danube in Europe. The meaning is the land of his realm, and his exaltation was stronger than the exaltation of the kings of the earth and the masters of peoples.

Al-shiyaʿ is the plural of shiʿa. The shiʿa is a group that supports another in what it desires, that is, follows it, obeys it, and aids it, as the Exalted said: "This is of his faction and this is of his enemy" [al-Qasas: 15]. It is applied to a faction of people by way of extension, through the relation of the general to the specific, as the Exalted said: ﴿Those who split their religion and became sects, each party rejoicing in what it has﴾ [al-Rum: 32].

Among the eloquent features is the choice of this word here, to indicate that he made the people of the land of the Copts into factions with tendencies, each faction partisan to him and hostile to the other faction, so that he could divide them and set some against others. He also incited enmity among them so that he could be safe from their uniting against him, as it is said: "Divide and you rule." This is a policy fit only for deception against an opponent or enemy, and not befitting the policy of the ruler of a single community.

(Ramesses) II had divided the land of Egypt into thirty-six provinces, and he appointed governors over each province as his deputies, so that he could accomplish what is related of him in this verse by His saying "﴿oppressing a group among them﴾," which occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "jaʿala" (made), and the clause "﴿slaughtering their sons and sparing their women﴾" is substituted for it as a comprehensive substitution (badal al-ishtimal). This is because he did not do that to them except

[Page 68]

because he regarded them as weak, that is, as humiliated. So he subjected them to torment and made them work at brick-making and hard labour. The oppressed group is the Children of Israel, and the pronoun in "minhum" refers to the people of the land, not to "shiyaʿan." The matter of the slaughter of the sons of the Children of Israel was discussed earlier in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾ is a causal explanation for the clause ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾. You have already learned, in the discussion of His saying ﴿He said, I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67] in al-Baqarah, that describing a matter with this form (predicate with kana) indicates the firm establishment of the attribute more than if it had been said "an akuna jahilan" (that I be ignorant). Likewise, His saying "﴿Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾" indicates the intense firm establishment of corruption in his character. Also, the verb "kana" (was) conveys the firm establishment of the predicate in its subject.

Thus there is confirmation of the meaning of corruption being firmly established in Pharaoh. His action here comprised great corruptions.

The first corruption: arrogance and tyranny, for it is a great psychological corruption from which numerous corruptions arise: contempt for people, disregard of their rights, bad treatment of them, spreading enmity among them, and a bad opinion of them; and not regarding in them any grounds for favour except what satisfies his desire and anger. When it is added to this that he is their ruler and shepherd, the trait of arrogance entails poor care for them, boldness in violating their rights, and looking at them with eyes of contempt, so that he does not concern himself with bringing them benefit or repelling harm from them; and he seizes their interests for himself, makes use of whoever he can among them for the service of his purposes, and does not show gentleness to them in governance, but treats them with harshness, which spreads terror in their souls of his violence and tyranny. This trait is the mother of corruptions and their sum, and for this reason it is placed first before what is mentioned after it, and then it is followed by the statement that he was among the corrupters.

The second corruption: he made the people of the kingdom into factions and divided them into categories, making some of them close to him, and it is understood from this that he made some of them the opposite of that. This is corruption within the community, for it stirs up envy and hatred between them, and causes some of them to watch for the misfortunes of others. Thus the favoured factions in his sight become arrogant toward the other factions, and the other factions strive to dislodge the favoured from their favour by casting slander and false accusations, so that they may take the place of the others. Thus time passes in plots of some against others, in strife,

[Page 69]

whereas it is the way of the righteous king to make all his subjects of one rank, like children to a father, loving good for them and correcting them with justice and gentleness, with no preference for one faction over another; and the nearness of the members of the community to him should be in proportion to their psychological and intellectual merits.

The third corruption: he humiliates a group among the people of his kingdom, making them despised and oppressed, with no equality between them and other factions, and no justice in treating them as he treats the other factions, although they have the same right in the land as others, because the land belongs to its people, its inhabitants who settled in it and grew up in it.

The group referred to is the Children of Israel, who had settled in the land of Egypt with the consent of its king in the time of Joseph; they were given the land of (Jasan) (Goshen), cultivated it, multiplied in it, and four hundred years passed over them there. So they had the same right in the land of the kingdom as all its other inhabitants, and it was not just to place them in a status below the status of others. The Exalted's words ﴿a group among them﴾ point to this meaning, for He made them part of the people of the land whom Pharaoh had made into factions.

By His words "a group," He indicated that he oppressed a complete community, which conveys that the oppression did not apply to particular individuals for reasons that would justify their oppression, such as their being agents of corruption, or not being deserving of consideration because of the baseness of their morals and deeds. Rather, his oppression proceeded on the basis of racial and tribal distinction, and this is corruption, for it places the superior on a par with the inferior.

On account of that racial oppression, he applied its severity to the individuals of that group without distinguishing between the deserving and others, and he did not observe the distinction of sex, male or female. This is the fourth corruption: that he slaughters their sons, that is, orders their slaughter. The attribution of the slaughter to him is a metaphor of attribution (majaz ʿaqli). The sons here means the male children. This was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. His purpose in this was that the Children of Israel should not have strength through the men of their tribe, so that authority in the land would belong only to his own people.

The fifth corruption: he spares the women, that is, he preserves the lives of the female children. He called them "women" by consideration of their future state, alluding to the fact that he spares them so that they become women, fit for what women are fit for, namely that they become prostitutes, since they have no husbands. And since their humiliation was by barring his people from marrying them, there remained for them no share of the men of the people except the satisfaction of lust. On account of this purpose, sparing them turned into a corruption, on the same level as the slaughter of the sons, since all of that is transgression against right. The position of the clause "﴿Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾" has already been discussed above.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verses 5–6:

﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land, and to make them leaders and make them the inheritors,﴾ ﴿and to establish them in the land, and to show Pharaoh and Haman and their armies from them that which they had feared.﴾

He conjoined the clause "wa-nuridu" (and We wish) to the clause ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4], because of the connection between what that clause contains, the account of the slaughter of the sons and the sparing of the women. That exaltation of Pharaoh in the land is part of the account, and it explains the story of Moses and Pharaoh. God's will for good toward those whom Pharaoh had subjugated is part of the complete account of Moses and Pharaoh, and it is a place of great lesson among the lessons of this story.

The present tense was used for describing a will that had already occurred, in order to bring that time to mind as though it were present, because the meaning is that Pharaoh was tyrannising over them while God, at that time, wished to nullify his work and to make them a great nation. For this reason the clause "wa-nuridu" may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the pronoun in "yastad'ifu" (he subjugates), on the basis that this will was concurrent with the time of Pharaoh's subjugation of them. So the meaning under both possibilities is: "And We, at that time, are willing to bestow favour, at a future time, upon those who were oppressed."

Al-mann (the bestowing of favour) means al-in'am (bounty). Its present form came with the ʿayn vowelled with a ḍamma, contrary to analogy (al-qiyas): "yamunnu".

﴿Those who were oppressed in the land﴾ are the group whom Pharaoh subjugated. "The land" is the same land as in His words ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4].

The reason for stating ﴿those who were oppressed﴾ explicitly, rather than using a pronoun for the group, is to draw attention to the reason contained in the relative clause: God is merciful to His servants, and He helps the oppressed, the wronged, who cannot devise a plan and do not find a way.

He singled out four things from the favour, conjoined to the verb "namunnu" by the conjunction of the specific to the general. They are: making them leaders (a'immah), making them the inheritors, establishing them in the land, and that the removal of Pharaoh's dominion should be at their hands, among other numerous blessings, many of which are mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

As for making them leaders, it means that He brought them out of the humiliation of slavery and made them a free nation, possessing its own affairs, having a just law and a code for its dealings, a power by which it repels its enemies, a sovereign realm exclusively its own, and a complete civilisation surpassing the civilisation of its neighbours, to the extent that it becomes a model for the nations in matters of perfection and the pursuit of well-being. This is the meaning of "making them leaders", that others follow them and they call people to good. Consider what the king of Israel attained in the time of Solomon, peace be upon him.

As for making them the inheritors, it means that God gives them the dwellings of other peoples and makes them rulers over them. Thus "inheritance" is used figuratively for succession to other nations.

The definite article in "al-warithin" (the inheritors) is the definite article of genus, indicating that they are the people of the special inheritance, which is the inheritance of authority in the land after those who were before them of the people of power. God caused them to inherit the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites and the Aramaeans, and settled them in their place, in the greatness they had possessed, to the point that they were known as the giants (al-jabbarun). He, exalted is He, said ﴿They said: O Moses, indeed in it there is a people of giants﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22].

"Establishing them in the land" means consolidating their authority over what they possessed of it, which is the land of al-Sham, if the lam is a substitute for the genitive pronoun that was omitted. It is possible that the meaning is strengthening them among the nations of the earth, if the definite article is taken as the genus of land restricted to a single instance, or as the definite of previous reference, that is, the land known to people.

The original sense of "tamkin" is "placing in a place". It was discussed earlier at His words ﴿Indeed We established him in the land﴾ [al-Kahf: 84] in Surat al-Kahf, and the discussion of the derivation of "tamkin" and its inflections was given earlier at His words ﴿We had established them in the land as We had not established you﴾ [al-An'am: 6] in Surat al-An'am.

﴿That which they had feared﴾ is the loss of their dominion through a man from the Children of Israel, as the soothsayers (al-kuhhan) had warned them of that.

[Page 72]

The meaning of showing them that is showing them its preliminaries and its causes.

The Pharaoh who was shown that is the king of Egypt, Merneptah (Mintahat) the Third, who ruled Egypt after Ramesses (Ra'masis) the Second, in whose time Moses was born, and who was the one who feared the emergence of a man from Israel who would have a great station. As for Haman, the commentators said he was Pharaoh's vizier. The apparent meaning of the verses of this surah requires that he was Pharaoh's vizier. I suppose that Haman is not a proper name, but a title of office, like Pharaoh, Kisra, Caesar, and Negus. The apparent meaning is that Haman was the title of the king's vizier in Egypt in that age. In the Book of Esther, one of the Jewish books appended to the Torah, the vizier of Ahasuerus (Ahshu-yarush), king of the Persians, is called Haman, so they took it as a proper name and claimed that there was no vizier of Pharaoh named Haman, and they took this assumption as a basis for attacking this verse. This is a confusion on their part, for proper names are not limited, and titles of offices may also be shared among nations, especially neighbouring nations. It is possible that Haman was a proper name of a man from Egypt, since proper names recur among nations and ages. It is also possible that it was a title of office in Egypt, and the Jews transferred this title to the land of the Persians during the period of their captivity.

Similar to this objection is the objection of some contemporary Orientalists, Christians, to His words, concerning Mary, when He related the words of her family to her: ﴿O sister of Aaron﴾ [Maryam: 28]. They said: this is an error arising from the fact that the father of Mary was named Imran, so it was assumed that Imran was the father of Moses, the Messenger, peace be upon him, and following that assumption came the assumption that Mary was the sister of Moses and Aaron. This is a baseless claim, for the Christians do not know the name of Mary's father. Is it impossible that he was named after the father of Moses and Aaron? Is it impossible that Mary had a brother named Aaron? We have discussed this in Surat Maryam.

"Al-junud" is the plural of "al-jund". The word "jund" is also applied to a nation, as He said ﴿Has there come to you the story of the hosts﴾ [al-Buruj: 17] ﴿of Pharaoh and Thamud﴾ [al-Buruj: 18].

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-nuriya" with the nun of majesty and the verb in the accusative, and Pharaoh and what is conjoined to him in the accusative. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "wa-yara" with the third-person ya' vowelled with a fatha and the ra' vowelled with a fatha, as the present tense of ra'a, and "Fir'awnu" and what is conjoined to it in the nominative. The ultimate meaning of the two readings is one.

[Page 73]

"Al-jund" is a collective noun with no singular from its own form. It is a group of people who gather around a matter they follow. For this reason it is applied to an army, since their work is one, namely serving their commander and obeying him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verses 5–6:

﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land, and to make them leaders and make them the inheritors,﴾ ﴿and to establish them in the land, and to show Pharaoh and Haman and their armies from them that which they had feared.﴾

He conjoined the clause "wa-nuridu" (and We wish) to the clause ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4], because of the connection between what that clause contains, the account of the slaughter of the sons and the sparing of the women. That exaltation of Pharaoh in the land is part of the account, and it explains the story of Moses and Pharaoh. God's will for good toward those whom Pharaoh had subjugated is part of the complete account of Moses and Pharaoh, and it is a place of great lesson among the lessons of this story.

The present tense was used for describing a will that had already occurred, in order to bring that time to mind as though it were present, because the meaning is that Pharaoh was tyrannising over them while God, at that time, wished to nullify his work and to make them a great nation. For this reason the clause "wa-nuridu" may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the pronoun in "yastad'ifu" (he subjugates), on the basis that this will was concurrent with the time of Pharaoh's subjugation of them. So the meaning under both possibilities is: "And We, at that time, are willing to bestow favour, at a future time, upon those who were oppressed."

Al-mann (the bestowing of favour) means al-in'am (bounty). Its present form came with the ʿayn vowelled with a ḍamma, contrary to analogy (al-qiyas): "yamunnu".

﴿Those who were oppressed in the land﴾ are the group whom Pharaoh subjugated. "The land" is the same land as in His words ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4].

The reason for stating ﴿those who were oppressed﴾ explicitly, rather than using a pronoun for the group, is to draw attention to the reason contained in the relative clause: God is merciful to His servants, and He helps the oppressed, the wronged, who cannot devise a plan and do not find a way.

He singled out four things from the favour, conjoined to the verb "namunnu" by the conjunction of the specific to the general. They are: making them leaders (a'immah), making them the inheritors, establishing them in the land, and that the removal of Pharaoh's dominion should be at their hands, among other numerous blessings, many of which are mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

As for making them leaders, it means that He brought them out of the humiliation of slavery and made them a free nation, possessing its own affairs, having a just law and a code for its dealings, a power by which it repels its enemies, a sovereign realm exclusively its own, and a complete civilisation surpassing the civilisation of its neighbours, to the extent that it becomes a model for the nations in matters of perfection and the pursuit of well-being. This is the meaning of "making them leaders", that others follow them and they call people to good. Consider what the king of Israel attained in the time of Solomon, peace be upon him.

As for making them the inheritors, it means that God gives them the dwellings of other peoples and makes them rulers over them. Thus "inheritance" is used figuratively for succession to other nations.

The definite article in "al-warithin" (the inheritors) is the definite article of genus, indicating that they are the people of the special inheritance, which is the inheritance of authority in the land after those who were before them of the people of power. God caused them to inherit the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites and the Aramaeans, and settled them in their place, in the greatness they had possessed, to the point that they were known as the giants (al-jabbarun). He, exalted is He, said ﴿They said: O Moses, indeed in it there is a people of giants﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22].

"Establishing them in the land" means consolidating their authority over what they possessed of it, which is the land of al-Sham, if the lam is a substitute for the genitive pronoun that was omitted. It is possible that the meaning is strengthening them among the nations of the earth, if the definite article is taken as the genus of land restricted to a single instance, or as the definite of previous reference, that is, the land known to people.

The original sense of "tamkin" is "placing in a place". It was discussed earlier at His words ﴿Indeed We established him in the land﴾ [al-Kahf: 84] in Surat al-Kahf, and the discussion of the derivation of "tamkin" and its inflections was given earlier at His words ﴿We had established them in the land as We had not established you﴾ [al-An'am: 6] in Surat al-An'am.

﴿That which they had feared﴾ is the loss of their dominion through a man from the Children of Israel, as the soothsayers (al-kuhhan) had warned them of that.

[Page 72]

The meaning of showing them that is showing them its preliminaries and its causes.

The Pharaoh who was shown that is the king of Egypt, Merneptah (Mintahat) the Third, who ruled Egypt after Ramesses (Ra'masis) the Second, in whose time Moses was born, and who was the one who feared the emergence of a man from Israel who would have a great station. As for Haman, the commentators said he was Pharaoh's vizier. The apparent meaning of the verses of this surah requires that he was Pharaoh's vizier. I suppose that Haman is not a proper name, but a title of office, like Pharaoh, Kisra, Caesar, and Negus. The apparent meaning is that Haman was the title of the king's vizier in Egypt in that age. In the Book of Esther, one of the Jewish books appended to the Torah, the vizier of Ahasuerus (Ahshu-yarush), king of the Persians, is called Haman, so they took it as a proper name and claimed that there was no vizier of Pharaoh named Haman, and they took this assumption as a basis for attacking this verse. This is a confusion on their part, for proper names are not limited, and titles of offices may also be shared among nations, especially neighbouring nations. It is possible that Haman was a proper name of a man from Egypt, since proper names recur among nations and ages. It is also possible that it was a title of office in Egypt, and the Jews transferred this title to the land of the Persians during the period of their captivity.

Similar to this objection is the objection of some contemporary Orientalists, Christians, to His words, concerning Mary, when He related the words of her family to her: ﴿O sister of Aaron﴾ [Maryam: 28]. They said: this is an error arising from the fact that the father of Mary was named Imran, so it was assumed that Imran was the father of Moses, the Messenger, peace be upon him, and following that assumption came the assumption that Mary was the sister of Moses and Aaron. This is a baseless claim, for the Christians do not know the name of Mary's father. Is it impossible that he was named after the father of Moses and Aaron? Is it impossible that Mary had a brother named Aaron? We have discussed this in Surat Maryam.

"Al-junud" is the plural of "al-jund". The word "jund" is also applied to a nation, as He said ﴿Has there come to you the story of the hosts﴾ [al-Buruj: 17] ﴿of Pharaoh and Thamud﴾ [al-Buruj: 18].

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-nuriya" with the nun of majesty and the verb in the accusative, and Pharaoh and what is conjoined to him in the accusative. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "wa-yara" with the third-person ya' vowelled with a fatha and the ra' vowelled with a fatha, as the present tense of ra'a, and "Fir'awnu" and what is conjoined to it in the nominative. The ultimate meaning of the two readings is one.

[Page 73]

"Al-jund" is a collective noun with no singular from its own form. It is a group of people who gather around a matter they follow. For this reason it is applied to an army, since their work is one, namely serving their commander and obeying him.

The following is the translation of the passage from Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 28, verse 7:

﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: "Suckle him; but when you fear for him, cast him into the river. Do not fear and do not grieve. We will surely return him to you and make him one of the messengers."﴾ This is coordinated with the clause ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed﴾ [al-Qasas: 5], since all of it is part of the account (naba'). This verse elaborates on the general statement ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed﴾ [al-Qasas: 5]: when the divine will was directed at rescuing the Children of Israel from humiliation, God created the one who would rescue them.

The revelation (wahy) here is revelation by inspiration (wahy ilham), which brings to her such expansion of the breast (inshirah al-sadr) that she becomes certain it is a thought from divine inspirations. True inspiration (ilham) comes to the righteous and places in their souls a certainty by which they are moved to act on what they have been inspired to do. This revelation may also have come through a true dream that she saw. The name of the mother of Moses is not known in the books of the Jews, and the exegetes mentioned names for her that are not reliably authenticated.

His saying ﴿Suckle him﴾ explains "We revealed." The command to suckle him implies omitted steps: when God willed this, He decreed that the means by which His will would be manifested would be the infant in the womb of the mother of Moses. She gave birth to him, feared for him the aggression of Pharaoh's partisans against her child, was perplexed about her situation, and so was inspired, or shown, what God related here and in other places.

The suckling she was commanded to do includes this: keep him hidden for a period during which you nurse him; then, when you fear that his news will become known, cast him into the river.

God commanded her to nurse him so that his body would be strengthened by his mother's milk, for a child is better nourished in the first part of his life by his mother's milk than by that of another woman. Also, so that from the last suckling before she cast him into the river he would have sustenance that would strengthen his body during the interval between his being cast into the river and the family of Pharaoh picking him up and bringing him to Pharaoh's house, and during the search for wet-nurses, and the sister's guiding them to his mother, until he was brought to be nursed and was returned to her after having been separated from her for part of a day.

The Jewish books report that the mother of Moses hid him for three months, then feared that his matter would spread, so she placed him in a waterproofed basket (safat muqayyar) and cast him into the river. God had given her good news that would remove her anxiety, by telling her that He would return him to her, and He added to this good news of the high station that would be his in this world and the Hereafter, by telling her that he would be one of the messengers.

It is apparent that this revelation to her was at the time of his birth, and that she was commanded to cast him into the river only in case of necessity, to avert a certain harm by a doubtful harm. Then it was cast into her certainty that there was no harm to him.

Al-yamm (the river/sea) means the sea, and here it is the Nile, which flowed through the city of Pharaoh where the Children of Israel lived. In Arabic usage, yamm is a synonym of bahr (sea), and bahr in their speech applies to any great expanse of water; a great river is called a bahr. God says ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, palatable, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty and bitter﴾ [Fatir: 12], and the yamm is among the rivers.

This verse has been an example of the subtle aspects of the inimitability of the Qur'an (i'jaz al-Qur'an). 'Iyad, in al-Shifa, and al-Qurtubi, in his Tafsir, with one of them adding to what the other says, report from al-Asma'i that he heard a Bedouin slave-girl reciting:

I seek God's forgiveness for all my affairs, for I have killed a man unlawfully,
Like a gazelle, soft in its tenderness... The night has passed midway and I have not prayed.

She intended by this a double meaning (tawriyah) with the Qur'an. He said to her: "May God fight you, how eloquent you are!" meaning how rhetorically effective (baligh) you are, for they used to call eloquence fasahah. She said to him: "Is this considered eloquence alongside His saying, ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: 'Suckle him; but when you fear for him, cast him into the river. Do not fear and do not grieve. We will surely return him to you and make him one of the messengers'﴾? He has combined in one verse two reports, two commands, two prohibitions, and two glad tidings."

[p. 75]

The two reports are ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses﴾ and His saying ﴿but when you fear for him﴾, because it indicates that she will be afraid for him.

The two commands are: "Suckle him" and "Cast him."

The two prohibitions are: "Do not fear" and "Do not grieve."

The two glad tidings are ﴿We will surely return him to you and make him one of the messengers﴾.

Fear (khawf) is the anticipation of something disliked. Grief (huzn) is a state of the soul that arises from an event disliked by the soul, such as the loss of something loved, or the loss of a beloved, or distance from him, or the like.

The meaning is: do not fear for him destruction from being cast into the river, and do not grieve over his separation from you.

The prohibition against fear and against grief is a prohibition against their causes, which are the anticipation of harm and the reflection on the loneliness of separation.

The clause ﴿We will surely return him to you﴾ stands in the position of a reason (illah) for the two prohibitions, because the guarantee of his return to her requires that he will not perish, and that she will not long for him through a long absence. As for His saying ﴿and make him one of the messengers﴾, it is the introduction of joy for her.

The family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he would become for them an enemy and a grief. Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners.

Iltiqat (picking up) is an iftial form derived from luqt, which means taking hold of something lying on the ground or the like, either deliberately or inadvertently. The picking up is attributed to the family of Pharaoh because the extraction of Moses' chest from the river was done by one of the women surrounding Pharaoh's daughter, when she was with her companions and nurses on the bank of the Nile, as is mentioned in the second chapter of the Book of Exodus.

The lam in ﴿لِيَكُونَ لَهم عَدُوًّا﴾ is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), known among grammarians as lam kay ("the lam of kay"). It is a preposition like "kay" ("in order that"), and it is connected to "iltaqatahu." The proper function of lam kay is to govern a verbal noun formed from an implied "an" placed after the lam together with the verb it governs, and that verbal noun is the motive that prompts the agent to perform the action. In this verse, the particle is used in a manner that follows the figure of speech of metaphor (isti'ara) rather than its literal sense, since it is evident that their motive for picking him up was not that he would become an enemy and a grief to them. Rather, they picked him up out of compassion for him and love for him, because of the pity that was placed in their hearts toward him. However, since the outcome of their picking him up was that he became an enemy to them, and a cause of grief for them, the outcome was likened to the motive in being the result of the action, just as a motive is. This is a subsidiary metaphor (isti'ara taba'iyya), meaning that the meaning of the particle is borrowed for another meaning, and the particle is then borrowed as a consequence of borrowing its meaning, which then extends from the meaning to the particle. For this reason it is called a subsidiary metaphor according to the majority of scholars of rhetoric (ulama' al-ma'ani), in disagreement with al-Sakkaki.

The pronoun in ﴿لَهم﴾ refers to the family of Pharaoh in terms of the generic description, because Moses was going to become an enemy to a different Pharaoh after this one. That is, he would become an enemy and a grief to their dynasty and their nation, since Moses' mission took place during the reign of this Pharaoh's son.

Describing him as "a grief" (ḥazanan), which is a verbal noun, is with an implied complement, meaning "a grief to them," indicated by the earlier phrase ﴿لَهُمُ﴾. This is not a case of describing with a verbal noun for emphasis, like your saying "So-and-so is justice," because in that usage the verbal noun stands in the place of the active participle, and the meaning of the verbal noun subsists in the described subject. The meaning here is "that he might become a grief to them." The attribution is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because he is the cause of grief and is not grief itself.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿وحَزَنًا﴾ with a fatha on the ḥa' and the zay. Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a ḍamma on the ḥa' and a sukun on the zay, and both are dialectal forms, like ʿadam and ʿudm.

The clause ﴿إنَّ فِرْعَوْنَ وهامانَ﴾ to its end is in the position of a causal justification for the clause ﴿لِيَكُونَ لَهم عَدُوًّا وحَزَنًا﴾. That is, God decreed the rescue of Moses so that he would become an enemy and a grief to them, because they were criminals. God made that a punishment for them for their oppression of the Children of Israel and for their worship of idols.

Al-khati' is an active participle from khati'a, on the pattern of fariḥa, when one commits a khati'a (sin), which is a crime or wrongdoing. God the Exalted said ﴿ناصِيَةٍ كاذِبَةٍ خاطِئَةٍ﴾ ["a lying, sinning forelock"] (al-'Alaq: 16). Its verbal noun is al-khit' with a kasra on the kha' and a sukun on the ta'. This was discussed earlier in God's words ﴿إنَّ قَتْلَهم كانَ خِطْئًا كَبِيرًا﴾ ["Indeed, killing them is a great sin"] (al-Isra': 31) in Surat al-Isra'. As for khata' (error), which is the opposite of intention, its verb is akhta'a, and its active participle is mukhti', as God the Exalted said ﴿لَيْسَ عَلَيْكم جُناحٌ فِيما أخْطَأْتُمْ بِهِ ولَكِنْ ما تَعَمَّدَتْ قُلُوبُكُمْ﴾ ["There is no blame upon you for what you did in error, but [what matters is] what your hearts intended"] (al-Ahzab: 5). Accordingly, it is necessary that the eloquent speakers distinguished usage between the perpetrator of a sin (khati'a) and the perpetrator of an error (khata'). Naftawayh followed this distinction between akhta'a and khati'a, and al-Jawhari and al-Hariri followed him.

Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn Qutayba held that the two terms are synonyms and are two dialects. The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words here is that he follows the view of Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn Qutayba, for he interpreted this verse with both meanings. In al-Asas he said that akhta'a means to err in judgment, and khati'a means to deliberately commit a sin. It has also been said that they are one and the same.

It appears that their root is two dialectal forms with the meaning of departing from what is right, whether unintentionally or intentionally. Then the eloquent usage became established in specifying akhta'a for an act done unintentionally, and khati'a for committing a crime or sin. This is what the usage of the language has settled upon. Indeed, the distinctions between words are among the finest refinements of the language.

As for the meaning of the verse here, it cannot be fitting unless khati'in is from al-khati'a (sin), so that the statement serves as a justification for the causation of their grief over him, by the mention of their wrongdoing. Mention of Haman has already preceded a moment ago.

[Page 76]
[Page 77]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 9:

﴿Pharaoh's wife said: "A delight of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him. Perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son," while they did not perceive.﴾ The words indicate that those who pulled him out placed him before Pharaoh and his wife. Pharaoh's wife felt compassion for him and turned Pharaoh away from killing him, after he had intended to do so. This is because he (Pharaoh) knew that the child was not one of the Copts' sons, by the color of his skin and the features of his face. He also knew that the Nile had not carried him from a distant place, as is evident from the fact that his chest-box (tabut) had not stayed long in the water, nor had it been tossed about much by frequent movement. So he knew that the placing of the child in the chest was intended to save him from slaughter. This was at the time he was lifted out of the water and taken out of the chest. Pharaoh's wife was a woman inspired toward goodness, and God decreed Musa's rescue through her. God, the Exalted, has said about her: ﴿And God presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, "My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people."﴾ (Surah al-Tahrim: 11).

[p. 78]

She had not seen Musa's enmity toward the family of Pharaoh, nor had she grieved because of him, since she passed away before the mission of Musa.

Pharaoh's wife was named Asiya, as in the hadith related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Many men have reached perfection, but among women none has reached perfection except Maryam the daughter of 'Imran and Asiya the wife of Pharaoh." Her words indicate that when Pharaoh saw him he admired him, then fear of the consequences of his affair overcame him. Therefore his wife warned him with her words, ﴿A delight of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him.﴾

﴿Qurrat 'ayn﴾ is in the nominative because it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), whose estimated form is: "This child." It was omitted because his presence before them indicates it. It is also an elliptical construction with an omitted noun, meaning: he is the cause of a delight of the eye for me and for you.

"Qurrat al-'ayn" is a metaphor by implication (kinaya) for joy, and it is a kinaya arising from its opposite, which is the heat of the eye, the effect of weeping that results from sorrow and grief. Thus the Arabs used heat of the eye as a figure for grief, as in their supplication against someone: "May God heat his eye." And as in the words of the rajiz (poet):

"Alas! May He tan the hide of his honor, and heat his eye after the sleep of eyes."

Then they followed that by using the opposite of this figure to express joy, saying: "Qurrat 'ayn" and "May God cool his eye." So the Qur'an conveyed what is in the speech of Pharaoh's wife, namely the indication of the meaning of delight felt in the soul, by means of the most eloquent expression the Arabs used for this, which is ﴿qurrat 'ayn﴾. One of its subtleties in the verse is that the delight intended is the delight that comes from seeing the beauty of the child, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha: 39).

It is also permissible that her saying ﴿qurrat 'ayn﴾ is an oath, as one says "Aymun Allah" (By God's right). The Arabs swear by this, meaning: "I swear by that by which my eye is cooled." In the authentic hadith, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq hosted a group of men and was late for their evening meal. In it there is an account, until the narrator said: they did not eat a morsel except that it swelled from beneath it, more than it had been. Abu Bakr said to his wife: "O sister of Banu Firas, what is this?" She said: "By the coolness of my eye, it is now more than before." So Pharaoh's wife would have sworn to Pharaoh by that which is the delight of her eye, and the delight of his eye is that he not kill Musa. The nominative of ﴿qurrat 'ayn﴾ would then be the subject (mubtada') with an omitted predicate, and omission of the predicate is common in the wording of an oath, like "la 'amruka" (by your life).

She began with herself in ﴿A delight of the eye for me﴾ before mentioning Pharaoh, as a display of her favor with him because of her status with him. She wished to forestall him with this, so that no command to kill the child would come from him.

The plural pronoun in her saying ﴿Do not kill him﴾ may refer to Pharaoh alone, placing him in the position of a group out of respect, as in His saying: ﴿He said: "My Lord, send me back"﴾ (Surah al-Mu'minun: 99). It may also refer to addressing Pharaoh while including within it the people of his state: Haman and the soothsayers who had cast into Pharaoh's mind that a youth from the Children of Israel would corrupt his kingdom. This is the better view, because it paves the way for granting her request, when she attributed most of the killing to the people of the state and made for Pharaoh a share of it equal to one of the group. It is as though she hinted that this should not be by his opinion, and so she made light for him his deviation regarding this child from what had been established of killing the children. It has been said that ﴿Do not kill him﴾ is an iltifat (shift in address) from addressing Pharaoh to addressing those entrusted with killing the children of the Children of Israel, like His saying: ﴿Joseph, turn away from this, and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ (Surah Yusuf: 29).

The clause ﴿A delight of the eye for me and for you﴾ is positioned as a preface (tamhid) and introduction to the proposal. The clause ﴿Do not kill him﴾ is positioned as a consequence derived from the introduction, and for this reason it is separated from it.

As for the clause ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾, it is positioned as the reason (illa) for the content of the clause ﴿Do not kill him﴾, and its connection to it is like the connection of the clause ﴿A delight of the eye for me and for you﴾ to it. However, the composition of the speech required this eloquent order, by making the natural restraint from killing, which is the restraint of love, the preface, because it is more firmly attached to the soul, and so it resembles self-evident knowledge. The rational restraint was placed after the prohibition as a reason, because it needs reflection. Thus there is a pause for thought after hearing the prohibition, prepared for by the natural restraint, so that the listener's recoil from the prohibition and his rejection of it is not feared.

Her saying ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ includes the removal of what had crept into Pharaoh's soul of fear that his kingdom would be corrupted at the hand of an Israelite youth, by indicating that this child would not be the one feared from him. For when he was joined to their household and would be raised among them, it is hoped that he would benefit them and be to them like a son. She persuaded Pharaoh by an analogy with tested circumstances in the relationship of upbringing, companionship, adoption and kindness, and that good does not come from evil. Therefore after it came the interjected clause, God's words ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ (Surah al-Qasas: 11), meaning: Pharaoh and his people did not know the hidden will of God regarding the vengeance upon the Coptic nation through Musa.

[p. 80]

Perhaps God made true for Pharaoh's wife her hope, so that Musa became a delight of the eye for her and her husband. When they both died and another Pharaoh came after them, what God had decreed of the victory of the Children of Israel came to pass.

The word "yash'uruna" (they perceive) was chosen here because it belongs to hidden knowledge, meaning: they do not know this hidden matter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 10:

﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became empty; she was about to disclose him, had We not fortified her heart so that she would be among the believers.﴾ "Asbaha" (أصْبَحَ) is used in the sense of "ṣāra" (became), so it implies a transition from one state to another, i.e., her heart had not been empty, and then it became empty.

"Al-fu'ād" (الفُؤادُ) is used in the sense of intellect and mind.

"Al-faraγ" (الفَراغُ) is figurative. The emptiness of the mind from a matter means, metaphorically, that the mind does not contain that matter in a figurative sense, i.e., the meaning of that matter does not circulate in the mind, meaning the abandonment of thinking about it.

Since it is not stated why the heart of Moses' mother became empty, the verse admits of meanings that return to the possibilities of what the object of emptiness is. Therefore the exegetes differed about this in earlier times, and their statements return to two directions: one direction indicates the steadfastness of Moses' mother and the firmness of her heart, and another direction indicates that weakness and doubt crept into her soul.

As for what returns to the first direction, it is that she was empty of fear and grief, so she became confident of its good outcome, following what was inspired to her, that she should not fear nor grieve, so it returns to praise of her. This is more fitting with His saying, may He be exalted, afterwards ﴿had We not fortified her heart so that she would be among the believers﴾, because that fortification is among the consequences of what Allah inspired to her, that she should not fear nor grieve.

So the meaning: when she cast him into the river as Allah had inspired her, what she had feared for him, of his being discovered by her and being killed, departed from her; for when she was able to cast him into the river and no one noticed him, she knew that he had been saved. This interpretation is also supported by the common saying: "So-and-so is khaliyy al-bāl" (free of mind), when there is no concern in his heart. This is the explanation of Abu 'Ubayda, al-Akhfash, and al-Kisa'i, and this is the best that it has been explained by, and it is from the meaning of praise of her for her steadfastness. And from Ibn 'Abbas through various chains, he said: "Empty of everything except the remembrance of Moses." In this there is something of the firmness of her heart, since her mind became empty of every thought that occurs concerning the affair of Moses.

As for the addition conveyed by the exception in his saying "except the remembrance of Moses," perhaps he derived it from the verse ﴿she was about to disclose him, had We not fortified her heart﴾; otherwise there is nothing in the verse indicating that exception.

This explanation requires combining praise of her for the good quality of her trust in Allah with an indication of the weakness of motherhood through longing for her child, even though she knew that he would move among good conditions, with him and with her.

As for the statements returning to the second direction, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi, citing Ibn al-Qasim from Malik, said: "The emptiness is the departure of the intellect." Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is like His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and their hearts are void (hawā')﴾ [Ibrahim: 43], i.e., there is no intellect in them. In al-Kashshaf: i.e., when she heard of his falling into the hand of Pharaoh, her intellect flew away because of what overwhelmed her of excessive anguish. Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, and Ibn Ishaq said: she became empty of remembering the promise that Allah had made to her, when a satanic thought crept into her, and she said to herself: "I feared for him from being killed, so I cast him with my own hand into the hand of the enemy who ordered his killing." Ibn 'Atiyya said: a group said: empty of patience. Perhaps he means empty of patience over his loss. All the statements returning to this direction aim at the point that Moses' mother was not steadfast in carrying out what Allah, may He be exalted, had commanded her, and that Allah rectified her by placing certainty in her soul.

The clause ﴿she was about to disclose him, had We not fortified her heart﴾ is, according to the first interpretation, an explanatory resumption (isti'nāf bayānī) for what the verb "asbaha" implies, that she had been in a state other than emptiness, so it was explained that she was about to reveal the matter of her son out of intense agitation, for agitation betrays a person. The meaning: her heart became empty, and before that she had almost disclosed the news of Moses during the period of his nursing, out of intense panic and anxiety that he might be killed. According to the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, the clause ﴿she was about to﴾ stands in the position of an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān) to the meaning of "empty." It is also an indication of the omitted exception.

So the estimate: empty except from the remembrance of Moses, so she was about to reveal the remembrance of Moses and speak his name because of the frequency of his remembrance in her soul.

As for the statements returning to the second direction, the clause ﴿she was about to disclose him﴾ is an explanation of the clause "her heart became empty," i.e., she was about to reveal the matter of Moses because of the weakness of her heart's firmness.

From Mujahid: when she saw the waves carrying the chest, she was about to cry out.

The "bā'" in "bihi" is either to emphasize the attachment of the object to its verb, the original being "latubdīhi," or it is for the implicit inclusion of "tabūḥu" (to reveal) in "tubdī," and this is better. "In" (إنْ) is the lightened form of the heavy one. The "lām" in "latubdī" distinguishes the lightened "in" from the negating "in."

"Al-rabṭ 'alā al-qalb" (binding upon the heart) is its strengthening against weakening, as a weak limb is bound, i.e., We bound her heart by creating patience in it. The answer to "lawlā" is the clause ﴿she was about to disclose him﴾.

What is meant by "the believers" is those who affirm Allah's promise, i.e., had We not reminded her, We would not have given her the promise, and her heart would not have been at rest. Thus "faith" here is used in its linguistic meaning, not its legal one, because she was among the believers before; or it is intended as the perfect among the believers.

The "lām" is for causation, i.e., so that she would attain the rank of the believers by Allah's command, who are not afflicted by doubt regarding what comes to them of divine occurrences.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 11:

﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him up," so she watched him from afar while they did not perceive.﴾ The apparent order of the reports is that they follow the order of their contents in occurrence, and this favors that the occurrence of the content of ﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became empty﴾ [al-Qasas: 10] preceded the occurrence of the content of ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him up"﴾. That is, she said to his sister that after her heart had been reassured by what had been inspired to her about casting him into the river; that is, when she cast him into the river she said to his sister: "Watch where the river will deposit him, and when will he be taken out from it?" She knew that the river would not deposit him far from her, because that is the requirement of God's promise to return him to her.

Page 83

The sister of Moses was named Maryam, and the story has already been mentioned in Surah Ta-Ha.

And al-qass (qaṣṣ) means following a trace; it has been used for tracking a person by sight, and therefore it is transitive to the pronoun of Moses without mentioning the trace. It has already been discussed in Surah al-Kahf at His saying ﴿So they both returned, retracing their footsteps﴾ [al-Kahf: 64].

And baṣura bi-l-shay' means he became one who has sight of it; that is, one who looks at it. It indicates the strength of seeing, that is, the strength of using the sense of sight, which is staring at the object seen; so "baṣura" is stronger than "abṣara". The bāʾ entering on its object is the bāʾ of causality, to indicate intense care in seeing the thing seen, until it is as if she became one who sees by means of it. You may also take the bāʾ as superfluous, for emphasizing the verb, and it then gives the meaning of increased exaggeration in the sense of the verb. It was discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "I perceived what they did not perceive"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 96] in Surah Ta-Ha.

And al-junub (junub), with two dammas, means "distant." It is an adjective of a noun understood from the context; that is, from a place that is distant.

And ʿan is for transition (al-mujāwaza), and the genitive phrase is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun of "baṣurat," because the transition here is from the states of his sister, not from the attributes of the place.

And "hum," that is, the family of Pharaoh, at the time they picked him up, do not perceive that his sister was observing his condition, and that is from the skill of his sister in how she observed him.

[Page 84]

The waw in "*wa-harramna*" is for circumstance (*wāw al-ḥāl*), referring back to the pronoun in "*li-ukhtihi*" (to his sister).

*Taḥrīm* (prohibition) means preventing. It is a *taḥrīm takwīnī* (a prohibition by creative decree), meaning that God decreed in the infant's own nature a refusal to take the breasts of wet-nurses and an aversion to them, so that the family of Pharaoh would be compelled to search for a wet-nurse whose breast he would accept. This is because Pharaoh and his wife were eager for the child's life. Among the preliminaries to this was that God caused him to be nursed by his mother for a period during which he became accustomed to her breast.

The meaning of "*min qablu*" (before that) is "before his being taken up," and it indicates that this prohibition was among the things that God's knowledge and will encompassed from eternity.

The *fa* in His words "*fa-qālat*" (so she said) is *fāʾ faṣīḥa* (the eloquent *fa*, a *fa* that signals an implied clause), meaning: so his sister revealed herself, as though she had passed by them without intent. She said this only after the seeking of wet-nurses for him had spread among the people, and after the replacing of one wet-nurse with another had become frequent, until he was presented to a large number in a short time. This was due to the speed of the family of Pharaoh's capacities and the intensity of their searching for wet-nurses, so that they found a large number in a short time. Also, the wet-nurses presented themselves to the family of Pharaoh once it became known that they were seeking a wet-nurse.

She offered her effort in this matter through the form of a question used for offering (*istifhām mustaʿmal fī al-ʿarḍ*), with gentleness toward the family of Pharaoh and to remove suspicion from herself.

The meaning of "*yakfulūnahu*" (they will undertake him) is that they will take on his protection and nursing. This indicates that their custom in nursing was that the infant be handed over to the woman who nurses him, so that he would stay with her, as was the custom of the Arabs, because free women did not agree to leave their homes and move to the homes of the families of nursing infants. This is as came in the report of the nursing of Muhammad (ﷺ) with Halimah bint Wahb in the clan of Banu Saʿd ibn Bakr. The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: So Pharaoh handed him over to her, and provided for her, and she took him to her house.

The shift from the verbal sentence to the nominal sentence in His words "*wa-hum lahu nāṣiḥūn*" (and they are sincere to him) is intended to stress that sincerity is among their qualities and something established for them. Therefore He did not say "*wa-yanṣaḥūna lahu*" (and they will advise him) as was said in "*yakfulūnahu lakum*", because undertaking the care is an easy matter, unlike sincerity and attentive concern.

Attaching "*lahu*" (to him) to "*nāṣiḥūn*" (sincere) is not for the sake of restriction; rather, it is because it narrates what is the case. The meaning is that sincerity is among their attributes, so it is present for him just as it is present for their like, according to their disposition. *Nuṣḥ* (sincerity) is pure work free from negligence and corruption.

[Page 85]

﴿So We returned him to his mother, that her eye might be comforted, and she would not grieve, and that she might know that the promise of God is true, but most of them do not know.﴾

The like of His saying ﴿So We returned him to his mother, that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve﴾ has already been discussed in Surah Ta-Ha. As for His saying, ﴿and that she might know that the promise of God is true,﴾ it is a reinforcement of the particle *kay* ("so that") by its synonym, the *lam al-ta'lil* (the causal *lam*, "in order that"), to make the meaning explicit at first glance, and it is coordinated with the affirmative verb, not with the negated verb.

The pronoun in ﴿but most of them do not know﴾ refers to the people understood from the context, or to the subjects of Pharaoh, and among the people are the Children of Israel.

The exception (*istidrak*) arises from establishing the evidence for her that the promise of God is true. That is, she alone knew this, while most of the people did not know it, because they were between polytheists and believers. The period since their faith had been long, and their peoples had been left without scholars to instruct them in the meanings of the religion, so their faith had become close to disbelief.

The point of lesson in this story is that it contains matters of great significance, in which there is a reminder for the believers and an admonition for the polytheists.

The first and greatest of these is the manifestation that what God has known and decreed is certainly going to happen, as indicated by His saying ﴿And We wished to show favor to those who were oppressed in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 5] up to His saying ﴿they were wary,﴾ and that caution does not save one from destiny.

The second: the manifestation that true exaltation belongs to God the Exalted and to the believers, and that the exaltation of Pharaoh did not avail him anything in averting the consequences of tyranny and corruption, so that this would be a lesson for the tyrants among the polytheists of Makkah.

The third: the introduction of the story with Pharaoh's haughtiness and the corruption of his deeds points to the fact that this was the cause of his being punished, and of taking up the cause of the oppressed, so that the tyrants might beware the evil end of their oppression, and so that those who patiently endure oppression might hope that the final outcome will be theirs.

The fourth: the indication of the wisdom in ﴿It may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216] regarding the Children of Israel, and ﴿It may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216] regarding Pharaoh, since they were rejoicing in enslaving the Children of Israel and in planning to cut off their offspring.

[Page 86]

The fifth: that the striking of Pharaoh's people suddenly, by the hand of those from whom they had hoped for benefit, is a greater lesson for the one who takes heed and a more painful regret for the one who sees clearly, and more indicative that God's vengeance is greater than the vengeance of an enemy, as He said ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], together with His saying ﴿It may be that he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [al-Qasas: 9].

The sixth: that by the judgment of reason it is not permissible to uproot an entire community because of an expected corrupter among them, due to the lack of proportion between the two harms, and because it is impossible to encompass all the individuals of a whole community. Therefore the expected corruption will only be in the overlooked part of the individuals, and two harms result: seizing the innocent and letting the guilty escape.

The seventh: the teaching that God accomplishes His command by preparing the causes that lead to it. Had God willed, He would have destroyed Pharaoh and those with him by a heavenly event, and would not have decreed for their destruction this ordered form, and He would have rescued Moses and the Children of Israel with a swifter rescue. But He willed that this occur through witnessing the changing conditions, beginning with the casting of Moses into the river until He returned him to his mother. So in this is a lesson for the polytheists who said ﴿O God, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and so that they might discern, from the flashes of the manifestation of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and the progression of the conditions of his call through the stages of strength, that what he promised them is going to come to pass in the end.

The eighth: the lesson that the presence of righteous people among corrupters lessens the harshness of the corruption of the corrupters. For the presence of Pharaoh's wife was a cause of restraining Pharaoh from killing the infant, even though it was certain that he was an Israelite. So his wife said, ﴿Do not kill him; it may be that he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [al-Qasas: 9], as we have previously explained its interpretation.

The ninth: what is in His saying ﴿and that she might know that the promise of God is true﴾ is an allusion reminding the believers that their victory is coming after a while, and a warning to the polytheists that there is no escape for them from their threat.

The tenth: what is in His saying ﴿but most of them do not know﴾ is an indication that a person is brought down by his ignorance from looking into the proofs of reason.

[Page 87]

Because of the lessons in this story, Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr was content with its opening instead of the sermon that he should have delivered to the people when he arrived in Iraq on behalf of his brother 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, being content with the allusion together with the recitation. He said: ﴿Ta, Sin, Mim﴾ [al-Qasas: 1], ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ [al-Qasas: 2], ﴿We recite to you from the news of Moses and Pharaoh in truth, for a people who believe﴾ [al-Qasas: 3], ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4], and he pointed toward the direction of Syria, meaning 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan. ﴿And made its people into factions, oppressing a group among them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive. Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾ [al-Qasas: 4]. ﴿And We wished to show favor to those who were oppressed in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 5], and he pointed with his hand toward the Hijaz, meaning his brother 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and his supporters. (﴿And to make them leaders and to make them the inheritors﴾ [al-Qasas: 5], ﴿and to establish them in the land and to show Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers﴾ [al-Qasas: 6]). And he pointed toward Iraq, meaning al-Hajjaj: ﴿from them that which they had feared﴾ [al-Qasas: 6].

This is a digression (*istitrad*) inserted between the parts of the story, which are arranged according to the order in which they occurred in reality. The digression arose from the phrase ﴿so that she may know that the promise of God is true﴾ (al-Qasas 28:13), since God's promise to her had already been related in His words ﴿We shall return him to you and make him one of the messengers﴾ (al-Qasas 28:7). When the narrative reached the account of his return to his mother, with His words ﴿So We returned him to his mother, that her eye might be comforted﴾ (28:13) and through to the end of that passage, it completed what was in it of the fulfilment of God's promise to her, through this digression in His words ﴿When he reached his maturity and became fully grown, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾. He was given judgment, meaning prophethood, only after he left the land of Madyan, as will come in His words ﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term and set out with his family﴾ (28:29).

A parallel to this verse occurred in Surah Yusuf, except for His words "and became fully grown" (*wa-istawa*). It was said that *istawa* here means *balagha ashuddahu* (he reached his *ashudd*), so it is an emphasis. The truth is that *al-ashudd* is the completeness of strength, because its origin is the plural of *shidda* with a kasra on the *shin*, on the pattern of *ni'ma* and *an'um*, and it is a form (*hay'a*) meaning strength, which was then treated as a singular. *Al-istiwa'* is the completeness of structure, as in His words about the crop ﴿then it grew thick and stood firm on its stalk﴾ (al-Fath 48:29). For this reason Musa is described with *istiwa'*, whereas Yusuf was described only with reaching *al-ashudd*, because Musa was a tall man, as in the hadith "as if he were one of the men of Shanu'a". So he had complete limbs, and for this reason his striking of the Copt (*al-qibti*) was decisive against the one who was struck (*al-mawkuz*).

*Al-hukm* is *al-hikma* (wisdom), and *al-ilm* is knowledge of God (*al-ma'rifa billah*).

[Page 88]

﴿He entered the city at a time of heedlessness among its people, and found in it two men fighting: one of his own party and the other of his enemy. The one of his party sought his help against the one of his enemy, so Musa struck him and killed him. He said, "This is from the work of Satan. Indeed, he is an enemy, a misleading, manifest one."﴾

Many reports, which this narrative alludes to, have been omitted. Musa grew up and matured in the palace of Pharaoh, so he was counted among the household of Pharaoh. It is also said that he was called "Musa, son of Pharaoh."

The clause ﴿He entered the city﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Musa: suckle him﴾ (28:7). The narrative is thus joined part to part. Musa knew that he was from the Children of Israel, perhaps because his mother was in contact with him in Pharaoh's palace and used to relate to him his entire story.

The city (al-madīna) is Memphis, the northern capital of Egypt.

The phrase ﴿at a time of heedlessness﴾ is connected to "entered." The particle "ʿalā" (upon) here expresses figurative elevation, as in His saying, ﴿upon guidance from their Lord﴾ (2:5), meaning: established in a time of heedlessness.

The time of heedlessness is the period during which the people of the city are unaware of what is happening in it. It is the time of people's rest, their dispersal, and the emptiness of the road of people. It is said that this was at the time of the midday rest (qaylūla), and that Musa was passing through the city alone. It is said that he was going to join Pharaoh, since Pharaoh had passed through that city. The purpose of mentioning this time is to indicate that no one noticed his killing of the Copt, as a preparation for His saying afterwards, ﴿He said, "O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?"﴾ (28:19) and so on, and as an introduction to the mention of his departure from the land of Egypt.

The two demonstratives in His saying ﴿this one is from his party and this one is from his enemy﴾ are an elaboration of what was stated generally in His saying ﴿two men fighting﴾.

The demonstrative noun (ism al-ishāra) in such contexts is not regarded as indicating near or far. Therefore the two demonstratives may be identical, as here and as in His saying, ﴿neither to these nor to those﴾ (4:143). They may also differ, as in the verse of al-Mutalammis:

*And none submits to oppression directed at him except the two most abased: the donkey of the tribe and the peg.*

*This one, bound by its rope to humiliation, and that one, struck and wounded, and no one has pity for it.*

The "shīʿa" (party) is the group affiliated to someone. It was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿and He made its people into factions﴾ (28:4). The "ʿadūw" (enemy) is the group whom Musa opposes, that is, he hates them. Thus, by "the one of his party" is meant a man from the Children of Israel, and by "the one of his enemy" is meant a man from the Copts, the people of Pharaoh. "ʿAduww" is a descriptive term that applies to both singular and plural, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾ (26:77) in Surah al-Shuʿarāʾ.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿this one is from his party and this one is from his enemy﴾, it is possible that these two descriptions mean that Musa knew he was from the Children of Israel through the account of his being picked up from the river, and that his mother had informed him of her story and his, as was mentioned earlier. Thus Musa grew up with enmity toward the Copts and with concealed love for the Children of Israel.

As for his striking the Copt, it was nothing but support for the truth under every interpretation. For this reason, when the quarrel between that Israelite and another Copt was repeated, and Musa wished to attack the Copt, the Copt did not say to him, "You only want to be a helper to your people," but rather said, ﴿You only want to be a tyrant in the land﴾ (28:19).

It is said that the Copt was one of the workers at Pharaoh's bakery. He wanted to carry firewood to the oven, so he called an Israelite to carry it, but the man refused. He then wanted to force him to carry it and to place it on his back. They quarreled and struck each other severely, and this is what is expressed as "fighting" by way of metaphor.

"Istighātha" (seeking rescue) is requesting relief, namely deliverance from hardship or assistance in repelling difficulty. The request is ordinarily made by calling out.
