Mentioning the "seeking rescue" indicates that the Israelite was overpowered and that the Copt pressed hard upon him, and that the Copt was an oppressor, since no one may be compelled to do work that he does not wish to do.

"Wakz" (striking) is striking with the hand by gathering its fingers, in the shape of forming the number seventy-three. It is called "jumʿ" (gathering), with a damma on the jīm and a sukūn on the mīm.

The clause ﴿so he decreed against him﴾ is a phrase used with the meaning of "he died," which is not altered. The subject of "qaḍā" (decreed) is therefore always omitted, meaning: "a decreer decreed against him," and that decreer is death. It is also possible that it refers to God, the Exalted, understood from the context, since none decrees death except Him, as in His saying, ﴿When We decreed death upon him﴾ (34:14). It has also been said that the pronoun in ﴿so he decreed﴾ refers to Musa, but this is not clear. The meaning is: Musa struck him, and the Copt died. This was an accidental killing, in that the blow happened to strike a vital place of the Copt, and Musa did not intend to kill him.

In the Book of Exodus of the Torah, in the second chapter, it is recorded that when Musa saw the Egyptian striking the Hebrew, he looked this way and that, and seeing that no one was there, he killed the Egyptian and buried him in the sand.

The clause ﴿He said, "This is from the work of Satan"﴾ is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf bayānī, an explanatory resumption), as if a questioner had asked: what happened with Musa when he was confronted with the death of the Copt? The narration of this is to draw attention to the fact that at that moment nothing occurred to Musa's mind except consideration of the religious consequence. The phrase "he said" is his speech within himself.

The demonstrative "this" refers either to the severe blow which caused the death, or to the death witnessed from his blow, or to the anger which caused the Copt's death. The meaning is that Satan kindled his anger until he exceeded the limit in the severity of the striking. Musa said this because the killing of a soul is considered abhorrent in human laws, since preserving a protected soul is one of the foundations of all religions. Musa knew the religion of his forefathers, perhaps through what he received from his mother, the righteous woman, during his nursing period and during his visits to her.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he is an enemy, a misleading, manifest one﴾ is a causal explanation for the fact that the severity of his anger was from the work of Satan. Had it not been for the satanic impulse, he would have limited himself to the Copt, or would have restrained himself from the one of his party. Since Satan is an enemy to humankind and has pathways into souls, Musa inferred from his act, which led to the killing of a soul, that it was an act arising from the whisper of Satan; had it not been so, his action would have been proceeding in permissible states.

In this there is evidence that the fundamental state of the human soul is goodness, and that this is the natural disposition (fiṭra), and that deviation from it requires a cause that is not natural, namely the intrusion of Satan's incitement into the soul.

The object of "ʿaduww" (enemy) is omitted, as indicated by the context, meaning: an enemy to Adam and the descendants of Adam.

[Page 91]

Following the statement about him as an enemy, he is described as misleading, because the enemy works to inflict harm upon his enemy. "Mubīn" (manifest) is a descriptive modifier of "muḍill" (misleading), not a second or third predicate.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 16:

﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me." So He forgave him. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ This is a *badal al-ishtimal* (inclusive apposition, a substitute that is included within the meaning of the preceding clause) for the clause ﴿He said, "This is from the work of Satan."﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]. This is because affirming with certainty that what proceeded from him was an act of Satan and his deception includes that this was a wrong done to himself, and that he turned to God by acknowledging his error, and from this follows the request for His forgiveness. He called his action a wronging of himself because it resulted from excessive anger on behalf of a man of his own party, and he was able to restrain his anger. So his hastening to strike the Copt with a deadly blow was a wrong that he brought upon himself. In Surat al-Shu'ara' he called it error (*dalal*): ﴿He said, "I did it then while I was of those who are astray."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 20].

By his wronging of himself he meant that he caused harm to himself by the Copts' intention to kill him, and that he exceeded the limit in punishing the Copt for his beating of the Israelite. Perhaps he did not seek out the wrongdoer between the two of them, and that was a tribal (*jahili*) form of support, as Wadak ibn Thumayl al-Mazini said in praise of his people:

"When they are called for help, they do not ask who summoned them,
to what war, or to what place."

Moses was guided to all of this by inspiration, since at that time there was no divine law among the Copts. It is also possible that his knowledge of this came from what he received from his mother and her people, of a religiosity based on the remnants of the religion of Isaac and Jacob.

No attention is to be paid here to the permissibility of a sin proceeding from a prophet, because he was not a prophet at that time. Nor is the question of a sin proceeding from a prophet before prophethood relevant, because that is hypothetical regarding sins whose ruling is established according to the law of that prophet, or the law of a prophet whom he follows, such as Jesus, peace be upon him, before his prophethood, since the Torah's law existed and he was one of its followers.

The *fa'* in His saying ﴿so He forgave him﴾ indicates sequence, meaning that He answered his plea for forgiveness and quickly granted him forgiveness.

The clause ﴿so He forgave him﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD*) between the clause ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself"﴾ and the clause ﴿He said, "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me"﴾ [al-Qasas: 17]. Its insertion serves to inform the people of the Qur'an of the honor Moses, peace be upon him, had with his Lord.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is a justification for the clause ﴿so He forgave him﴾. He justified the forgiveness by saying that He is abundant in forgiveness and merciful to His servants, and this is emphasized by the form of restriction (*qasr*), suggesting that what came from him was a wronging of himself, along with the circumstances surrounding it that we have mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 17:

﴿He said, "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals."﴾ The repetition of "He said" serves to emphasize the verb of "﴿He said, 'My Lord, I have wronged myself'﴾ [al-Qasas: 16]". The statement is repeated to draw attention to the continuity of Musa's speech, since a separation occurred between it and the two sentences "﴿So He forgave him; indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾" [al-Qasas: 16]. The structure of the speech is: "He said, 'My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me,' 'My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals.'" His saying "He said, 'My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me'" is not a new sentence following his saying "So He forgave him," because Musa did not know that Allah had forgiven him, since no revelation had yet come to him on that day.

The ba' in "﴿by what You have bestowed upon me﴾" indicates cause, and "mā" is a relative pronoun. The returning pronoun of the relative clause has been omitted, because it is a pronoun governed by the same preposition that governs the relative pronoun, and such omission is common in this construction. The estimated sense is: "by that with which You have bestowed upon me." It is also possible that "mā" is a verbal noun (masdariyyah), and the referent of the bestowal is what he was given of wisdom and knowledge, so that realities became clear to him, and customs and traditions no longer had influence over his feelings. Thus he no longer viewed things except through the lens of truth, and among that is that he would not be a supporter or helper of the criminals.

He meant by "the criminals" those who are suspected of committing crime, and he meant by them those who oppress people and subjugate them, because the Copt humiliated the Israelite by forcing him to carry firewood against his will.

Perhaps this statement was made in the sense of reflection upon his killing of the Copt, being confident that he had killed him by mistake.

The joining of the sentence "﴿then I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾" with the particle fa' is because the relative pronoun is often treated like a conditional noun, so its predicate and its complement are joined with fa', likening it to the response of a conditional clause, especially when the relative pronoun is a preposed prepositional phrase, since a preposed prepositional phrase may be intended with the meaning of a condition and is treated as a condition, as in his saying in the hadith, "As you are, so you will be ruled over," with the verb "takunu" in the jussive and giving it a jussive response.

The "zahir" means the helper.

This structure indicates that Musa intended to make his not supporting the criminals a repayment for the blessing of wisdom and knowledge, by making the thanks for that blessing the defense of truth and the changing of falsehood; for if one does not change falsehood and wrongdoing, and leaves them as they are, he has flattered their doer, and flattery is a form of support. Among what supports this interpretation is that when Musa, on the following morning, found the man who had called for his help the day before calling for his help against another Copt, he wanted to strike the Copt, fulfilling his promise to his Lord when he said "﴿then I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾"; because the Copt was a polytheist and the Israelite a monotheist.

Many of the early scholars (salaf) took this verse as evidence for prohibiting aiding the people of injustice in any of their affairs. Perhaps the basis of their argument is that Allah related it from Musa in a context of praising him, and so this indicates that it is part of the true speech.

﴿So he became in the city, fearful and watchful, when behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was calling out to him for help. That is, he became fearful that he would be held accountable for the blood of the Qibti (the Egyptian) whom he had killed, "and he was watchful" (yataraqqab), meaning he was observing what was being said about his affair, so that he would be ready to go into hiding or to leave the city. This is because news of the killing of the Qibti had not spread, since it happened at a time when the alleys of the city were empty, as was explained earlier. Therefore Musa was watching for the affair of the murdered Qibti to come to light.

The particle "idhā" (إذا) is li-l-mufājaʾa (for sudden surprise), meaning: suddenly he was surprised that the one who had sought his help the day before was seeking his help again today.

The definite article in "al-ams" (الأمس, "yesterday") is a replacement (ʿiwaḍ, compensation) for the genitive noun that is omitted, meaning "his yesterday," since it was not "yesterday" at the time the verse was revealed.

Al-istiṣrākh (الاستصراخ) means an intensified crying out, that is, calling out (al-nidāʾ). In the earlier narrative it is expressed by al-istighātha (الاستغاثة, seeking help), and the two expressions were varied for the sake of stylistic variety (li-l-tafannun).

Musa's words to him, "Indeed, you are clearly a misguided person," are a rebuke of the Israelite, since his earlier call for help had been the cause of a man's death. This does not require that his call for help should not be answered; rather, it is in the nature of a reproach and blame directed at him for the frequency of his quarrels.

Al-ghawiyy (الغويّ) means one who is intensely in error (al-ghawāya), and ghawāya is misguidance and poor judgment. That is, "You provoke someone you cannot withstand, and then you seek rescue from me day after day." It is not meant that he is a wrongdoer or a corrupter, for if he were such, Musa would not have wanted to strike his enemy.

Al-baṭsh (البطش) means seizing with violence, and what is meant here is striking. The apparent sense of his words "an enemy to both of them" is that he was a Qibti. It may be that he was described as an enemy to both of them because his enmity toward the Israelite was well known and widespread among the Copts. As for his enmity toward Musa, it is because he intended to wrong a man, and wrongdoing is an enemy to the soul of Musa, since he grew up upon the purity of a soul that God had prepared for the message. The interrogative is used here to express denial (al-inkār).

Al-jabbār (الجبّار) is one who does whatever he wills in ways that harm people, and who holds people to account with severity rather than gentleness. Its occurrence was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Ra'd in His words, ﴿And every obstinate tyrant has failed﴾ [Ibrahim: 15], and in Surat Maryam in His words, ﴿and has not made me a tyrant, wretched﴾ [Maryam: 32].

The meaning is: "You are trying to be one who acts arbitrarily through retaliation and severity, and you are not trying to be one of the reformers who make peace between the two disputants by working toward reconciliation between them." Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verses 20–21:

Page 95

﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city, running. He said, "O Moses, indeed the chiefs are conferring about you, to kill you, so leave; indeed I am to you among the sincere advisers."﴾ ﴿So he left from it, fearful, watchful. He said, "My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people."﴾

The apparent arrangement of the verses indicates that the man came during the exchange between Moses and the Copt, and so the matter of their dispute was set aside, since in the course of it there occurred something more important and more useful for the story.

It is apparent that "the farthest part of the city" is the area of the palaces of Pharaoh and his people, for it is the custom of kings to dwell at the edges of cities, guarding against revolts and raids, so that their dwellings are closest to escape when fear arises. It has been said: "The outskirts are the dwellings of the nobles." As for the saying of Abu Tammam:

"It was the protected middle, then events connected with it until it became an edge."

that is another meaning, referring to the diminishing of the civilization, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They say, "Indeed our houses are exposed."﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13].

By this the reason for mentioning the place from which the man came becomes clear, and that the man knew Moses.

Al-Mala' (the chiefs): the assembly of people of standing. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The chiefs of his people said﴾, i.e., of Noah, in al-A'raf, and by them is meant the people of Pharaoh's state. So the meaning is: the people of authority are conferring about you, i.e., they are consulting about killing you. This implies that the matter was referred to Pharaoh, and in the Book of Exodus, chapter 2: ("Pharaoh heard this matter and sought to kill Moses"). When this man learned of that, he hastened with the news to Moses, because he was impressed by Moses and his uprightness. It has been said that this man was from the Children of Israel. It has also been said that he was from the Copts but was a believer who concealed his faith, perhaps because God inspired him with knowledge of the corruption of polytheism through the soundness of his nature, and prepared him to rescue Moses from the hand of Pharaoh.

Al-Sa'y: quick walking. It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿Then behold, it was a serpent, moving swiftly﴾ [Ta-Ha: 20] in Surat Ta-Ha. Its literal and figurative meanings were explained earlier at His saying ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its due striving﴾ [al-Isra': 19] in Surat al-Isra'. The clause "yas'a" (running) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "rajul" (a man)

Page 96

described as being "from the farthest part of the city." "Ya'tamiruna bika" means: they are conferring. It is treated as implying the meaning of "yahummuna" (they intend), so it takes the preposition "bi" as if it had been said: they confer and intend to kill you.

The original sense of al-i'timar is accepting the command of the one who commands, so it is the reflexive of "amara" (to command). Imru' al-Qays said:

"And he who is led by his own will transgresses against himself"

meaning: what harms him is what he obeys in his own self's command. Then the use of i'timar for consultation became common, because those who consult take one another's counsel, so all of them act upon it, as He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And confer among yourselves in kindness﴾ [al-Talaq: 6].

The clause "Qala ya Musa" (he said, "O Moses") is a substitutive clause of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause "Ja'a rajul" (a man came), because his coming includes his saying that. The object of "leave" is omitted, indicated by the context, i.e., "so leave the city." The clause "Indeni laka mina al-nasihin" (indeed I am to you among the sincere advisers) is a justification for his command to leave. The "lam" in His saying "laka min al-nasihin" is an extra particle (silah), because the verb "nasaha" is most often used with the "lam" as its transitive particle; one says "nasahtu laka" (I advised you). He, exalted is He, said ﴿When they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91] in Surat al-Tawbah, and some have erroneously said "nasahtuka." The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for the sake of the rhyme (ri'aya) before the closing word (fasila).

Al-taraqqub: its literal meaning is waiting, and it is derived from "raqiba," when one looks at the conditions of a thing. From it the high place is called "marqaba" and "murtaqab." Here it is used metaphorically for caution.

The clause "Qala rabbi najjini" (he said, "My Lord, save me") is a substitutive clause of inclusion for the clause "yataraqqabu" (watchful), because his watchfulness includes supplication to God that He save him.

"The wrongdoing people" are the people of Pharaoh. He described them with wrongdoing because they are polytheists, and because they sought to kill him in retaliation for an accidental killing, which is an injustice, since an accidental killing does not, in the view of reason and the Law, call for the penalty of death.

The point of lesson from the story of Moses with the Copt and his departure from the city, from His saying "And when he reached his maturity" up to here, is that God chooses whom He wills from among His servants, that He knows best where to place His messages, and that when His will attaches to something, He prepares its causes by His power, bringing it forth in the most perfect arrangement.

﴿When he turned his face towards Madyan, he said, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way."﴾

This is a prophetic migration (hijrah nabawiyyah), resembling the migration of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Indeed, I am migrating to my Lord﴾ (Surat al-'Ankabut: 26). Allah inspired Musa, peace be upon him, to head for the land of Madyan, where he would find a prophet who would instruct him in the etiquette of prophethood. Musa did not know where he was heading or whom he would find at his destination, as is indicated by his saying: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way.﴾

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When he turned his face towards Madyan﴾, is connected (ʿaṭf) to omitted clauses, since the intended meaning is: when he left the city, wandering aimlessly, it happened that his journey was on a road leading to the land of Madyan, and at that moment he said: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: Musa set out with no knowledge of the road, relying only on good opinion of his Lord.

Tawajjaha (توجه) means he turned his face toward something, i.e., he directed his journey towards Madyan.

Tilqā' (تلقاء): its origin is a verbal noun on the pattern tif'āl with a kasra on the tā', and it has no parallel with a kasra on the tā' except timthāl. It means meeting or nearness. The use of this noun to denote direction became common, so it became one of the adverbs of place that are put in the accusative as adverbs of place. The intended meaning is: when he turned in the direction of the meeting-point of Madyan, that is, the direction of the lands of Madyan. The saying of God, exalted is He, ﴿And when their eyes are turned towards the companions of the Fire﴾ (Surat al-A'raf: 47), has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

[Page 98]

Madyan: a people descended from Madyan ibn Ibrahim. Their affairs were discussed at the verse ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ (Surat al-A'raf: 85) in Surat al-A'raf.

The land of Madyan lies on the western shore of the Red Sea. When Musa left the city of (Ra'amses) or (Memphis), he took a route heading west-south, and he traveled across desert passing through the lands of the Amalekites, the lands of the Edomites, and then the lands of the Nabataeans, until he reached the land of Madyan. That is a distance of approximately eight hundred and fifty miles. Since Musa was travelling on foot during that journey, that distance requires about forty-five days. He would certainly have spent the nights in the desert. He was a strong, hardy man, and Allah had inspired him with the right way, so he did not go astray on his journey.

Al-sawā' (السواء): the straight path, which has no crookedness. Allah inspired him with this supplication, within which lies His granting him success in the true religion.

[Page 98]

His words ﴿When he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ indicate that he reached the land of Madyan, and that was when he arrived at their water. Here *al-wurud* (arrival) means reaching and attaining, as in His words, ﴿And there is not one of you but will arrive at it﴾ [Maryam: 71]. By "the water" is meant the place of the water. The water of a people is what identifies their dwellings, because tribes used to settle by water sources, and they would refer to the land of a tribe by "the water of the sons of so-and-so." So the meaning is: "When he arrived," that is, when he reached the lands of Madyan.

It is fitting for a stranger who comes to the dwellings of a people to head for the water, because it is the gathering place of people, and there he becomes known to those who accompany him and host him.

*Lamma* (when) is a particle of timing, indicating that the existence of one thing coincides with the existence of another. That is, when he arrived in the land of Madyan, he found a community (*ummah*).

[Page 99]

*Ummah* means a large group of people, and it has been discussed in His words, ﴿Mankind were one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213], in al-Baqarah. The object of *yasqun* (they water) has been omitted in order to generalize what is watered, which is livestock and people. Also, the purpose does not depend on knowing what is watered, but on what follows it: the two women holding back from watering, as in *al-Kashshaf*, following *Dala'il al-I'jaz* (Proofs of Inimitability). So this is a case of treating a transitive verb as if it were intransitive. Alternatively, the omission here is for brevity, as al-Sakkaki chose, and his commentators, Sa'd (al-Taftazani) and al-Sayyid (al-Jurjani), supported this. As for the omission of the objects of *tadhudan* (you drive away) and *la nasqi* (we do not water), and *fasaqa lahuma* (so he watered for them), what is definite about them is what the two shaykhs (al-Zamakhshari and al-Sakkaki) held. As for what *Miftah al-'Ulum* and its commentators held, it is a matter for which there is no evidence in the Qur'an that would require positing an omitted element. The information that they were driving away sheep comes from the books of the Israelites.

The meaning of *min dunihim* (apart from them) is in a place other than the area around the water, that is, on a side away from the community of people. This is because the true meaning of the word *dūna* (below/beside) is that it describes a thing that is lower than another. From this branch several figurative meanings with different relations, and among them is what occurs in this verse. So *dūna* here means a direction that a person reaches after the place where the watering people are. It compares the place that the walker reaches after another place to the lower place relative to the other, as though the walker descends to it, since walking is likened to ascending and descending depending on the perspective.

The noun described by *dūna* is omitted due to frequent usage, so *dūna* takes the place of that omitted noun.

The particle *min* (from) with *dūna* may be used for location in time, as in His words, ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9]. It may also mean *'inda* (at/near), a meaning that Abu 'Ubayda affirmed in His words, ﴿Neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10]. The meaning is: he found two women in a direction away from the direction of those watering.

*Tadhudan* means "driving away." The true meaning of *dhawd* is driving animals away from water. For this reason they called a herd of camels a *dhawd*. It is not said "*dhudtu al-nas*" (I drove the people away) except as a figurative metonymy (*majaz mursal*). From this is His saying in a hadith: "Some people will indeed be driven away from my Basin..." (the hadith continues).

The meaning in the verse is: they were holding back camels from the water. In the Torah, Shu'ayb was the owner of sheep, and Moses herded his sheep. So the use of *tadhudan* here would be a metonymy, or the true meaning of *dhawd* is driving all livestock away from the water basin. The statements of the linguists are not explicit in clarifying the true meaning of this.

[Page 100]

In the Book of Exodus it says that they had sheep. *Dhawd* is used only for livestock. The purpose of bringing livestock to the water is to water them. When Moses saw the two women holding back their livestock from drinking, he asked them: "What is your affair?" This is a question about their story and their situation, since they came to the water and did not push in to water their sheep.

The sentence "He said, 'What is your affair?'" is a *badal al-ishtimal* (inclusive substitution) of the sentence "And he found, apart from them, two women driving away."

*Khatb* means affair, or an important event. It has been discussed at His words, ﴿He said, "What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?"﴾ [Yusuf: 51]. They replied that they disliked watering while the place was crowded with shepherds, and that they would continue not watering, as the use of the present tense implies, until the shepherds leave.

*Ri'a'* (shepherds) is the plural of *ra'i* (shepherd).

*Al-Isdar* means causing to return from watering, that is, until the shepherds have watered and sent their livestock away. So *al-isdar* means making others depart, that is, until the camel herders take their livestock away and the crowding ends. Their holding back from the crush was their habit, as they were women of dignity and noble upbringing.

The majority of reciters read *yusdira* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *dal*. Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Ja'far read *yasdura* with a *fatha* on the initial letter of the present tense and a *damma* on the *dal*, attributing the action of departing to the shepherds: until they return from the water, that is, with their livestock. This is because the description of them as shepherds implies that they had livestock. This implies that this was their habit every day of watering, but the wording does not indicate that it was a habit.

Their words, ﴿And our father is a very old man﴾, were an excuse for their presence at the watering alongside the men, because they did not find a man to water for them. The only man for them was their father, and he is a very old man who cannot come to the water because of his weakness in competing.

[Page 101]

The names of the two women were Layya and Safurah. In the Book of Exodus, their father is described as a priest of Madyan. In that book he is first called Ra'uwil, then the account returns to him and he is called Yathrun, and described as the father-in-law of Moses (*hamiyy*). So the named person is one. Ibn al-'Ibri said in his history: "Yathrun ibn Ra'uwil had seven daughters, and two of them went out to water." So Shu'ayb is the one called Yathrun by the Jews.

Referring to a prophet as a priest (*kahin*) is a technical usage, because a *kahin* informs about the unseen, and because it is applied among the Jews to one who manages religious affairs. To affirm definitively that he is Shu'ayb the Messenger, our scholars treated what came from him in this story as a previous law (*shar' sabiq*), and they derived from it issues based on the principle that the law of the messengers of God before us is a law for us unless an abrogating ruling (*nasikh*) is revealed. Among these issues are a woman's engaging in work and seeking means of livelihood, the obligation of her modesty, the guardianship of a father in marriage, making physical labour a dowry, combining marriage and hire in a single contract, and the legitimacy of hiring. Al-Qurtubi has fully discussed these matters. Yet the evidences of the Islamic law are sufficient without deriving these matters from what is in this verse, except that some of these rulings do not have their evidence in the Qur'an. So in this verse there is evidence for them from the Book according to those who hold that the law of those before us is a law for us.

In his permitting his two daughters to water, there is evidence for the permissibility of a woman dealing with her own affairs and appearing in public gatherings of people, provided she covers what must be covered. This is because the law of those before us is a law for us if our law narrates it and there is nothing in our law that abrogates it. As for people avoiding such things, that is a matter of dignity (*muru'a*). People differ over what dignity and customs require, and they vary in this, and the conditions of nations differ in it, especially the differences between the manners of the Bedouins and the settled folk.

The entry of the temporal *lamma* indicates that his arrival coincided with the presence of the watering people. The attachment of the verb *saqa* (he watered) with *fa* (then) indicates that he hastened and watered for them, and that was at the moment of his arrival.

The meaning of *fasaqa lahuma* (so he watered for them) is that he watered what they had come to water for their sake. So *li* (for) is for purpose, that is, nothing motivated him to do it except them, out of compassion for them and to help them. This is part of the strength of his dignity, that he undertook this difficult task despite the exhaustion he had upon arrival.

*Tawalla* means returning along his path. This indicates that he had been sitting earlier in the shade and then returned to it. It appears that *tawalla* is synonymous with *wallā*, but an increase in the form usually implies an increase in meaning, so *tawalla* is stronger than *wallā*. This has been discussed under His words, ﴿and turned back retreating﴾ in Surat al-Naml.

[Page 102]

He remembered all of that while enjoying the blessing of the coolness of the shade and rest from fatigue. So he uttered a comprehensive sentence combining thanks, praise, and supplication, which is ﴿I am in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾. *Faqir* means needy. So his words, ﴿I am in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾, are thanks for favours already bestowed.

His words, ﴿I am in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾, are also praise of God, as He is the Giver of good.

*Khayr* (good) is that which has benefit and suitability for the one it concerns. Some of it is the good of this world, and some is the good of the Hereafter, which may appear in the form of hardship, because the outcome is what matters. God, Exalted is He, says, ﴿Do not be impressed by their wealth and their children; Allah only intends to punish them through them in this world, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 85]. The first of this good is the granting of wisdom and knowledge.

The best good for a stranger is finding a shelter where he can eat and spend the night, and a wife with whom he can feel at ease and settle.

So God's response to him was that He inspired Shu'ayb to send for him to bring him to his house and marry him to his daughter, as the particle *fa* (then), indicating sequence, in His words, ﴿Then one of them came to him﴾ suggests.

It is fitting for a stranger who comes to the dwellings of a people to head for the water, because it is the gathering place of people, and there he becomes known to those who accompany him and host him.

*Lamma* (when) is a particle of timing, indicating that the existence of one thing coincides with the existence of another. That is, when he arrived in the land of Madyan, he found a community (*ummah*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 25:

﴿Then one of the two women came to him, walking shyly. She said, "Indeed my father invites you, so that he may reward you with the wage for what you gave us to drink."﴾ You know that the fa' (فاء, the particle of sequence) indicates that God answered his supplication, so He made it easy for Shu'ayb to send for Musa in order to host him and marry him to his daughter. This guarantees him companionship in a land of exile, a shelter, and a righteous companion. The fa' also indicates that Shu'ayb did not delay in sending for him, so he sent one of the two daughters for whom he had watered the flock, and she was Safurah. She came to him while he was still in his place in the shade.

He mentioned "tamshi" (تَمْشِي, "walking") so that he could build upon it his statement "ʿalā istiḥyāʾin" (عَلى اسْتِحْياءٍ, "shyly"). Otherwise, the verb "jāʾathu" (جاءَتْهُ, "came to him") is sufficient without mentioning "tamshi."

The "ʿalā" (عَلى) is for the figurative sense of elevation, borrowed to mean being firmly characterized by the description. The meaning is that she was shy in her walking, i.e., she walked not in a swaggering manner, nor swaying, nor displaying adornment. It is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that she was covering her face with her garment; that is, covering the face was not obligatory for her, but it was an exaggeration in modesty. And "al-istiḥyāʾ" (الِاسْتِحْياءُ) is an intensive form of "al-ḥayāʾ" (الحَياءُ, modesty), like "al-istijābah" (الِاسْتِجابَةُ, response). God said: ﴿And tell the believing women to lower their gaze﴾ [al-Nur: 31] up to His words ﴿so that it may be known what they conceal of their adornment﴾ [al-Nur: 31].

The clause "qālat" (قالَتْ, "she said") is an appositive (بَدَلٌ) of "jāʾathu." She only explained to him the purpose of her father's invitation by way of hastening to honour him.

The "jazāʾ" (الجَزاءُ, reward) is recompense for a good or bad deed with something similar in goodness or in evil. God said: ﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾ [al-Rahman: 60], and God said: ﴿That is how We repaid them for their disbelief﴾ [Saba: 17].

The emphasis of the clause in her words "Indeed my father invites you" is a report of what was in her speech of affirming the news, for the sake of giving it importance and bringing joy to the one informed of it.

The "ajr" (الأجْرُ, wage/reward) is compensation for a beneficial deed to the one compensated, and from it the reward for acts of obedience is called "ajr." God said: ﴿And if you believe and fear God, He will give you your rewards﴾ [Muhammad: 36]. "Ajra mā saqayta lanā" (أجْرَ ما سَقَيْتَ لَنا, "the wage for what you gave us to drink") is put in the accusative as an absolute object (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq) to clarify the type of recompense, that it is a recompense of good, which is that he intended to host him. And it is not the absolute object to clarify the type of recompense, that it is a recompense of good, which is that he intended to host him, it is not from the meaning of hiring a hired worker, because it was not by mutual agreement, nor by condition, nor by custom.

The recompense is honour, and hiring is a contract. This is supported by His words after it: ﴿One of them said, "O my father, hire him"﴾ [al-Qasas: 26], for it is evidence that her father had not previously resolved to hire Musa. The act of Musa was pure kindness that did not seek any reward for it, because he did not know the two women or their house. The act of Shu'ayb was pure generosity and love for hosting every stranger, and hosting the stranger is from the tradition of Ibrahim, so it is no wonder that two men from the descendants of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, would practise it. The "mā" (ما) in His words "mā saqayta lanā" is verbal-nominal (maṣdariyyah), meaning "your watering (for us)," and the "lām" (لام) in "lanā" is the lām of cause.

* * *

﴿So when he came to him and related to him the narrative, he said, "Fear not; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾
It was customary that the guest be greeted by being asked about his condition and the reason for his coming. Therefore Musa related to him the story of his departure and his arrival to Shu'ayb. That requires that Shu'ayb had asked him about the reason for his coming. The "qaṣaṣ" (القَصَصُ) means the news. And "qaṣṣa ʿalayhi" (قَصَّ عَلَيْهِ) means he informed him.

The definite article in "al-qaṣaṣa" (القَصَصَ) is a substitute for the genitive (عِوَضٌ عَنِ المُضافِ إلَيْهِ), that is, "qaṣaṣahu" (his story), or it is for prior reference, that is, the narrative mentioned just before. Its parallel was mentioned at the beginning of surah Yusuf.

Shu'ayb then reassured him that he would remove the fear from himself, because he had come into a place of safety from being struck by the judgement of Pharaoh, since the land of Madyan belongs to the rule of the Canaanites, who are a people of might and valour. The meaning of his prohibition of fear is his prohibition of thinking that the hand of Pharaoh would reach him.

The clause ﴿you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾ is a reason for the prohibition of fear. The description of Pharaoh's people as "wrongdoers" confirms what Musa had told him of their intention to kill him as retribution for an accidental killing, and what preceded that of their enmity towards the Children of Israel.

﴿One of the two women said: "O father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy."﴾ ﴿He said: "Indeed, I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine on condition that you serve me for eight years. But if you complete ten, it is from you. And I do not wish to burden you. You will find me, God willing, among the righteous."﴾ ﴿He said: "That is between me and you. Whichever of the two terms I fulfill, there will be no injustice against me. And God is Witness over what we say."﴾

He omitted what Musa received from Shu'ayb in terms of reward by way of his hospitality and feeding him, and moved on to the offer of one of the two women to her father that he hire him for work with his livestock, since there was no man in their household who could do that, and their father had grown old. When she saw his trustworthiness and piety, she saw that he was the best one to be hired for work with them, owing to his strength for the work and his trustworthiness.

The ta' in "abati" (my father) is a substitute for the ya' of the first person in the vocative specifically, and it may be pronounced with a kasra, and this is how the majority recited it. It may also be pronounced with a fatha, and this is how Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far recited it.

The clause ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾ is a reason for her advice to hire him, meaning: because one like him is the one who should be hired. It came in a comprehensive, unrestricted expression as a proverb, because of its generality and its exact correspondence to reality without exception. The definite article in "al-qawiyy al-amin" (the strong, the trustworthy) is for the genus, intended in the sense of generality. The address in "man istajarta" (whom you hire) is directed to Shu'ayb, and is suitable to include everyone who is fit to be addressed, so that the saying may be fully valid to be sent forth as a proverb. Thus the estimate is: whoever hires the one who hires. "Man" is a relative pronoun in the sense of the definite by the article of genus, since the relative clause here does not intend a specific description of a particular individual.

The placing of "best of whom you hire" as the predicate-subject, by making it a noun, while making "al-qawiyy al-amin" the predicate, is equally valid to make "al-qawiyy al-amin" the subject, since both are equal in definiteness, in that the definiteness in the relative clause after "khayr" and in the definite article here both intend generality in both. So what is given precedence in the two parts of the sentence is what is more important and deserving of attention, namely the best of hired workers; because the sentence was brought as a justification for the statement "hire him," so the description of the worker is more important in the context of its justification, and the hearer's soul is more eager to learn his condition.

The coming of this generality right after speaking of a specific person indicates that the one spoken of is among those covered by that generality. This was in line with the core of eloquence, since attributing trustworthiness and strength to this person spoken of is establishing the ruling with evidence. So the estimate of the meaning of the speech is: hire him, for he is strong and trustworthy, and indeed the best one who hires a hired worker is the strong and trustworthy. Thus the sentence contained the special feature of placing the more important first, the brevity of omission, and the rhetorical mode, and with this it fulfilled the full requirement of the situation, being eloquent to the limit of inimitability.

It is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "I complain to God of the weakness of the trustworthy and the treachery of the strong." He meant: I ask Him to support me with a strong, trustworthy person whom I may rely upon.

The demonstrative in His words "hatayn" (these two) refers to the two women for whom he watered (the flocks), if both were present together, to the exclusion of the other daughters of Shu'ayb, because the matter is connected to their affair; or the demonstrative refers to them because they were present in Musa's mind, given the recency of his watering for them, if the other was absent at that time.

In this is the permissibility of a man offering his female ward to one who would marry her, out of desire for his righteousness. He left to Musa the choice of one of them, because he had known them, and the one Musa chose was Safurah, who was the younger, as came in the narration of Abu Dharr from the Prophet (ﷺ). He chose her rather than her sister because he knew her manners through her modesty and her speech, and this was a preference for her in his eyes.

This offer was before the conclusion of the marriage contract, so there is no ignorance of the one contracted upon in it. His words ﴿on condition that you serve me for eight years﴾: the particle "'ala" (on) is among the forms of conditions in contracts. "Ta'jurani" is the present tense of "ajarahu," like "nasarahu," when he is a hired worker for him. "Hijaj" is the plural of "hijjah," with a kasra on the ha', which means a year, derived from the name "hajj," because the Hajj occurs every year, and the season of Hajj falls in the last month of the Arabic year.

The binding of making his marriage conditional on the hiring contract between them is an offer from him to Musa, and not yet a marriage contract nor a hiring contract until Musa agrees. In this offer there is evidence for the question of combining a marriage contract with a hiring contract. The root of this question in the Sunnah is the hadith of the woman who offered herself to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not marry her, but married her to a man who was present in his assembly, and he had nothing to give her as dower, so he married her to him for what he had of the Qur'an, that is, on condition that he teach it to her.

The well-known position of the school of Malik is that a condition attached to a marriage contract, if it contradicts the nature of the marriage contract, is void, and the marriage is annulled before consummation and stands after it with the customary dower (mahr al-mithl). As for a condition that does not contradict the marriage contract, the marriage is not annulled because of it, but the condition is nullified. It is also reported from Malik: all conditions are disliked at the outset, but if they occur, they stand. Ashhab and Asbagh said: the condition is permissible, and Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi chose this, and it is the truth, because of the verse and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The conditions most worthy of being fulfilled are those by which you have made lawful the private parts."

The apparent meaning of the verse is also that the mentioned hiring was made the dower of the daughter. It is possible that what was stipulated was only the binding of the hiring, and as for the dower, it follows what is regarded in their law as a pillar of marriage, and laws may differ in the meanings of legal realities. If we take the apparent meaning of the verse, it indicates that they made the dower the benefits of the husband's service to Shu'ayb, and it is possible that this was with her consent, since she heard and remained silent, based on customs accepted among them, that her father would benefit from those services.

It is possible that it was for the woman's guardian by original right, if he was the one entitled to the dower in that law, since the customs of nations differ regarding the marrying off of their wards. And since the verse contains generality, it is not sufficient as a proof for the permissibility of making a woman's dower the benefits of her husband's labor. So the question of the validity of making the dower a hiring contract returns to derivation from the principles of the Shari'ah, and entry under the general meaning of dower, since the benefits of hiring have value, so there is no barrier to making them a dower. The verified position of the school of Malik is that it is disliked but stands. Al-Shafi'i and 'Abd al-Malik ibn Habib of the Malikis permitted it. Abu Hanifah said: it is not permissible to make the dower the benefits of a free person, but it is permissible for it to be the benefits of a slave. He did not see in the verse a proof, because according to him it may be that the marriage fulfilled its conditions, so the generality entered into it. Ibn al-Qasim, one of Malik's companions, agreed with him.

Since the ruling of the law of those before us is disputed as to whether it is a law for us, it was a disputed proof among the scholars of usul al-fiqh, and the generality that entered this verse added weakness to it, so it is necessary to return to other evidences from the law of Islam. The evidence for permissibility is included under the general meaning of dower. If the benefits made as dower are obtained before consummation, the matter is clear; but if some or all of them are not realized except after consummation, as in this verse, the matter returns to marriage with a deferred dower, which is disliked but not void, and to hiring for a consideration that is not divisible by dividing the work. So if the hired worker does not complete the work in this case, it returns to the question of a worker being unable to do the work after having received the wage. It is reported in the Sahih, and in the hadith of the woman who gave herself to the Prophet (ﷺ), that he did not accept her, and a man of his companions said to him: "If you have no need of her, marry her to me." He said: "Do you have anything to give her as dower?" ... until he said to him (ﷺ): "Seek, even an iron ring." He said: "I have nothing, not even an iron ring." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "What do you have of the Qur'an?" He said: "I have such-and-such surah and such-and-such surah," naming surahs. He said to him: "I have married her to you for what you have of the Qur'an." And in one narration, the Prophet ordered him to teach her twenty verses of what he had of the Qur'an, and she would be his wife. If this addition is authentic, the hadith is in accordance with what is in this verse, and it is evidence for the validity of making the dower a hiring for work. If it is not authentic, as is well known in the books of Sahih, then the story is a particular case, confined to its specific instance.

The verse does not address the work for which he was hired. The Book of Exodus mentions that he herded the sheep of Jethro, who is Shu'ayb, but the Qur'an has no purpose in explaining that. The verse does not address the wage, and you know that the apparent meaning is that it was his marrying off of the daughter. If we do not take this apparent meaning, the verse does not address the wage, since there is no purpose in it from the narration of the story, so it follows what is customary among them regarding the wages of works, and tribes had customs in that. I found, since the beginning of this fourteenth century, that a shepherd of sheep receives each year a shirt and sandals, called "balghah," and similar things, which I cannot specify now.

His words ﴿If you complete ten, it is from you﴾ made that matter subject to Musa, as a favor from him in choosing him and entrusting him to what his condition would be at the end of the eight years, out of desire for the increase.

The "min" is for origin. "'Inda" is used figuratively for the self and essence, and the prepositional phrase is the predicate of a deleted subject, and the estimate is: the completion of the ten is from yourself, meaning not from me. The meaning is that completion is not included in the contract, which is binding on both sides, so the implication of the adverbial phrase is considered here.

Malik argued from His words ﴿Indeed, I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine﴾ that a father has the right to marry off his virgin daughter without her permission. This is taking the apparent meaning, since it did not address seeking her permission. Those who prohibit this may say: the absence of mention of it does not require its non-occurrence.

His words ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the righteous﴾ mean the righteous among people in good dealing and gentleness of manner. He intended by this to make his character known to his companion, and this is not the self-praise that is forbidden, because what is forbidden is what the speaker intends by boasting and self-glorification. As for what is for the purpose of religion or dealing, that is established for a good reason, as Yusuf said: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land; indeed I am a knowing guardian﴾ [Yusuf: 55].

"Ashuqqa 'alayka" means: I would be burdensome to you, that is, impose on you a hardship. Hardship means difficulty, fatigue, and hardship in work. The original usage is to describe toilsome work as burdensome, so attributing "ashuqqa" to his self is a metaphorical attribution, since he is the cause of the hardship, meaning: I do not wish to stipulate on you what involves your hardship. This is from the leniency mentioned in the hadith: "May God have mercy on a man who is lenient when he sells, lenient when he buys." . . .

The clause ﴿He said: "That is between me and you"﴾ relates Musa's answer to Shu'ayb's speech. The demonstrative refers to what was mentioned, namely ﴿on condition that you serve me for eight years﴾ to the end of it. This is Musa's acceptance of what Shu'ayb required, and with it the contract for the marriage and for the hiring was completed. That is, the matter is as you stipulated upon me and upon yourself. "Bayni wa baynaka" (between me and you) is used figuratively for the meaning of firmness, obligation, and binding, meaning each is responsible for what is his part of the work.

"Ayyamā" is in the accusative governed by "qadaytu" (I fulfil). "Ayyu" is a relative noun of indeterminate reference, like "mā". "Mā" is added after it for emphasis, so that the relative noun resembles conditional particles (asmā' al-shart), because emphasising the indeterminacy in the relative noun gives it generality, and so it resembles the conditional; for this reason it is given a response like the response of the conditional. The whole clause is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause "that is between me and you," because the choice of the end of the term is among what the contract, conveyed by the clause "that is between me and you," includes. "Al-'udwan" with a damma on the 'ayn: transgression against the right, i.e., "so let there be no transgression against me." Thus he negated the category of transgression, of which is the transgression of the one who hires him. Moses called God as witness over himself and over Shu'ayb.

The root of "al-wakil" is: the one to whom a matter is entrusted. Here he means that he was entrusted with fulfilling what they had contracted upon, so that if either of them failed in something, God would be the one who holds him to account. Since "al-wakil" was given the meaning of "al-shahid" (witness), it was made to take the preposition "'ala," whereas its proper construction would have been with "ila."

The lesson from the telling of this part of the story, which begins with the words of the Exalted ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 22] down to His words ﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say﴾, is what it contains of the virtues of deeds and the excellences of people of perfection, and how God Almighty prepared Moses to receive the message by turning him through stages of virtues, the greatest of which is keeping company with a messenger from among the messengers of God and becoming his son-in-law, and what it includes of the qualities of manliness and chivalry that were lodged in his soul: doing good, relieving the distressed, compassion toward the weak, asceticism, contentment, gratitude to his Lord for what He bestowed upon him, chastity, desire for the company of the righteous and working for them, fulfilling the contract, and steadfastness upon the covenant. Ultimately this led to his being honoured with prophethood, and what it contains of the prophetic qualities that Shu'ayb displayed: love of hospitality, granting security to the fearful, and gentleness in dealings. This is so that the polytheists may take heed from it, if they have any capacity for taking heed, by comparing those states with their kinds of states of the Prophet (ﷺ), and so that they may come to see that what they knew him for of pure qualities before his mission, and the rectifying of his conduct, and his assistance in the calamities of truth, and his marriage to the best woman among his people, are only singular qualities in him among his people, and are only flashes for the pouring of the cloud of revelation upon him. And God knows best where He places His message. And so that the Muslims may follow the good example set by the character of the people of prophethood and righteousness.

The lesson from the telling of this part of the story, which begins with the words of the Exalted ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 22] down to His words ﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say﴾, is what it contains of the virtues of deeds and the excellences of people of perfection, and how God Almighty prepared Moses to receive the message by turning him through stages of virtues, the greatest of which is keeping company with a messenger from among the messengers of God and becoming his son-in-law, and what it includes of the qualities of manliness and chivalry that were lodged in his soul: doing good, relieving the distressed, compassion toward the weak, asceticism, contentment, gratitude to his Lord for what He bestowed upon him, chastity, desire for the company of the righteous and working for them, fulfilling the contract, and steadfastness upon the covenant. Ultimately this led to his being honoured with prophethood, and what it contains of the prophetic qualities that Shu'ayb displayed: love of hospitality, granting security to the fearful, and gentleness in dealings. This is so that the polytheists may take heed from it, if they have any capacity for taking heed, by comparing those states with their kinds of states of the Prophet (ﷺ), and so that they may come to see that what they knew him for of pure qualities before his mission, and the rectifying of his conduct, and his assistance in the calamities of truth, and his marriage to the best woman among his people, are only singular qualities in him among his people, and are only flashes for the pouring of the cloud of revelation upon him. And God knows best where He places His message. And so that the Muslims may follow the good example set by the character of the people of prophethood and righteousness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verses 26–28 (part 1 of 2):

﴿One of the two women said: "O father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy."﴾ ﴿He said: "Indeed, I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine on condition that you serve me for eight years. But if you complete ten, it is from you. And I do not wish to burden you. You will find me, God willing, among the righteous."﴾ ﴿He said: "That is between me and you. Whichever of the two terms I fulfill, there will be no injustice against me. And God is Witness over what we say."﴾

He omitted what Musa received from Shu'ayb in terms of reward by way of his hospitality and feeding him, and moved on to the offer of one of the two women to her father that he hire him for work with his livestock, since there was no man in their household who could do that, and their father had grown old. When she saw his trustworthiness and piety, she saw that he was the best one to be hired for work with them, owing to his strength for the work and his trustworthiness.

The ta' in "abati" (my father) is a substitute for the ya' of the first person in the vocative specifically, and it may be pronounced with a kasra, and this is how the majority recited it. It may also be pronounced with a fatha, and this is how Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far recited it.

The clause ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾ is a reason for her advice to hire him, meaning: because one like him is the one who should be hired. It came in a comprehensive, unrestricted expression as a proverb, because of its generality and its exact correspondence to reality without exception. The definite article in "al-qawiyy al-amin" (the strong, the trustworthy) is for the genus, intended in the sense of generality. The address in "man istajarta" (whom you hire) is directed to Shu'ayb, and is suitable to include everyone who is fit to be addressed, so that the saying may be fully valid to be sent forth as a proverb. Thus the estimate is: whoever hires the one who hires. "Man" is a relative pronoun in the sense of the definite by the article of genus, since the relative clause here does not intend a specific description of a particular individual.

The placing of "best of whom you hire" as the predicate-subject, by making it a noun, while making "al-qawiyy al-amin" the predicate, is equally valid to make "al-qawiyy al-amin" the subject, since both are equal in definiteness, in that the definiteness in the relative clause after "khayr" and in the definite article here both intend generality in both. So what is given precedence in the two parts of the sentence is what is more important and deserving of attention, namely the best of hired workers; because the sentence was brought as a justification for the statement "hire him," so the description of the worker is more important in the context of its justification, and the hearer's soul is more eager to learn his condition.

The coming of this generality right after speaking of a specific person indicates that the one spoken of is among those covered by that generality. This was in line with the core of eloquence, since attributing trustworthiness and strength to this person spoken of is establishing the ruling with evidence. So the estimate of the meaning of the speech is: hire him, for he is strong and trustworthy, and indeed the best one who hires a hired worker is the strong and trustworthy. Thus the sentence contained the special feature of placing the more important first, the brevity of omission, and the rhetorical mode, and with this it fulfilled the full requirement of the situation, being eloquent to the limit of inimitability.

It is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "I complain to God of the weakness of the trustworthy and the treachery of the strong." He meant: I ask Him to support me with a strong, trustworthy person whom I may rely upon.

The demonstrative in His words "hatayn" (these two) refers to the two women for whom he watered (the flocks), if both were present together, to the exclusion of the other daughters of Shu'ayb, because the matter is connected to their affair; or the demonstrative refers to them because they were present in Musa's mind, given the recency of his watering for them, if the other was absent at that time.

In this is the permissibility of a man offering his female ward to one who would marry her, out of desire for his righteousness. He left to Musa the choice of one of them, because he had known them, and the one Musa chose was Safurah, who was the younger, as came in the narration of Abu Dharr from the Prophet (ﷺ). He chose her rather than her sister because he knew her manners through her modesty and her speech, and this was a preference for her in his eyes.

This offer was before the conclusion of the marriage contract, so there is no ignorance of the one contracted upon in it. His words ﴿on condition that you serve me for eight years﴾: the particle "'ala" (on) is among the forms of conditions in contracts. "Ta'jurani" is the present tense of "ajarahu," like "nasarahu," when he is a hired worker for him. "Hijaj" is the plural of "hijjah," with a kasra on the ha', which means a year, derived from the name "hajj," because the Hajj occurs every year, and the season of Hajj falls in the last month of the Arabic year.

The binding of making his marriage conditional on the hiring contract between them is an offer from him to Musa, and not yet a marriage contract nor a hiring contract until Musa agrees. In this offer there is evidence for the question of combining a marriage contract with a hiring contract. The root of this question in the Sunnah is the hadith of the woman who offered herself to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not marry her, but married her to a man who was present in his assembly, and he had nothing to give her as dower, so he married her to him for what he had of the Qur'an, that is, on condition that he teach it to her.

The well-known position of the school of Malik is that a condition attached to a marriage contract, if it contradicts the nature of the marriage contract, is void, and the marriage is annulled before consummation and stands after it with the customary dower (mahr al-mithl). As for a condition that does not contradict the marriage contract, the marriage is not annulled because of it, but the condition is nullified. It is also reported from Malik: all conditions are disliked at the outset, but if they occur, they stand. Ashhab and Asbagh said: the condition is permissible, and Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi chose this, and it is the truth, because of the verse and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The conditions most worthy of being fulfilled are those by which you have made lawful the private parts."

The apparent meaning of the verse is also that the mentioned hiring was made the dower of the daughter. It is possible that what was stipulated was only the binding of the hiring, and as for the dower, it follows what is regarded in their law as a pillar of marriage, and laws may differ in the meanings of legal realities. If we take the apparent meaning of the verse, it indicates that they made the dower the benefits of the husband's service to Shu'ayb, and it is possible that this was with her consent, since she heard and remained silent, based on customs accepted among them, that her father would benefit from those services.

It is possible that it was for the woman's guardian by original right, if he was the one entitled to the dower in that law, since the customs of nations differ regarding the marrying off of their wards. And since the verse contains generality, it is not sufficient as a proof for the permissibility of making a woman's dower the benefits of her husband's labor. So the question of the validity of making the dower a hiring contract returns to derivation from the principles of the Shari'ah, and entry under the general meaning of dower, since the benefits of hiring have value, so there is no barrier to making them a dower. The verified position of the school of Malik is that it is disliked but stands. Al-Shafi'i and 'Abd al-Malik ibn Habib of the Malikis permitted it. Abu Hanifah said: it is not permissible to make the dower the benefits of a free person, but it is permissible for it to be the benefits of a slave. He did not see in the verse a proof, because according to him it may be that the marriage fulfilled its conditions, so the generality entered into it. Ibn al-Qasim, one of Malik's companions, agreed with him.

Since the ruling of the law of those before us is disputed as to whether it is a law for us, it was a disputed proof among the scholars of usul al-fiqh, and the generality that entered this verse added weakness to it, so it is necessary to return to other evidences from the law of Islam. The evidence for permissibility is included under the general meaning of dower. If the benefits made as dower are obtained before consummation, the matter is clear; but if some or all of them are not realized except after consummation, as in this verse, the matter returns to marriage with a deferred dower, which is disliked but not void, and to hiring for a consideration that is not divisible by dividing the work. So if the hired worker does not complete the work in this case, it returns to the question of a worker being unable to do the work after having received the wage. It is reported in the Sahih, and in the hadith of the woman who gave herself to the Prophet (ﷺ), that he did not accept her, and a man of his companions said to him: "If you have no need of her, marry her to me." He said: "Do you have anything to give her as dower?" ... until he said to him (ﷺ): "Seek, even an iron ring." He said: "I have nothing, not even an iron ring." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "What do you have of the Qur'an?" He said: "I have such-and-such surah and such-and-such surah," naming surahs. He said to him: "I have married her to you for what you have of the Qur'an." And in one narration, the Prophet ordered him to teach her twenty verses of what he had of the Qur'an, and she would be his wife. If this addition is authentic, the hadith is in accordance with what is in this verse, and it is evidence for the validity of making the dower a hiring for work. If it is not authentic, as is well known in the books of Sahih, then the story is a particular case, confined to its specific instance.

The verse does not address the work for which he was hired. The Book of Exodus mentions that he herded the sheep of Jethro, who is Shu'ayb, but the Qur'an has no purpose in explaining that. The verse does not address the wage, and you know that the apparent meaning is that it was his marrying off of the daughter. If we do not take this apparent meaning, the verse does not address the wage, since there is no purpose in it from the narration of the story, so it follows what is customary among them regarding the wages of works, and tribes had customs in that. I found, since the beginning of this fourteenth century, that a shepherd of sheep receives each year a shirt and sandals, called "balghah," and similar things, which I cannot specify now.

His words ﴿If you complete ten, it is from you﴾ made that matter subject to Musa, as a favor from him in choosing him and entrusting him to what his condition would be at the end of the eight years, out of desire for the increase.

The "min" is for origin. "'Inda" is used figuratively for the self and essence, and the prepositional phrase is the predicate of a deleted subject, and the estimate is: the completion of the ten is from yourself, meaning not from me. The meaning is that completion is not included in the contract, which is binding on both sides, so the implication of the adverbial phrase is considered here.

Malik argued from His words ﴿Indeed, I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine﴾ that a father has the right to marry off his virgin daughter without her permission. This is taking the apparent meaning, since it did not address seeking her permission. Those who prohibit this may say: the absence of mention of it does not require its non-occurrence.

His words ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the righteous﴾ mean the righteous among people in good dealing and gentleness of manner. He intended by this to make his character known to his companion, and this is not the self-praise that is forbidden, because what is forbidden is what the speaker intends by boasting and self-glorification. As for what is for the purpose of religion or dealing, that is established for a good reason, as Yusuf said: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land; indeed I am a knowing guardian﴾ [Yusuf: 55].

"Ashuqqa 'alayka" means: I would be burdensome to you, that is, impose on you a hardship. Hardship means difficulty, fatigue, and hardship in work. The original usage is to describe toilsome work as burdensome, so attributing "ashuqqa" to his self is a metaphorical attribution, since he is the cause of the hardship, meaning: I do not wish to stipulate on you what involves your hardship. This is from the leniency mentioned in the hadith: "May God have mercy on a man who is lenient when he sells, lenient when he buys." . . .

The clause ﴿He said: "That is between me and you"﴾ relates Musa's answer to Shu'ayb's speech. The demonstrative refers to what was mentioned, namely ﴿on condition that you serve me for eight years﴾ to the end of it. This is Musa's acceptance of what Shu'ayb required, and with it the contract for the marriage and for the hiring was completed. That is, the matter is as you stipulated upon me and upon yourself. "Bayni wa baynaka" (between me and you) is used figuratively for the meaning of firmness, obligation, and binding, meaning each is responsible for what is his part of the work.

"Ayyamā" is in the accusative governed by "qadaytu" (I fulfil). "Ayyu" is a relative noun of indeterminate reference, like "mā". "Mā" is added after it for emphasis, so that the relative noun resembles conditional particles (asmā' al-shart), because emphasising the indeterminacy in the relative noun gives it generality, and so it resembles the conditional; for this reason it is given a response like the response of the conditional. The whole clause is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause "that is between me and you," because the choice of the end of the term is among what the contract, conveyed by the clause "that is between me and you," includes. "Al-'udwan" with a damma on the 'ayn: transgression against the right, i.e., "so let there be no transgression against me." Thus he negated the category of transgression, of which is the transgression of the one who hires him. Moses called God as witness over himself and over Shu'ayb.

The root of "al-wakil" is: the one to whom a matter is entrusted. Here he means that he was entrusted with fulfilling what they had contracted upon, so that if either of them failed in something, God would be the one who holds him to account. Since "al-wakil" was given the meaning of "al-shahid" (witness), it was made to take the preposition "'ala," whereas its proper construction would have been with "ila."
