Ultimately this led to his being honoured with prophethood, and what it contains of the prophetic qualities that Shu'ayb displayed: love of hospitality, granting security to the fearful, and gentleness in dealings. This is so that the polytheists may take heed from it, if they have any capacity for taking heed, by comparing those states with their kinds of states of the Prophet (ﷺ), and so that they may come to see that what they knew him for of pure qualities before his mission, and the rectifying of his conduct, and his assistance in the calamities of truth, and his marriage to the best woman among his people, are only singular qualities in him among his people, and are only flashes for the pouring of the cloud of revelation upon him. And God knows best where He places His message. And so that the Muslims may follow the good example set by the character of the people of prophethood and righteousness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 29:

﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term and set out with his family, he perceived a fire from the side of the Mount. He said to his family, "Wait here, for I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I can bring you news from it, or a burning brand from the fire, that you may warm yourselves."﴾

The Qur'an does not mention which of the two terms Musa fulfilled, since specifying it has no bearing on the purpose within the context of the story. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "He fulfilled the more complete and the finer of the two, for when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ promised, he acted." That is, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he made a promise, would not deliver from someone like him anything but complete fulfillment. This is also reported from the Prophet ﷺ in narrations with weak chains of transmission, that he was asked about this and answered with the same as what Ibn 'Abbas said.

"Ahl" (family), in its general usage, includes the wife, as in the hadith: "By Allah, I know nothing about my family except good."

In the Book of Exodus, it is mentioned that he asked his father-in-law's permission to go to Egypt to check on his brothers and his kin. The rest of the story has already been discussed in Surah al-Naml, except for the addition of his words: ﴿he perceived a fire from the side of the Mount﴾, which is equivalent to his words here: ﴿when he saw a fire and said to his family, "Wait here, for I have perceived a fire"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 10].

"Al-jidhwah" (a burning brand) has three vowel forms for its initial letter (jim): it is read with kasra by the majority, with fatha by 'Asim, and with damma by Hamzah and Khalaf. It means a thick piece of wood. It has been said to mean this in general, and it has been said to mean a piece of wood that is kindled, which is the meaning in the Qamus. If the first meaning is intended, then describing the brand as "from the fire" is a restrictive description (wasf mukhassas); if the second meaning is intended, then it is a clarifying description (wasf kashif). And "min" (from) in the first case is explicative (bayaniyyah), and in the second case partitive (tab'idiyyah).

[p. 112]

﴿When he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, out of the tree: "O Moses, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"And throw down your staff." But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in flight and did not return. "O Moses, come forward and do not fear. Indeed, you are among the secure."﴾ ﴿"Put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without harm. And draw your arm close to your side against fear."﴾ [al-Qasas: 32]

This has been mentioned previously in Surah al-Naml, except for differences in wording, such as "atāhā" (came to it) here and "jā'ahā" (came to it) there, and "innī anā Allāh" (indeed I am Allah) here, and "innahu anā Allāh" (indeed it is I, Allah) there, with a pronoun referring to the Divine Name in that place and the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n) here. Both are equivalent in position, because the pronoun of the Divine Name signifies something great. His saying here "Lord of the worlds" and his saying there "the Mighty, the Wise." This implies that the three attributes were addressed to him at that time.

The discussion of the wisdom behind mentioning the attribute of God before His command to him to throw down the staff is like the discussion that preceded in Surah al-Naml, because the description "Lord of the worlds" indicates that all creatures are subjugated to Him, so as to steady Moses' heart against the terror of receiving the message.

"Wa-an alqi" (and that you throw down) here and "alqi" (throw down) there, and "usluk" (insert) here and "adkhil" (put) there. This variation is an embellishment (tafannun) in repeating the story, to renew the listener's attentiveness to it. Otherwise, the addition of "from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, out of the tree" is a valley on the slope of Mount Ṭūr. Its shāṭi' (shore) means its side and its bank.

As for describing the shore as "right" (al-ayman): if "al-ayman" is understood as the opposite of "al-aysar" (left), then it is "right" in the sense that it lies on the right of one who faces the qibla, according to the Arab manner of making the qibla the principal direction for fixing location. The Arabs describe directions as right and left and mean this sense. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Upon Qaṭan at al-Shaym, its right-hand rain, and its left-hand upon al-Sitār and Fayḍhul."

On this basis the usage of the Muslims in determining geographical locations and the positions of lands has proceeded, so "al-ayman" means the western side of the mountain, that is, the direction of the sunset from Ṭūr.

[p. 113]

Do you not see that they named Yemen "Yaman" because it lies on the right of one facing the gate of the Ka'ba, and named Syria "Shām" because it lies on the "shām" (left) of one facing its gate, that is, on his left? Thus they took the facing of the Ka'ba as the reference. This is what suits His later saying, "And you were not on the western side."

As for taking it to mean "more right-handed" for Moses, this does not agree with God's saying, "And We appointed for you the right side of Mount Ṭūr" [Ṭā-Hā: 80], since no mention of Moses occurred there.

If it is understood as an elative from "yumn," meaning blessing, then it is like His description of it as "the holy" in Surah al-Nāzi'āt: "When his Lord called to him in the holy valley, Ṭuwā" [al-Nāzi'āt: 16].

"Al-bu'qa" with a dammah on the bāʾ, and it may be pronounced with a fatḥah, is a piece of land distinguished from others.

"Al-mubāraka" (blessed) is because of its being chosen for the descent of revelation upon Moses. His saying "out of the tree" may be connected to the verb "nūdiya" (he was called), so that the tree is the source of this calling, and "min" is for origin, that is, he heard speech coming out of the tree. It may also be a stationary adverbial phrase, a second description of the valley, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), in which case "min" is for contiguity, that is, adjoining the tree, that is, near it, namely the place that adjoins the tree.

The definiteness in "al-shajara" (the tree) is definiteness of the genus, and it departs from indefiniteness to indicate that it is a specific tree. It is not definiteness of previous reference, since the tree was not previously mentioned. In the Torah it is said that this tree was of the bramble kind (which is of the ʿiḍāh shrubs), and it is said it was a hawthorn, and the hawthorn is also among the ʿiḍāh shrubs.

The addition of "aqbil" (come forward) is an explicit statement of the content of His saying "do not fear" in Surah al-Naml, because when he turned back in flight out of fear of the snake, the prohibition against fear indicated the meaning of asking him to come forward. So the discourse there was concise, and here it is expanded, for embellishment in narrating the two accounts. Likewise the addition of "indeed you are among the secure" here, which is not related in Surah al-Naml, is an emphasis on the meaning of "do not fear." In it is an added confirmation of his security, by what is indicated by the emphasis with "inna" and by placing him among those who are secure. This is stronger in confirming security than saying "you are secure," as preceded in His saying "that I should be among the ignorant" [al-Baqara: 67] in Surah al-Baqara.

His saying "And draw your arm close to your side against fear" [al-Qasas: 32]: in it the net meaning derived from its construction is obscure, so it became an area of divergence among the exegetes in clarifying it, and the possible senses of its words were entangled, so that whenever one possible sense of its words was established, another sense conflicted with it. These are the words: "janāḥ" (arm/wing), "rahab" (fear), and the particle "min" (from). So they followed paths that lead to no firm conclusion. These were fully discussed in the speech of al-Qurṭubī and al-Zamakhsharī. Some said: there is an inversion (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr) in the speech, and that His saying "from fear" is connected to His saying "turned back in flight," with "min" being a particle of causation, that is, he turned back because of the cause of fear. This should not be given attention, since there is no reason to invert what they claimed, given the long separation between the verb "walla" (turned back) and "min al-rahab" (from fear).

It was said that "janāḥ" means "hand," but it is not fitting that it be a metaphor for the hand, since this leads either to repeating the meaning of "usluk yadaka fī jaybika" (insert your hand into your bosom), and the conjunction particle prevents the possibility of emphasis. The claim that the repetition is for a difference of purpose between the first and the second, as in al-Kashshāf, is far-fetched. Or it is interpreted as meaning that placing the hand on the chest removes fear, as was reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn 'Abbās and from Mujāhid, and this interpretation is also far-fetched. This is an inclination toward the view that "janāḥ" is a metonymy (majāz mursal) intended to mean the human hand. "Janāḥ" has a literal meaning and figurative usages between metonymy (mursal) and metaphor (isti'āra), and it occurs in the Qur'an and elsewhere in various senses. Its occurrence in some places with a certain meaning does not oblige taking it in that sense wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. Therefore the preferred view is that His saying "and draw your arm close to your side" is an image (tamthīl) depicting the condition of a bird instead of flying away out of fear. This is taken from one of two possibilities mentioned by al-Zamakhsharī, and it is said that its origin belongs to Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī. "Al-rahab" is well known to mean fear, as in His saying "They call upon Us with desire and fear" [al-Anbiyā': 90].

The meaning: refrain from being fearful about the matter of the message. In the speech there is concision, indicated by His saying after it: "He said, 'My Lord, indeed I killed a soul among them, so I fear that they will kill me'" [al-Qaṣaṣ: 33]. So His saying "draw your arm close to your side against fear" has the same meaning as His saying: "They shall not reach you by Our signs; you and whoever follows you are the victors" [al-Qaṣaṣ: 35].

Al-Jumhūr read "al-rahab" with a fatḥah on the rāʾ and the hāʾ. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim and Khalaf read it with a ḍammah on the rāʾ and sukūn on the hāʾ. Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read it with a fatḥah on the rāʾ and sukūn on the hāʾ. These are all eloquent dialects.

[p. 112]

﴿When he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, out of the tree: "O Moses, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"And throw down your staff." But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in flight and did not return. "O Moses, come forward and do not fear. Indeed, you are among the secure."﴾ ﴿"Put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without harm. And draw your arm close to your side against fear."﴾ [al-Qasas: 32]

This has been mentioned previously in Surah al-Naml, except for differences in wording, such as "atāhā" (came to it) here and "jā'ahā" (came to it) there, and "innī anā Allāh" (indeed I am Allah) here, and "innahu anā Allāh" (indeed it is I, Allah) there, with a pronoun referring to the Divine Name in that place and the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n) here. Both are equivalent in position, because the pronoun of the Divine Name signifies something great. His saying here "Lord of the worlds" and his saying there "the Mighty, the Wise." This implies that the three attributes were addressed to him at that time.

The discussion of the wisdom behind mentioning the attribute of God before His command to him to throw down the staff is like the discussion that preceded in Surah al-Naml, because the description "Lord of the worlds" indicates that all creatures are subjugated to Him, so as to steady Moses' heart against the terror of receiving the message.

"Wa-an alqi" (and that you throw down) here and "alqi" (throw down) there, and "usluk" (insert) here and "adkhil" (put) there. This variation is an embellishment (tafannun) in repeating the story, to renew the listener's attentiveness to it. Otherwise, the addition of "from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, out of the tree" is a valley on the slope of Mount Ṭūr. Its shāṭi' (shore) means its side and its bank.

As for describing the shore as "right" (al-ayman): if "al-ayman" is understood as the opposite of "al-aysar" (left), then it is "right" in the sense that it lies on the right of one who faces the qibla, according to the Arab manner of making the qibla the principal direction for fixing location. The Arabs describe directions as right and left and mean this sense. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Upon Qaṭan at al-Shaym, its right-hand rain, and its left-hand upon al-Sitār and Fayḍhul."

On this basis the usage of the Muslims in determining geographical locations and the positions of lands has proceeded, so "al-ayman" means the western side of the mountain, that is, the direction of the sunset from Ṭūr.

[p. 113]

Do you not see that they named Yemen "Yaman" because it lies on the right of one facing the gate of the Ka'ba, and named Syria "Shām" because it lies on the "shām" (left) of one facing its gate, that is, on his left? Thus they took the facing of the Ka'ba as the reference. This is what suits His later saying, "And you were not on the western side."

As for taking it to mean "more right-handed" for Moses, this does not agree with God's saying, "And We appointed for you the right side of Mount Ṭūr" [Ṭā-Hā: 80], since no mention of Moses occurred there.

If it is understood as an elative from "yumn," meaning blessing, then it is like His description of it as "the holy" in Surah al-Nāzi'āt: "When his Lord called to him in the holy valley, Ṭuwā" [al-Nāzi'āt: 16].

"Al-bu'qa" with a dammah on the bāʾ, and it may be pronounced with a fatḥah, is a piece of land distinguished from others.

"Al-mubāraka" (blessed) is because of its being chosen for the descent of revelation upon Moses. His saying "out of the tree" may be connected to the verb "nūdiya" (he was called), so that the tree is the source of this calling, and "min" is for origin, that is, he heard speech coming out of the tree. It may also be a stationary adverbial phrase, a second description of the valley, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), in which case "min" is for contiguity, that is, adjoining the tree, that is, near it, namely the place that adjoins the tree.

The definiteness in "al-shajara" (the tree) is definiteness of the genus, and it departs from indefiniteness to indicate that it is a specific tree. It is not definiteness of previous reference, since the tree was not previously mentioned. In the Torah it is said that this tree was of the bramble kind (which is of the ʿiḍāh shrubs), and it is said it was a hawthorn, and the hawthorn is also among the ʿiḍāh shrubs.

The addition of "aqbil" (come forward) is an explicit statement of the content of His saying "do not fear" in Surah al-Naml, because when he turned back in flight out of fear of the snake, the prohibition against fear indicated the meaning of asking him to come forward. So the discourse there was concise, and here it is expanded, for embellishment in narrating the two accounts. Likewise the addition of "indeed you are among the secure" here, which is not related in Surah al-Naml, is an emphasis on the meaning of "do not fear." In it is an added confirmation of his security, by what is indicated by the emphasis with "inna" and by placing him among those who are secure. This is stronger in confirming security than saying "you are secure," as preceded in His saying "that I should be among the ignorant" [al-Baqara: 67] in Surah al-Baqara.

His saying "And draw your arm close to your side against fear" [al-Qasas: 32]: in it the net meaning derived from its construction is obscure, so it became an area of divergence among the exegetes in clarifying it, and the possible senses of its words were entangled, so that whenever one possible sense of its words was established, another sense conflicted with it. These are the words: "janāḥ" (arm/wing), "rahab" (fear), and the particle "min" (from). So they followed paths that lead to no firm conclusion. These were fully discussed in the speech of al-Qurṭubī and al-Zamakhsharī. Some said: there is an inversion (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr) in the speech, and that His saying "from fear" is connected to His saying "turned back in flight," with "min" being a particle of causation, that is, he turned back because of the cause of fear. This should not be given attention, since there is no reason to invert what they claimed, given the long separation between the verb "walla" (turned back) and "min al-rahab" (from fear).

It was said that "janāḥ" means "hand," but it is not fitting that it be a metaphor for the hand, since this leads either to repeating the meaning of "usluk yadaka fī jaybika" (insert your hand into your bosom), and the conjunction particle prevents the possibility of emphasis. The claim that the repetition is for a difference of purpose between the first and the second, as in al-Kashshāf, is far-fetched. Or it is interpreted as meaning that placing the hand on the chest removes fear, as was reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn 'Abbās and from Mujāhid, and this interpretation is also far-fetched. This is an inclination toward the view that "janāḥ" is a metonymy (majāz mursal) intended to mean the human hand. "Janāḥ" has a literal meaning and figurative usages between metonymy (mursal) and metaphor (isti'āra), and it occurs in the Qur'an and elsewhere in various senses. Its occurrence in some places with a certain meaning does not oblige taking it in that sense wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. Therefore the preferred view is that His saying "and draw your arm close to your side" is an image (tamthīl) depicting the condition of a bird instead of flying away out of fear. This is taken from one of two possibilities mentioned by al-Zamakhsharī, and it is said that its origin belongs to Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī. "Al-rahab" is well known to mean fear, as in His saying "They call upon Us with desire and fear" [al-Anbiyā': 90].

The meaning: refrain from being fearful about the matter of the message. In the speech there is concision, indicated by His saying after it: "He said, 'My Lord, indeed I killed a soul among them, so I fear that they will kill me'" [al-Qaṣaṣ: 33]. So His saying "draw your arm close to your side against fear" has the same meaning as His saying: "They shall not reach you by Our signs; you and whoever follows you are the victors" [al-Qaṣaṣ: 35].

Al-Jumhūr read "al-rahab" with a fatḥah on the rāʾ and the hāʾ. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim and Khalaf read it with a ḍammah on the rāʾ and sukūn on the hāʾ. Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read it with a fatḥah on the rāʾ and sukūn on the hāʾ. These are all eloquent dialects.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 32:

Page 115
﴿So these two are proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Indeed they are a people who are defiantly disobedient.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of His saying, ﴿And draw your arm close to your side against fear﴾. The reference is to the staff and the whiteness of the hand. The burhan (proof) is the decisive argument. The "min" (from) indicates the starting point, and the "ila" (to) indicates the figurative endpoint, meaning: two arguments upon which I send you with them to them.

The clause ﴿Indeed they are a people who are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Naml: 12] is a reason (ta'lil) for the clause ﴿So these two are proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, because it implies that they are of such a kind that they are confronted with proofs. He then explains that the cause of this is that disbelief has become firmly rooted in their souls, to the point that it became like an innate disposition in them, and their collective identity as a people is sustained by it, as indicated by His saying "they were" (kanu). As for His saying "a people" (qawman), it is as previously explained in His saying, ﴿Surely there are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] in Surat al-Baqarah. And fisq (defiant disobedience) means associating partners with Allah.

The majority of readers recited (fa-dhanika) with a light nun, from (dhanika), according to the original form of the dual. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ruways from Ya'qub recited it with a doubled nun in (fa-dhannika), and this is the dialect of Tamim and Qays. The grammarians explained it by saying that doubling the nun is a compensation for the alif in (dha) and (ta), which were elided for the sake of the dual form. In al-Kashshaf, it is stated that the doubling is a compensation for the lam of distance that attaches to the demonstrative noun, and for this reason he said: "The light form is the dual of dhaka, and the doubled form is the dual of dhalika." And this is the better view.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 33:

﴿He said: "My Lord, indeed I killed a soul from among them, so I fear that they will kill me."﴾

The emphasis (al-ta'kid) was applied to what is usual in the use of such reports that are unusual, so that the listener may be certain of their occurrence. Otherwise, God already knew that when He said to him, "Draw your hand close to your side against fear" (according to the reading of al-rahab, i.e., terror). The meaning is: "so I fear that they will mention my killing of the Copt and then kill me." This is like an excuse, and he knows that the message of God cannot be escaped by an excuse; but he wanted to be in a divine security from his enemies. This is an allusive supplication (ta'rid bi-al-du'a'), and a preface to asking that he be strengthened by his brother Harun.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 34:

Page 116
﴿And my brother Aaron, he is more eloquent in tongue than I, so send him with me as a helper (ridan) to confirm me. Indeed I fear that they will deny me.﴾ This is an explicit request which shows that Musa did not intend by the first (statement) a disavowal of conveying the message, but rather he wished to have it reinforced by his brother. He specified him and did not ask for just any supporter, either because of his knowledge of his trustworthiness and his sincerity toward God and toward his brother, and his knowledge of the eloquence of his tongue.

And "ridan" with a light pronunciation is like "ridʾin" with a hamza at its end: an aid, support. Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read "ridan" with a light pronunciation. The rest read "ridʾan" with the hamza, according to the original form.

And "yuṣaddiqnī" was read by the majority in the jussive, as a response to the imperative in his saying "fa-arsilhu maʿī" (so send him with me). ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read it in the nominative, on the basis that the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun (hāʾ) in "arsilhu."

The meaning of his confirming him (taṣdīqihi iyyāhu) is that he would be a cause of Pharaoh and his chiefs confirming him, by clarifying the proofs which Musa would present in the setting of disputing with Pharaoh, as his saying "he is more eloquent in tongue than I, so send him with me as a helper to confirm me" requires. For he made the request that he be sent with him conditional upon his being more eloquent in tongue, and made his confirmation the answer to that request or a circumstantial clause of what is requested. So it is a derivation upon a derivation, and it is inevitable that its meaning be suited to the meaning of what it derives from, namely that he is more eloquent in tongue. Eloquence has no effect on confirmation except in this sense.

Confirmation does not mean that he says to them, "Musa has spoken the truth," because that is something in which the eloquent and the one with a speech impediment are equal. Therefore the attribution of confirmation to Aaron is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), since he is its cause, while those who truly confirm are those in whom knowledge arises that Musa is truthful in what he has brought.

The clause "indeed I fear that they will deny me" is a justification for the request for his support with Aaron. This is a second fear of denial, while the first was a fear of being killed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 35:

Page 117
﴿He said: "We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and We will give you both authority, so they shall not reach you. With Our signs, you two and whoever follows you shall be the victors."﴾

Allah granted him both of his supplications and added to them a favour beyond what he had asked. The granting of the second supplication is in His saying, "We will strengthen your arm through your brother," and the granting of the first is in His saying, "so they shall not reach you," and the favour is in His saying, "and We will give you both authority." Thus Musa was given the same capacity as Harun to establish proof, when He said, "and We will give you both authority." This is indicated by the arguments that Musa, peace be upon him, spoke in his debate with Fir'awn, as in Surat al-Shu'ara' and here, and by what he addressed to the Children of Israel, as related in Surat al-A'raf. It is not reported in the Qur'an that Harun spoke the call to Fir'awn, while Musa had asked Allah, exalted is He, to loosen a knot from his tongue, as in Surat Ta-Ha. And there is no doubt that Allah answered him.

Al-shadd (ash-shadd) is binding. The manner of one who works with a limb, when he wants to make it perform a tiring task, is to bind it so that it does not come apart or suffer a break. The opposite of this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: "And when they regretted (sa-qut fi aydihim)," and the saying of people: "He broke his arm (fatta fi 'adudihi)." The brother here is placed in the position of the binding by which the arm is tied. The meaning is that he supports him with his eloquence, so attaching the strengthening to the binding is included under the figurative use of the rational (majaz 'aqli). All of this is an image: the clarification of his proof is compared to the strengthening of one who wishes to undertake a great deed, by having his hand bound, which is the ta'yid (support) that has become common in the sense of aid and assistance. Otherwise, ta'yid is also derived from the hand (yad). The original meaning of ayyada is "he made a hand," so it is a metaphor for bringing about aid.

Al-sultan here is a verbal noun meaning dominance over hearts and souls, that is, awe in the hearts of the enemies and terror of you two, just as He cast love for Musa into the hearts when the family of Fir'awn picked him up. The literal meaning of sultan was previously discussed in His saying, exalted is He: "We have indeed given his heir authority" (17:33), in Surat al-Isra'.

Upon the granting of authority, He says, "so they shall not reach you," meaning they shall not harm you with evil, which is killing or the like. Thus "reach" is used metaphorically for striking. The meaning is striking with evil, by the indication of the context.

His saying, "With Our signs, you two and whoever follows you shall be the victors," may permit that "with Our signs" be connected to a deleted element indicated by His saying, "to Fir'awn and his chiefs" (7:103), its estimate being: go with Our signs, in the manner estimated in His saying, exalted is He, "among nine signs to Fir'awn" (27:12), and His saying in Surat al-Naml after His saying, "Insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without harm, among nine signs" (27:12), meaning: go among nine signs. This is stated explicitly in His saying in Surat al-Shu'ara': "He said: 'No! Go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed, We are with you, listening'" (26:15).

It may also be connected to "We will give you both authority," meaning authority over them by Our signs, so that their dread of you two becomes one of Our signs. It may also be connected to "so they shall not reach you," meaning they will be turned away from harming you by signs from Us, like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I have been helped by terror (nusirtu bil-ru'b)." It may also be connected to "the victors," meaning you will overcome and subdue them by Our signs with which We support you both. Placing the prepositional phrase before its governed element in this aspect is for emphasis on the greatness of the signs with which We support you both. And placing the prepositional phrase before its governed element in this aspect is for emphasis on the greatness of the signs which the two of them will be given. It is also possible that the particle bi- is an oath particle, affirming to them that they are the victors and steadying their hearts.

In all these aspects, the signs include the observed extraordinary events of custom, such as the nine signs, and they include the hidden miracles, such as the turning of Fir'awn's people away from proceeding to harm them, despite their power and the enmity they harboured, such that, were it not for the diversion from Allah, they would have destroyed Musa and his brother.

The lesson to be drawn from this part of the story is an alert that prophethood is an outpouring from Allah upon whomever He chooses from among His servants; that the message of Muhammad ﷺ was like the message of Musa, which came to him suddenly, so Muhammad was called in the cave of Mount Hira, just as Musa was called at the side of Mount Tur; that he was seized by fear just as Musa was; that Allah steadied him just as He steadied Musa; and that Allah suffices him against his enemies just as He sufficed Musa against his enemies.

**[Page 119]**

﴿So when Moses came to them with Our signs, as clear proofs, they said, "This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we have not heard of this among our earliest forefathers."﴾ What lay between God's calling out to him and his presence before Pharaoh has been left out of the account of events, because no lesson depends on it. The coming with the signs is attributed to Moses, peace be upon him, alone, and not to Aaron, because he is the original Messenger, through whose hands the miracles came. This differs from His saying, "﴿Go, then, with Our signs﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 15]," in Surat al-Shu'ara, and His saying, "﴿With Our signs, you two and whoever follows you will be the victors﴾ [al-Qasas: 35]," where He linked the signs to both of them through their two pronouns. This is because the sense of association (mulabasah) is broad: whoever accompanies the bearer of the signs is associated with them.

The "clear signs" (al-ayat al-bayyinat) are the extraordinary events that break customary norms (khawariq al-'adat) which he displayed. That is, he came to them with them, one sign after another, in various situations. At each sign they said, "﴿This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we have not heard of this among our earliest forefathers.﴾"

Al-muftara means "the fabricated," that is, "the false." The meaning of the signs being "fabricated magic" is that it is false to claim that they come from God, and that they are magic is concealed.

The demonstrative in their saying "and we have not heard of this" refers to the claim of messengerhood from God, because that is what can be heard. As for the signs, they cannot be heard. Thus the two demonstratives have different referents. The sense is: "We have not heard of anyone calling our forefathers to what you call to." The sentence therefore contains an omitted noun, indicated by the adverb of time, so that the meaning is "in the time of our forefathers." They made the absence of such a call reaching their forefathers, so that it would reach them through their earliest forefathers, a proof of its falsehood. This is the last refuge to which one who has been refuted and defeated resorts when he cannot find any acceptable proof to repel the truth. So he turns to such fabrications and stupefying falsehoods.

[Page 120]

﴿Moses said: "My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him, and who will have the good outcome of the abode. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper."﴾ When they made their statement denying him, and relied on their claim that what Moses brought was something their forefathers had never known, Moses answered their speech with its like in confirming his truthfulness. He said that God knows it, so the knowledge of their forefathers counts for nothing beside the knowledge of God. When they held to the knowledge of their forefathers, Moses held to the knowledge of God, Exalted is He. Thus Moses argued on his own behalf and did not leave that to Aaron.

The usage required that Moses' words be reported with the verb "qala" (said) without a conjunction (waw), as is the case in reporting dialogues, as we have mentioned more than once. This was departed from here by bringing the conjunction in the reading of the majority, other than Ibn Kathir, because he intended here to balance the argument of Pharaoh's chiefs with the argument of Moses, so that the hearer would see the difference between them in hitting upon the truth, and would perceive the corruption of one and the soundness of the other. Things are made clear by their opposites. For this reason the sentence was joined with a conjunction, following the original rule rather than the more common usage, to draw attention to considering the meaning of both. Ibn Kathir read "qala Musa" without a waw, which is also how it is written in the codex of the people of Makkah, following the original form of reporting dialogues. From the combination of the two readings, the requirements of both aspects of the reporting are fulfilled. God is referred to by the attribute of lordship (rubbubiyyah) joined to His pronoun, to make explicit that the One who knows the truth is the true God, not their supposed deities.

It appears that the Copts had in their language no name for the true, necessarily existent Lord, but only names of supposed gods.

In the case of ﴿who has come with guidance﴾ [al-Qasas: 85] he used the past tense, and in the case of ﴿who will have the good outcome of the abode﴾ [al-An'am: 135] he used the present tense. This is because the coming with guidance, whether true or supposed, is a matter that has already been realised and has passed, whether the one who brought it was Moses or their forefathers and scholars. As for the existence of the good outcome of the abode for someone, it is awaited, to be manifested later. So in his saying ﴿My Lord knows best who has come with guidance﴾ there is a calling of God as witness and a fair statement, meaning: my Lord knows best who it is that has come with guidance, whether it is I or you, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24].

In His saying ﴿and who will have the good outcome of the abode﴾ there is a committing of the matter to what will become apparent of the victory of one of the two parties over the other, and it is a counter-threat with the warning of the evil end awaiting them.

And ﴿ʿāqibat al-dār﴾ ("the good outcome of the abode") is a phrase that has become like a proverb for the final good after hardship, comparing the one who does a deed to the traveller seeking pasture who reaches a land of fertility and settles there: ﴿And they will say: "Praise be to God"﴾ [Fatir: 34] ﴿"who has settled us in the abode of permanence from His bounty"﴾ [Fatir: 35]. The original form of ﴿ʿāqibat al-dār﴾ is "al-dār al-ʿāqibah" (the abode that comes after), and the adjective was then made into a genitive construction with the noun it qualifies.

And al-ʿāqibah is the state that comes after (ʿāqibah), that is, that which follows something else. This word therefore indicates a change of state to something better, which is why it is not applied to a praiseworthy outcome in every case. His saying ﴿So you will surely know who will have the good outcome of the abode﴾ [al-An'am: 135] has already been mentioned in Surat al-An'am, and in Surat al-Ra'd His saying ﴿For them is the good outcome of the abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 22], and His saying "And the disbeliever will know to whom belongs the good outcome of the abode."

The majority read (takūnu) with a feminine (taʾnīth) ta' above the line, following the original feminine gender of the phrase ﴿ʿāqibat al-dār﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a ya' below the line, which is permissible for a verb whose subject is a figurative (majazi) feminine.

All of this is confirmed by the clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾, which indicates his confidence that he is upon the truth. This breaks their resolve and casts the terror of doubt about salvation into their hearts. The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ ("indeed he") is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), since the clause following it has a meaning that gives the matter weight and significance.

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 28, verse 38:

﴿Pharaoh said, "O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself. So kindle for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay, and make for me a tower that I may look upon the god of Moses, though I think him among the liars."﴾

The speech of Pharaoh related here takes place in a setting other than the dialogue with Moses. It is a speech he addressed to the people of his assembly after the exchange with Moses. For this reason it is related with the conjunction (*harf al-'atf*), linking one narrative to another. This is a narrative of a dialogue between Pharaoh and his chiefs concerning Moses' call, so the conjunction is appropriate, as is clear.

Pharaoh intended by his address to his chiefs to confirm them in the belief in his divinity. So he said, ﴿I know of no god for you other than myself﴾, as a refutation of Moses' statement related in Surat al-Shu'ara, ﴿[Moses] said, "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones"﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 26], and his statement there, ﴿"Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you are certain"﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 24]. Thus Pharaoh showed them that Moses' call had not found acceptance with him and that he did not believe in it, so he said, ﴿I know of no god for you other than myself﴾.

The intended meaning of the negation of his knowledge of such a god is the negation of the existence of any god other than himself, by way of *kinayah* (metonymy), showing them that his knowledge encompasses everything real; so if there were another god, he would know it.

The object of the negation of the existence of another god besides him is the negation of the existence of the god whom Moses affirmed, who is the Creator of all. As for the gods they claim, these are among the things that Pharaoh's divinity entails, because Pharaoh, in their view, is the manifestation of the gods they assert, since in their belief he is the son of the gods and the essence of their secret, and "all the game is in the belly of the wild ass" (*kullu al-sayd fi jawf al-fara*).

When Moses said that the true god is the Lord of the heavens, Pharaoh supposed, in a distorted conception, that the realm of this Lord is the sky. So he based on the negation of any other god, and on the presumption that the alleged Lord resides in the sky, his command to Haman, his minister, to build for him a tower that would reach the clouds of the sky, so that he might see the god whom Moses claimed. When he did not find him, he returned to his people and established for them the non-existence of a god in the sky by way of direct observation. He wanted to appear to his people in the guise of one who seeks the truth and thoroughly investigates the worlds, so that when he later informed his people that the result of his search had turned out to be the lie of Moses, they would increase in confidence in the falsity of Moses' words, upon him be peace.

In this handful of sophistic disputation there is a clear indication of the poor ordering of his thinking and that of his chiefs, or the extent of his trickery and the weakness of his people's opinions.

"Haman" is a title or a name for Pharaoh's minister, as was mentioned just above. By his words ﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay﴾ he intended that Haman should order the workers to fire the clay so that it becomes baked brick (*al-ajurr*), and build with it. He therefore referred to the building by its preliminaries, namely the kindling of the kilns to dry the clay made into bricks. They used to build their houses with baked brick, making moulds of clay which hardened when fired, and they would mix it with straw so that it would hold together before being put into the kiln (*tannur*), as the description of the making of clay is given in the fifth chapter of the Book of Exodus.

He began his command with the first of the tasks of building, to indicate concern for starting at the earliest time of the order, because the beginning of construction is delayed until after its materials are brought. Therefore he ordered him to begin bringing those materials, the first of which is the kindling, that is, lighting the ovens to fire the bricks. He expressed the baked brick by "the clay" because it is the basis of making the brick, and it is a known clay. It seems he did not order him to build with stone and lime, intending to hasten the erection of this high tower, since lasting durability through the solidity of its construction across the ages is not what was sought; rather the aim was swiftness in reaching its height so that people would witness it, and despair would arise, and then it would be torn down from its foundation.

He turned away from expressing it as "baked brick." Ibn al-Athir said in *al-Mathal al-Sa'ir*: "Because the word *ajurr* and similar words such as *qarmad* and *tub* are common words, so it was mentioned with the word *tin* (clay)." End of quotation. What appears from Ibn al-Athir's words is that the shift to *tin* was because it is lighter and more eloquent.

The attribution of the kindling upon the clay to Haman is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), on the basis that he is the one who gives the order for that, as they say: "The sultan built a bridge," and "al-Mansur built Baghdad."

Haman was mentioned just above and was Pharaoh's minister. In past eras, the commands of kings used to be issued through the minister, so the minister was the one who executed the king's commands through his aides, from scribes, commanders, agents and the like, each in what suits him.

The *sarh* (ṣarḥ) is a lofty palace, and it was mentioned previously at His saying, ﴿It was said to her, "Enter the ṣarḥ"﴾ [al-Naml: 44] in Surat al-Naml.

He hoped to reach the sky by this tower, where the god of Moses resides. This is from the corruption of his thinking, since he supposed that the sky can be reached by such a tower, however long its construction, and that God is settled in a place within the sky.

The *ittila'* (iṭṭilā') is a strong, laboured rising, because of its difficulty.

His words ﴿and I think him among the liars﴾ employ the word *zann* (ẓann, "thought/supposition") in the sense of certainty. So his attempt to reach the sky was to increase the verification of his supposition; or because he wanted to persuade his people of that. Perhaps he intended by this to disguise the matter from his people, so as to place in their belief that Moses claimed God is in a specific place which the height of his tower reaches. Then he would make the failure to find the god at that height a proof of the non-existence of the god Moses claimed. The beliefs of the people of misguidance were founded on corrupt imagination, and their proofs were founded on the deception of the impostors among their leaders.

His words ﴿among the liars﴾ indicate that he counts him among the group whose nature is lying, as was mentioned previously in His saying, ﴿[Moses] said, "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant"﴾ [al-Baqara: 67].

The Qur'an does not mention that this tower was built, and it is not one of the pyramids, because the pyramids were built of stone, not baked brick, and because they were made into tombs for the Pharaohs who built them. The commentators differed on whether the building of this tower took place and was completed or not. Some related that it was completed and Pharaoh ascended to its top, came down, and claimed that he had killed the Lord of Moses. Some related that the tower collapsed before its construction was completed, killing a great number of the builders and soldiers. Some related that he never began its construction. A different interpretation of the verse has occurred to me, which I will mention in Surat al-Mu'min.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 39:

﴿And he was arrogant, he and his soldiers, in the land without right, and they thought that they would not be returned to Us.﴾ Al-istikbar (arrogance) is stronger than al-kibr (pride); that is, he became exceedingly arrogant when he aspired to reach the Great Lord as the dominant one reaches his equal.

Junuduhu (his soldiers): his followers. His arrogance is the origin, and the arrogance of his soldiers follows from his arrogance, because they follow him and receive from him the beliefs he dictates to them.

Al-ard (the land) may refer to a specific land, namely the land of Egypt, or it may refer to the genus, that is, in the world of the earth, since they were, at that time, the greatest of the nations of the earth.

His saying ﴿without right﴾ is a necessary circumstantial clause attached to its operator, since arrogance can only be without right.

His saying ﴿and they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾ is known by implication from their disbelief in Allah, but He stated it explicitly because of the importance of refuting it, so the implication of the implicit meaning is not relied upon for it. Moreover, in stating it explicitly there is an allusion to the polytheists, that they and he are equal, so let them place themselves in whatever station of the stations of the people of disbelief. Abu Jahl was called by the Muslims "the Pharaoh of this nation," taking this from the allusions of the Qur'an.

The meaning of that is: they thought that there is no resurrection and no return, because they disbelieved in that to which they would return. The mention of ﴿to Us﴾ is for depicting the actual reality and is not a restrictive condition, so it should not be imagined that they denied the resurrection but did not deny the existence of Allah, like the polytheists. The placement of ﴿ilaynā﴾ before its operator is for the sake of the verse-ending (fasila).

It is also permissible that the meaning be: and they thought that they were secure from returning into the grip of Our power, as indicated by His saying in Surah ash-Shu'ara' ﴿He said: The Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if you are certain﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 24] ﴿He said to those around him: Do you not listen?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 25], in amazement at that. According to this possibility, the allusion to the polytheists remains as it is, for they thought that they were secure from annihilation, so they said: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky."

Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (لا يرجعون) with a fatha on the yā' of the imperfect, from raja'a. The rest read it with a damma on it, from (أُرجِعَ), when the act of returning is done to them.

So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea; so see how was the end of the wrongdoers. That is, they thought they would not be returned to Us, so We hastened their destruction. This is indeed a form of "return to God," since it is a return to His judgment and His punishment, and it is followed by the return of their souls to His punishment. Therefore, after mentioning their thought, He appended the information that he and his soldiers were seized. He made this appended clause like a parenthetical insertion between the narration of their circumstances.

In al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, Zamakhshari's commentary), this is counted among the sublime (fakhm) forms of speech, because it indicates the greatness of God's majesty. His words "So We cast them into the sea" contain an implicit metaphor (istiʿara makniyya): he and his soldiers are likened to pebbles that someone takes in his hand and throws into the sea. If the "seizing" (akhdh) is taken in its literal sense, it also contains an implicit metaphor, because it entails a comparison with a handful grasped by the hand, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the earth and the mountains will be lifted and crushed with one blow﴾ [al-Haqqa: 14], and His words: ﴿while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Zumar: 67]. It is also possible to consider all of this an allegorical metaphor (istiʿara tamthiliyya), as is not hidden.

His words "So see how was the end of the wrongdoers" are an exhortation (iʿtibar) through the evil of their end because of their wronging themselves by disbelief, and their wronging the Messenger by arrogance in refusing to listen to his call. This is the locus of the lesson (ʿibra) in relating this story, so that the polytheists may take heed: they should compare the situation of Muhammad's (ﷺ) call with the situation of Moses's (peace be upon him) call, and compare their own situation with that of Pharaoh, and thus be certain that the punishment which befell Pharaoh and his people will inevitably befall them. This is among the whole of the lesson in this part of the story, beginning from His words, exalted is He: ﴿So when Moses came to them with Our clear signs﴾ [al-Qasas: 36], so that people may take heed that the condition of the people of misguidance is one: they meet the callers to goodness with aversion, arrogance, and the fabrication of excuses. Just as Pharaoh and his people said ﴿This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we have not heard of this among our earliest forefathers﴾ [al-Qasas: 36], Quraysh said ﴿Rather, he has invented it; rather, he is a poet﴾ [al-Anbiya: 5], and they said ﴿We have not heard of this in the latter religion﴾ [Sad: 7], meaning the one we found (our fathers upon).

And just as Pharaoh, out of arrogance on earth, aspired to reach God, the polytheists said ﴿Why were the angels not sent down to us, or do we not see our Lord? Indeed they have been arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], and they thought they would not return to God, as those (earlier ones) thought. So there is near at hand for them of annihilation what befell those (earlier ones).
