Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 41:

﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿And he [Pharaoh] and his soldiers were arrogant﴾ [al-Qasas: 39], meaning: they were arrogant, so they supported misguidance and spread it. That is, We made him and his soldiers leaders (aʾimma, plural of imam) for the misguidance that leads to the Fire, so they are as though they were calling to the Fire. Each one calls with what his hand can reach: Pharaoh's calling was his command; the calling of his priests was the invention of the rules and illusions of misguidance; and the calling of his soldiers was the carrying out of that and the defending of it.

Aʾimma: the plural of imam, which is one who is followed in an action, whether good or evil. God the Exalted said (﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command﴾ [al-Anbiya: 73]). The meaning of making them leaders calling to the Fire is: creating their souls inclined toward evil and turned away from listening to right guidance, and their existence was among people whose condition was like that. So the "making" (jaʿl) is a creational making (jaʿl takwini) through making the causes of that. God sent the messengers to them to guide them, but that did not benefit them, so for this reason they persisted in disbelief.

Calling to the Fire is calling to the action that brings one into the Fire, so it is a calling to the Fire in its outcome (bil-maʾal). And since they were calling to the Fire, they are all the more among the people of the Fire. Therefore He said ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾, meaning they will not find anyone to help them, so as to ward off from them the punishment of the Fire.

The reason for the coordination of "﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾" is that calling requires soldiers and followers in whom they take pride in this world, but these will not avail them on the Day of Resurrection. He said: ﴿And those who followed said: "If only we had a return, so that we could disown them as they have disowned us"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 42:

Page 127
﴿And We made them follow up in this world with a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among those who are disfigured.﴾

Their being followed by the curse in this world means that the curse was made to cling to them in the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted. He decreed for them a destruction in which there is no mercy. He expressed that clinging by "following" (ittiba') in the manner of metaphor (isti'arah), because the follower (al-tabi') does not separate from the one he follows (matbu'uhu). The outcome of that curse was their being cast into the sea (al-yamm). It is also permissible that by "the curse" is meant the people cursing them, meaning that the people of faith curse them.

Their recompense on the Day of Resurrection is that they are among the "maqbuhin" (those who are disfigured). The maqbuh is one who is reviled with the word "qubbiha" (may he be made ugly), i.e., Allah or the people made him ugly, that is, made him ugly among people through his deeds, i.e., blameworthy. It is said: "qabahahu" with a light ba' (qabaha), so he is "maqbuh," as in this verse. And it is said: "qabbahahu" with a doubled ba' (qabbaha) when one attributes ugliness to him, so he is "muqabbah," as in the hadith of Umm Zar' when the tenth woman said: ("So when I speak in his presence, I am not reviled [la uqabbah]"), i.e., my speech is not made ugly and displeasing in his sight.

The indication to the world by "hadhihi" (this) is to belittle the matter of the world in comparison with the Hereafter.

The difference in form between his saying ﴿And We made them follow up﴾ and his saying ﴿they will be among those who are disfigured﴾ is because the curse in this world has ended with their drowning; or because the cursing of the believers against them in this world occurs at times when they mention them. Both possibilities do not require permanence, so the verbal sentence was used with it. As for the disfiguring of their condition on the Day of Resurrection, it is constant with them and clings to them, so the nominal sentence, which implies permanence and stability, was used in its place.

The pronoun "hum" in his saying "hum min al-maqbuhin" is not a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) but a pronoun of the subject (mubtada'), and by it the sentence became nominal, indicating the stability of the disfigurement for them on the Day of Resurrection.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 43:**

﴿Indeed, We gave Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the earlier generations, as insight for mankind, guidance and mercy, that they might remember.﴾

The purpose of the preceding verses, beginning from His words "When he came to it, he was called," up to this point, is to take warning from the end of those who denied, who said, ﴿We never heard of this among our forefathers of old﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24], so that like is compared with like.

Indeed, the polytheists used to say the same thing, intending to silence the Messenger (ﷺ) by arguing that if God had truly sent him, He would have sent him to the generations before him. And God would not leave the generations before them without a messenger and then send one to the last generation. So His words ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ complete the comparison of the Messenger Muhammad's (ﷺ) mission with the mission of Moses (peace be upon him). Both came after a long interval in which there was no messenger. At the same time, the verse points out that the prior sending of messengers to nations is an established fact, attested by tawatur (mass, continuous transmission), and that the destruction of the earlier generations followed from their nations' denial of their messengers. That destruction did not require messengers to be sent continually in succession; they came at scattered times.

If the polytheists, by their words ﴿We never heard of this among our forefathers of old﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24], sought to nullify the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the ground that its time was late, that is sophistry and delusion. Their argument is refuted by a refutation that turns it back on itself: messengers had come to the nations before, and then Moses came after an interval from the messengers.

When the matter of Islam overwhelmed them, the polytheists took refuge with the Jews, seeking their guidance in the methods of religious disputation. So the polytheists would mix what the Jews taught them of sophistries with what had become fixed in their souls through the misguidance of the leaders of polytheism. Thus they would utter statements that contradict one another. Once they said ﴿We never heard of this among our forefathers of old﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24], which is one of the arguments of the unlettered, and another time they said ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human being﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. The Qur'an would crush their falsehood with the proof of truth by holding them to the contradiction in their statements. This verse is part of that. It is a proof by comparing the mission of Muhammad with the mission of Moses (peace be upon them both), and its purpose is the mention of the earlier generations.

As for the mention of their destruction, it is an idmaj (embedding) of warning within the argument. The sentence ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ is a takhallus (transition) from the story of Moses' prophethood to the confirmation of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). The intended focus is His words (﴿after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾).

Furthermore, the Qur'an did not explain the wisdom behind the intervals (fatarat) that precede the sending of messengers. It confined itself to explaining the wisdom of sending after them, because that is what matters in the context of refuting the argument of the falsifiers against the message, or because it is content with the fact that this is an established matter that cannot be denied. This is what is intended here. As for the wisdom of separating messengers by intervals, it is beyond the level of their understanding. So by His words ﴿insight for mankind, guidance and mercy, that they might remember﴾ He points to the wisdom of sending after an interval. By His words "after We had destroyed the earlier generations" He points to the nations whom God uprooted for denying God's messengers.

The emphasis of the sentence with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and the particle of confirmation (harf al-tahqiq) is to treat the addressees as if they were deniers of this occurrence, so that emphasis by oath is needed with them. Thus the locus of emphasis is His words ﴿after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾.

"The Scripture" (al-Kitab) is the Torah, with which God addressed Moses (peace be upon him). "Insights" (basa'ir) is the plural of basirah, which is the perception of the intellect. It was named basirah by derivation from the sight of the eye. The Scripture is described as "insights" in view of the multiplicity of its proofs and the abundance of its clear evidences, as in the other verse where He said ﴿You know that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights﴾ [al-Isra': 102].

"The earlier generations" (al-qurun al-ula) are the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and the people of Lot. The qarn (generation) is the community. He, exalted is He, said ﴿How many generations have We destroyed before them?﴾ [Sad: 3]. And in a hadith: "The best of generations is my generation" (khayr al-qurun qarni).

"The people" (al-nas) are those to whom Moses was sent from the Children of Israel and the people of Pharaoh. It also includes those who wish to be guided by his guidance, like those among the Arabs of Yemen who became Jews, and it is guidance and mercy for them, and for whoever takes from them. He, exalted is He, said ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]. Among what the Torah contains is its warning against worshipping idols.

The pronoun in "that they might remember" (la'allahum yatadhakkarun) refers to the people who were addressed with the Torah. That is, likewise, the sending of Muhammad to you is guidance and mercy, that you might remember.

﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed the command to Moses, nor were you among the witnesses.﴾ When their doubt, by which they tried to deny the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), was refuted, the discussion moved to establishing his mission through a decisive proof. This was done through what Allah informed him of concerning the news of Moses's mission, which he could not have known by himself unless it was a revelation (wahy, divine inspiration) to him from Allah, exalted is He. Thus this is a transition from an indication by implication (dalalat al-iltizam) in the story of Moses to an explicit establishment of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The argument is presented in the manner of the theological school (al-madhhab al-kalami, the method of kalam, or systematic theological reasoning). The inference is built on the negation that the Prophet (peace be upon him) was present at the place where Allah decreed the revelation to Moses, so that it follows that someone like him would not know this except through direct observation. The way of knowing without observation was absent from him and from his people, since they were not people with knowledge of the news of the messengers, as the People of the Book were. When the usual way of knowledge for people like him was negated, it became certain that the way of his knowledge was Allah's informing him of the story of Moses.

Since His saying ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾ is a negation of his presence there and his attendance, it became certain that what is meant by ﴿the witnesses﴾ is the people of testimony (ahl al-shahada), i.e., those with certain reliable report (al-khabar al-yaqin), and they are the scholars of the Children of Israel, because they are the ones Allah made witnesses over the Torah and what it contains. Do you not see that He censured them for concealing some of what the Torah contains of good tidings concerning the Prophet (ﷺ), by His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 140]. The meaning is: you were not among the people of that time, nor among those who received the news of that through certain, widely transmitted report from their books at that time. So it became certain that the way of your knowledge of that is the revelation of Allah, exalted is He.

The decreed matter (al-amr al-maqdi) is the matter of prophethood given to Moses, when Moses received it.

His saying ﴿al-janib al-gharbi﴾ (the western side) is an idafa (genitive construction) of the qualified noun to its adjective; its original form is bi-l-janib al-gharbi (with the western side). This is common in Arabic speech, although the grammarians of Basra (nuhat al-Basra) denied it and resorted to many interpretations. The correct view is that it is permissible.

The western side (al-janib al-gharbi) is the one mentioned earlier, described as the right-hand bank of the valley, i.e., at the side of the sacred mountain.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 45:

﴿But We produced generations, and the age grew long over them.﴾ The connection of this istidrak (the "but" that corrects a preceding statement) with the speech before it is obscure, and how it can be an istidrak and a sequel to the first statement, by removing what might be suspected to be established, is unclear.

Its explanation: His saying "﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ [al-Qasas: 43]" is brought in order to refute the wonder of the polytheists at the message of Muhammad ﷺ, since no messenger had come to their forefathers of old, as you know from what has preceded just now. So He reminded them that God sent Moses in the same way after a great interval (fatrah), and that the people to whom Moses was sent raised the same doubt, saying ﴿We never heard of this among our earliest fathers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24]. Just as Moses' message (peace be upon him) came after a gap in the messengers, so too was the message of Muhammad ﷺ. The meaning is: the polytheists were worthy of having the message of Muhammad compared with the message of Moses, but God produced qurun (generations, i.e. nations) between the time of Moses and their time, so the time grew long and the polytheists forgot the message of Moses, and they said ﴿We never heard of this in the latter religion﴾ [Sad: 7]. The omission of the rest of the argument, which is the estimate "so they forgot", is for brevity, since it is evident from His saying ﴿so the age grew long over them﴾, as the Exalted said about the Jews when they began to distort words from their places: ﴿and they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13], and He said about the Christians: ﴿We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 14], and He said to the community of Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Do not be like those who were given the Book before, for the term grew long over them and their hearts hardened﴾ [al-Hadid: 16]. So the plural pronoun in His saying "'alayhim" refers to the polytheists, not to the generations.

Thus it becomes clear that the istidrak is connected to His saying "﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾", and that what lies between that and this is an digression (istitrad). This is better in explaining the connection of the istidrak than what al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) laboured over. May God grant him the reward of his insight, and thank him for the extent of his effort. And this is contrary to the position of the two istidraks that come after it, in His saying ﴿But We were senders of messengers﴾ and His saying ﴿But it is a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Qasas: 46]. The 'umur (lifespan) here means the long duration, as in His saying ﴿I had already lived among you a lifetime before it﴾ [Yunus: 16].

* * *

﴿And you were not dwelling among the people of Madyan, reciting to them Our verses, but We were senders of messengers﴾ This is a repetition of the proof by another example, like what is in His saying ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾ [al-Qasas: 44], meaning: you were not with Moses at the time of the speaking, nor were you among the people of Madyan when Moses came to them and what happened between him and Shu'ayb happened, which We have related to you.

And al-thawa' means residence.

The pronoun in "'alayhim" refers to the polytheists of Makkah, not to the people of Madyan, because the Prophet ﷺ recites the verses of God to the polytheists.

And by the verses is meant the verses containing the story of Moses among the people of Madyan, from His saying "and when he turned towards Madyan" to His saying ﴿So when Moses had fulfilled the term and set out with his family﴾ [al-Qasas: 29]. Mujahid said something with this meaning, and it is what the structure of the speech requires; had the pronoun been made to refer to the people of Madyan, it would have been said: "Our verses are witnessed among them."

The clause ﴿reciting to them Our verses﴾, according to Muqatil's interpretation, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "kunta", and it is a future-referring circumstance (hal muqaddarah) because its time differs from the time of its governing verb, as is evident. The meaning: you were not residing among the people of Madyan as travellers reside, such that when they return from their journeys they begin to tell their people about what they witnessed in other lands.

The istidrak in His saying ﴿But We were senders of messengers﴾ is clear, meaning: you were not present among the people of Madyan so that you would know the news of Moses from direct observation, but We were senders of You (messengers) by Our revelation, and so We taught you what neither you nor your people knew before this.

He turned away from saying "But We revealed this," to His saying ﴿But We were senders of messengers﴾, because the more important aim is to establish that the message came from God, in refutation of the polytheists in their saying and the saying of their like ﴿We never heard of this among our earliest fathers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24], and so that the message of Muhammad ﷺ would be known by implication, together with what comes later in His saying ﴿But it is a mercy from your Lord, that you may warn a people﴾ [al-Qasas: 46], and so the argument and challenge in this verse and the one before it is a challenge by what the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, knew of the news of the past story.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 46:

﴿And you were not on the western side of the mount when We called, but it was a mercy from your Lord, that you might warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, that they might remember.﴾

The side of the mount (*janib al-Tur*) is the western side, and it is the right-hand side that comes first. He described it with these two attributes, and so they are omitted here because it had become well known. The negated state is restricted by the adverbial clause "when We called" (*idh nadayna*), meaning at the time of Our calling.

The object of the calling is omitted because it is evident that it was the calling of Musa (Moses) by God, Exalted is He. This is the calling for the appointed time of forty nights, and the sending down of the tablets of the Torah following that intimate conversation, as is related in al-A'raf. That took place at the side of the mount, since the Children of Israel were around the mount, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿O Children of Israel, We had indeed delivered you from your enemy and made an appointment with you at the right side of the mount﴾ [Taha: 80]. It is the very place where Musa was called for the first time on his return from the land of Madyan, as has already been mentioned. Therefore the calling in His words here, "when We called," is other than the calling in His words ﴿Then when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley﴾ [al-Qasas: 30], up to His words ﴿O Musa, indeed I am God﴾ [al-Qasas: 30], and so on, so that there is no repetition with His words: "And you were not on the western side when We decreed to Musa the command." This argument is based on what the Prophet (ﷺ) knew of the report of Musa, peace be upon him, being summoned for the intimate conversation. That story is not mentioned in this surah, but it is mentioned in another surah, such as surah al-A'raf.

As for His words ﴿but it was a mercy from your Lord﴾, the word "lakin" (but) is here with a sukun on the nun, by agreement of the readers. It is therefore a particle with no governing effect, so it is not a conjunction of coordination, since it lacks its two conditions: that a negation or prohibition precede it, and that it not occur after the conjunction "wa." Accordingly, the particle "lakin" here is merely for corrective contrast (*istidrak*), has no governing effect, and is parenthetical (*i'tiradi*). The "wa" that precedes "lakin" is parenthetical as well.

The corrective contrast in His words ﴿but it was a mercy from your Lord﴾ arises from the implication of His words ﴿And you were not on the side of the mount﴾, meaning: your knowledge of that was not due to your presence, but your knowledge was a mercy from your Lord, that you might warn a people to whom no warner had come before you.

The accusative of "mercy" (*rahmatan*) indicates that it is governed by a verb in the accusative drawn from the context of the speech. It may be either by way of an omitted verb of being that is indicated by the negation of being in His words ﴿And you were not on the side of the mount﴾, the sense being: "but your knowledge was a mercy from Us"; or by way of the absolute object (*mafʿul mutlaq*) that comes in place of its verb, the sense being: "but We showed you mercy, by teaching you that through revelation as a mercy," the indication for this being His words "that you might warn a people."

[Page 134]

It is also permissible that "mercy" be in the accusative as an object of purpose (*mafʿul li-ajlihi*) governed by the verb in "that you might warn," so that the verb "that you might warn" is connected to an omitted verb of being, which is the place where the corrective contrast lands. In these possibilities there is a multiplicity of meanings, and this is among the eloquent kinds of brevity.

Instead of "a mercy from Us," the expression "a mercy from your Lord" is used, with the explicit noun in place of the pronoun. This is because the meaning of "Lord" (*Rabb*), when added to the pronoun of address, conveys the care of the Lord for the one He nurtures.

The phrase "that you might warn a people" is connected to what the verbal noun "mercy" implies, according to the aspects mentioned above. The "li-" is for causation. "A people" refers to Quraysh and the Arabs, who were the first addressed with the religion. All of them had not received a warner before Muhammad (ﷺ). As for Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, they were warners at a time when the tribe of Quraysh did not yet exist, nor the 'Adnanite Arab tribes. As for the Qahtanite tribes, Ibrahim was not sent to them, because the lineage of Quraysh traces back to 'Adnan, and between 'Adnan and Isma'il there are many generations.

It was limited to Quraysh or to the Arabs, rather than all the other nations to which the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, because the favour upon them was more complete, since no law had preceded them. Their order was disordered and not mixed with any stirring of a preserved law, so they were in need of a warner. It is also a veiled reproach for their ingratitude for this blessing. There is nothing in the speech that requires restricting the warning to them, nor anything that requires that those others whom Muhammad (ﷺ) warned, such as the Jews, Christians, and the people of Madyan, had not received a warner before him.

In His words "that you might warn" together with His words ﴿to whom no warner had come﴾ there is an indication that they had reached such a degree of disbelief that the forbearance of God, Exalted is He, does not pass beyond it.

Remembering (*tadhakkur*) is the rational consideration of the causes that led to the wisdom of warning them, and these causes are the extremity of their error beyond all the misguided nations. For they combined polytheism with many corruptions: killing souls, earning livelihood through raids and gambling, mixing of lineages, and violating honour. Therefore it was obligatory to remind them of what would set right their condition.

The like of His words "that they might remember" has already preceded just above.

[Page 135]

﴿And had it not been that a calamity would strike them for what their hands have put forward, and they would say, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your verses and be among the believers?"﴾

This is connected to His saying, ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, that they may remember﴾ [al-Qasas: 46], because warning occurs before a punishment.

The first "لَوْلا" (lawla) is a particle of prohibition due to existence (حَرْفُ امْتِناعٍ لِوُجُودٍ), meaning that its answer is negated because its condition exists. It is a particle that necessarily begins a sentence, so what follows it is a subject (مُبْتَدَأٌ). The predicate of the subject that follows "لَوْلا" must be omitted and is implied as a general verb of being (كَوْنٌ عامٌّ). The subject here is the verbal noun formed from (أنْ and the verb تُصِيبَهم), and the meaning is: "Had it not been for their being struck by a calamity." Since the verb that is turned into a verbal noun is followed by another verb, ﴿فَيَقُولُوا﴾ (fa-yaqulu), this following verb, which is joined to it, must also fall under the verbal noun, and it is conjoined by the fa of sequence (فاءُ التَّعْقِيبِ). Thus this conjoined verb is the intended meaning, like His saying, ﴿that if one of them errs, the other will remind her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], where the intended meaning is "that the other will remind her."

The structure of the speech was arranged in this manner, rather than saying: "Had it not been that they would say, 'Our Lord...' when a calamity strikes them," for the rhetorical purpose of emphasizing the warning against the striking of calamity. So it was placed in the position of the subject rather than the position of the adverbial phrase, to make the intended subject equal to the conditional clause of "لَوْلا," so that it and its adverbial phrase become two principal elements of the sentence. The implied meaning here is: "Had it not been for their being struck by a calamity that would be followed by their saying, 'Our Lord, why did You not send...' etc., we would not have paid attention to Your sending to them, because they are people of obstinacy and determination in fleeing."

The answer to "لَوْلا" is omitted, indicated by what preceded it, from His saying, ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾ up to His saying, ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ [al-Qasas: 46]. That is, "But We have given them an excuse by sending you, so as to cut off their excuse." The answer to "لَوْلا" is omitted and indicated by the preceding speech; that is, "Had it not been for mercy toward them through reminding and warning them, they would have deserved the calamity descending upon them."

The second "لَوْلا" is a particle of urging (حَرْفُ تَحْضِيضٍ, "tahdid"), meaning: "Would that You had sent to us before You seized us with punishment, so that You might set right our conditions, while You are free from our punishment." The word "فَنَتَّبِعَ" (fa-natabi'a) is in the accusative by an implied "an" (أنْ), obligatorily, as the answer to the urging.

[Page 136]

The pronoun in "تُصِيبَهم" refers to the people to whom no warner had come before. What is meant by "بِما قَدَّمَتْ أيْدِيهِمْ" (for what their hands have put forward) is the polytheism that preceded.

The "مُصِيبَة" (musibah, calamity) is what befalls a person, i.e., what descends upon him of conditions, but its use has come to be restricted to what befalls a person of punishment and harm.

The "ب" in "بِما قَدَّمَتْ أيْدِيهِمْ" is causal (لِلسَّبَبِيَّةِ), meaning: a punishment whose cause was what preceded of their evil deeds. What is meant by it here is the punishment of this world by annihilation and the like. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿So how, when a calamity strikes them for what their hands have put forward﴾ [al-Nisa': 62], in Surat al-Nisa'. It refers to the foul deeds they commit.

"مَا قَدَّمَتْ أيْدِيهِمْ" also means what they believed of polytheism and what they did of the effects of polytheism.

"The hands" is a metaphor for the minds that acquire the beliefs of disbelief. The inner conviction is thus likened to the action of the hand, a comparison of the intelligible to the perceptible.

This verse implies that the polytheists deserve punishment through calamities in this world, even if no messenger had come to them, because the proofs of the oneness of God are firmly established in the innate disposition (fitrah). Nevertheless, God's mercy overtook them, so He did not strike them with calamities until He sent them a messenger.

The meaning of the verse according to the principles of al-Ash'ari (al-Ash'ari), and as clarified by the adherents of his school, such as al-Qushayri and Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, is that the sin of polytheism has no excuse for its doer, because the oneness of God has been called to by the prophets and messengers from the time of Adam, to such an extent that no rational person is excused for ignorance of it. God has placed it in the innate disposition when He took its covenant from the descendants of Adam, as indicated by His saying: (﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify."﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]), as we explained in Surat al-A'raf.

But God is kind to His servants when years lengthen, generations pass away, and people become prone to heedlessness. So He takes care of them by sending messengers to remind them of what is in the innate disposition, and so that they may legislate for them what brings about the welfare of the community.

Therefore, the polytheists who passed away before the Muhammadan mission are held accountable for their polytheism and punished for it in the Hereafter. Had God willed, He would have punished them for it in this world by annihilation, but God gave them respite.

[Page 137]

The polytheists to whom the messengers came and whom they did not believe deserve the punishment of this world in addition to the punishment of the Hereafter. God said, ﴿And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment before the greater punishment, that they may return﴾ [al-Sajdah: 21].

As for the sects who consider the proof of God's oneness in divinity to be rational, such as the Maturidiyya and the Mu'tazila, the meaning of the verse is according to its apparent sense, and this is a view that is not far-fetched.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 48:

﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?" Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before? They said, "Two sorceries supporting each other," and they said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in both."﴾ "The fa' (فَ) here is eloquent (fasīḥah), like the fa' in the verse of 'Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf:

They said, "Khurasan is the farthest that is aimed at for us; then, the return; indeed we have come to Khurasan."

The sense of the speech is: if it is among their excuses that they should say this, then We have sent to them a Messenger with the truth. ﴿When the truth came to them﴾ they fabricated excuses and said: "We will not believe in him until we are given the like of what was given to Moses."

And al-Haqq (the Truth): it is what is in the Qur'an of guidance.

The attribution of coming to it (al-haqq) is a metaphor (isti'arah), by likening the truth to a person and likening its hearing to the coming of a person; or it is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), and the one who actually comes is the Messenger who conveys it from Allah. He expressed this by "the truth" in order to incorporate praise of him within the speech.

When the signs of the Messenger ﷺ dazzled them, they found no excuses except what the Jews had taught them, namely that they should say: ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ That is, that his signs should be like the signs of Moses which the Jews recount to them, and some of which the Qur'an has related.

The pronoun in "yakfurū" (they disbelieve) refers to the people mentioned in His saying "to warn a people" (li-tundhira qawman), so that the pronouns are consistent with His saying "lawla an tuṣībahum" (unless they are struck) and the pronouns after it of the same kind.

It is problematic, then, that those who disbelieved in what was given to Moses are the people of Pharaoh, not the polytheists of the Arabs.

Some exegetes said: this is from the argument of equals by an act of its like; because polytheism gathers the two groups, so their origins of thinking are one and their slander is united. The Copts were older than them in the religion of polytheism, so they were their origin in it, and the branch follows its origin and speaks with its speech, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Thus did no messenger come to those before them but they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 52] ﴿Did they bequeath it to one another? Rather, they are a transgressing people.﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 53] That is, they are alike in the cause of disbelief and transgression, so some of them do not need the advice of others regarding the foundations of disbelief. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ [ar-Rum: 2] ﴿in the nearest land, but they, after their defeat, will overcome﴾ [ar-Rum: 3], then He said: ﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice﴾ [ar-Rum: 4] ﴿in the victory of Allah﴾ [ar-Rum: 5]; that is, in Allah's victory for them, since He gave victory to those alike in not being polytheists, for the Romans on that day were upon the religion of the Messiah.

So their saying ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ is from the way of dialectical concession (al-taslim al-jadali), or from their inconsistency in their disbelief, so that at one time they are deniers (mu'attilun), and at another time they set conditions (mushtarituun). The apparent view is that the polytheists used to deny the messengership of all the messengers without exception. Likewise, the report of their saying "two sorcerers supporting each other" is from the speech of the polytheists of Makkah concerning Moses and Harun, when they heard their story; or concerning Moses and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them both. This is the more apparent, and it is what accords with His saying after it: ﴿And they said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in both."﴾ ﴿Say: "Then bring a book from Allah which is better guidance than both of them."﴾ [al-Qasas: 49].

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (ساحِرانِ) sāḥirān, the dual of sāḥir. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (سِحْرانِ) siḥrān, on the basis that it is a report using the verbal noun for emphasis (mubalaghah); that is, "they are two possessors of sorcery."

Al-tazahur (تَظاهُر) means: mutual cooperation.

The tanwin in "bi-kullin" (بِكُلٍّ) is the tanwin of compensation (tanwin 'iwad) for the omitted genitive complement; so the genitive complement is to be estimated according to the two possibilities: either "with each of the two sorcerers," or it is to be estimated as "with each one who claimed a messengership." The latter is more fitting to the speech of Quraysh, since they said: ﴿Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being﴾ [al-An'am: 91].

[Page 139]

﴿Say: "Then bring a Book from God that is better guidance than these two, and I will follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿But if they do not respond to you, know that they only follow their own desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from God? Indeed, God does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

That is: respond to their spoken words, as quoted from their saying "two sorcerers" (ساحران) and their saying ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in all of it﴾ [Al-Qasas: 48].

Describing "a Book" as ﴿from God﴾ is an incorporation (idmaj) that praises both the Qur'an and the Torah, in that they are both books from God. By the Torah is meant what the four books attributed to Moses contain of the speech of God to Moses, or of Moses' attribution to God of a matter, not everything those books contain. For those books contain stories and events that are not the speech of God. Thus it is said of the Muṣḥaf that it is the speech of God in the strict sense, whereas the books of the Two Testaments are called the speech of God only by way of predominance (taghlīb), since the two messengers did not claim that for the two Testament books. The Qur'an has challenged both of them in this verse with what the Qur'an contains of guidance, through the eloquence of its composition. This is evidence that what it contains of knowledge and truths is among the ways of its inimitability (i'jaz), as we have stated in the Tenth Introduction.

So the meaning of ﴿if they do not respond to you﴾ is: if they do not respond to your call, that is, to the religion after the proof has been established against them by this challenge. Know then that their persistence in disbelief after that is nothing but following desire, and they have no doubt (shubha) in their religion.

It is also possible that by non-response is meant not bringing a Book better than the Qur'an, because the act of responding (istijāba) requires a call, and there is no call in His words ﴿Bring a Book from God that is better guidance than these two﴾, but rather it is an assertion of incapacity (ta'jīz). So the sense is: if they are unable and do not respond to your call after being unable, ﴿then know that they only follow their desires﴾, that is, it cannot be changed. And know that the verb istajāba, with the added sīn and tā', transitively takes the call directly and takes the caller with the preposition lām. In that case the word "call" is usually omitted, so it is rarely said: "God answered his supplication (istajāba Allāhu lahu duʿāʾahu)," but rather one says only "God answered him (istajāba Allāhu lahu)." When they say "he called him and he answered him (daʿāhu fa-istajābahu)," the meaning is "he answered his call." This is like His words ﴿If they do not respond to you, then know that it was sent down with the knowledge of God﴾ [Hūd: 14] in Surat Hūd.

[Page 140]

And "annamā" with a fatḥa on the hamza gives the sense of restriction (ḥaṣr), like "innamā" with a kasra on the hamza, because the fatḥa-hamza form is a derivative (far') of the kasra-hamza form both in wording and in meaning, so there is no escape from its meaning. Thus the sense is: "know that they follow nothing but their desires." The particle "inna," which is usually used for a doubtful condition, is employed here by way of mockery (tahakkum), or because it is the original particle. The insertion of the verb "fa-iʿlam (know)" is for emphasis on the statement that follows it, as was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿And know that God comes between a man and his heart﴾ [Al-Anfāl: 24] in Surat al-Anfāl.

His words "attabiʿhu (I will follow it)" are the answer to "fa-ʾtū (bring)," that is: if you bring it, I will follow it. This is an intensification of the challenge, because when he promises them that he will follow whatever they bring, he is in effect following them, and that stirs their motives to try to bring a Book better than His Book, if they were able. If they do not do so, then the truth has been established against them and defeat has become binding upon them, and this is more indicative of their incapacity and more firmly establishes the inimitability of the Qur'an.

This is conditional speech concerning something whose non-occurrence has been ascertained, so the conditioned thing is then impossible to occur, like His words ﴿Say: If the Merciful had a son, I would be the first to worship﴾ [Al-Zukhruf: 81]. Because it is impossible to occur, God commanded His Messenger to say it. It has been understood from His words ﴿if they do not respond﴾ and from the insertion of "fa-iʿlam" that they will never bring such a thing at all, and this is part of the inimitability through reporting of the unseen.

At the end of the speech comes a remarkable appended conclusion (tadhyīl): there is no one more astray than one who follows his desire, which contradicts the guidance of God.

"Man" (مَن) is an interrogative noun about an undefined entity, and it is an interrogative of denial, so it conveys negation, and the nominal meaning it contains is in the sense of an indefinite noun in the context of negation, which conveys generality, so it includes those who followed their desires and others. By this generality it becomes an appended conclusion, like His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God?﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 140] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The term "following" (ittibāʿ) is applied to acting upon what a person's will dictates, which arises from his inclination toward corruptions and harms, by likening the action to walking behind a traveller. In it there is a comparison of desire (hawā) to a traveller. And "hawā" is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, as in the verse of Jaʿfar ibn ʿUlba:

"My desire goes with the Yemeni caravan, ascending."

[Page 141]

His words ﴿without guidance from God﴾: the bāʾ here is for accompaniment (mulābasa), and it is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the agent of ﴿followed his desire﴾. It is a circumstantial phrase that clarifies, to emphasize the meaning of desire, because desire cannot accompany divine guidance, nor can its possessor accompany it, since guidance returns to the sense of reaching the good aim.

God made the guidance His, because it is the true guidance, since it comes from the One who knows everything, and so it is free from error and mistake.

The reason why he is not more astray than this is that error (ḍalāl), originally, is missing the path, and it occurs in varying conditions, with consequences ranging from hardship, or danger, or complete ruin, according to the degree of severity of the error. Following desire, while disregarding the use of reason and reviewing it for salvation, casts its follower into many states of harm without limit or confinement.

Therefore, this following that departs from the very nature of guidance is necessarily the greatest error, and its follower is the most astray of those who are astray.

Then this appended conclusion is followed by what completes it, for in it is the identification of this undefined group, who are the most astray of the astray. They are the people who were wrongdoers (ẓālimīn), that is, wrongdoing was their condition and the foundation of their collective identity, and for this reason He referred to them as "a people" (qawm).

By "the wrongdoers" is meant those who are complete in wrongdoing, which is wronging oneself and wronging people, the greatest of which is associating partners with God, committing indecencies, and aggression. God does not create in their souls the capacity for guidance, as a punishment from Him for their wrongdoing, so they remain in error, floundering in it, and so they are the most astray of the astray. Yet they vary in the degree to which God's guidance is denied them, according to their varying firmness in their wrongdoing. One of them may persist in his error for a time, then God decrees guidance for him and creates faith in his heart. Because of this variation in readiness to abandon error, the Prophet's ﷺ call to them to believe continued among all those addressed, since none knows the extent of people's variation in accepting guidance except God. So the guidance denied here in regard to its attachment to them is the creative guidance (al-hudā al-takwīnī).

As for guidance in the sense of direction (irshād), it falls within the general scope of the call. This is the meaning of the saying of the Ash'ari [Ashʿarite] imams

[Page 142]

that God addresses with faith those whom He knows will not believe, like Abū Jahl, because the creative attachment (al-taʿalluq al-takwīnī) is different from the legislative attachment (al-taʿalluq al-tashrīʿī).

Between "hawāhu" and "hudan" there is a paronomasia (jinās) that is imperfect (muḥarraf) and a graphic paronomasia (jinās khaṭṭ).

[Page 139]

In it there is a comparison of desire (hawā) to a traveller. And "hawā" is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, as in the verse of Jaʿfar ibn ʿUlba:

"My desire goes with the Yemeni caravan, ascending."

[Page 141]

His words ﴿without guidance from God﴾: the bāʾ here is for accompaniment (mulābasa), and it is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the agent of ﴿followed his desire﴾. It is a circumstantial phrase that clarifies, to emphasize the meaning of desire, because desire cannot accompany divine guidance, nor can its possessor accompany it, since guidance returns to the sense of reaching the good aim.

God made the guidance His, because it is the true guidance, since it comes from the One who knows everything, and so it is free from error and mistake.

The reason why he is not more astray than this is that error (ḍalāl), originally, is missing the path, and it occurs in varying conditions, with consequences ranging from hardship, or danger, or complete ruin, according to the degree of severity of the error. Following desire, while disregarding the use of reason and reviewing it for salvation, casts its follower into many states of harm without limit or confinement.

Therefore, this following that departs from the very nature of guidance is necessarily the greatest error, and its follower is the most astray of those who are astray.

Then this appended conclusion is followed by what completes it, for in it is the identification of this undefined group, who are the most astray of the astray. They are the people who were wrongdoers (ẓālimīn), that is, wrongdoing was their condition and the foundation of their collective identity, and for this reason He referred to them as "a people" (qawm).

By "the wrongdoers" is meant those who are complete in wrongdoing, which is wronging oneself and wronging people, the greatest of which is associating partners with God, committing indecencies, and aggression. God does not create in their souls the capacity for guidance, as a punishment from Him for their wrongdoing, so they remain in error, floundering in it, and so they are the most astray of the astray. Yet they vary in the degree to which God's guidance is denied them, according to their varying firmness in their wrongdoing. One of them may persist in his error for a time, then God decrees guidance for him and creates faith in his heart. Because of this variation in readiness to abandon error, the Prophet's ﷺ call to them to believe continued among all those addressed, since none knows the extent of people's variation in accepting guidance except God. So the guidance denied here in regard to its attachment to them is the creative guidance (al-hudā al-takwīnī).

As for guidance in the sense of direction (irshād), it falls within the general scope of the call. This is the meaning of the saying of the Ash'ari [Ashʿarite] imams

[Page 142]

that God addresses with faith those whom He knows will not believe, like Abū Jahl, because the creative attachment (al-taʿalluq al-takwīnī) is different from the legislative attachment (al-taʿalluq al-tashrīʿī).

Between "hawāhu" and "hudan" there is a paronomasia (jinās) that is imperfect (muḥarraf) and a graphic paronomasia (jinās khaṭṭ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 51:

﴿And We have certainly caused the Word to reach them, that they may remember.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And had it not been that a calamity should afflict them for what their hands had sent forth...﴾ [al-Qasas: 47] and what follows it, namely His saying ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us, they said: "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 48].

Al-Tawsil (causing to reach, connecting): it is an intensive form of al-wasl (connecting), which is joining some part of a thing to another part. It is said: "He connected (wassala) the rope" when he joined its strands, one part to another, until it became one rope.

The "word" (al-qawl) here refers to the Qur'an. God, the Exalted, says ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾ [al-Tariq: 13] and ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble Messenger﴾ [al-Haqqah: 40]. So the definite article is for prior reference (al-ʿahd), meaning "the known word." The connecting (al-tawsil) has many aspects. In respect of its wording, parts of it were connected to one another, and it was not revealed all at once. In respect of its meanings, it connected kinds of speech: promise and warning, encouragement and deterrence, narratives, admonitions, lessons, and advice, one following another, and moving from one subject to another. In all of this there is help for the mind's vigour toward remembrance and reflection.

Both the lam (of emphasis) and "qad" are for emphasis, as a response to them, since they were ignorant of the wisdom behind the gradual revelation (tanjim) of the Qur'an. The wisdom of its gradual revelation is mentioned here in what returns to their benefit, by His saying ﴿so that they may remember﴾. Another wisdom is mentioned in the verse of Surat al-Furqan, returning to the benefit of the Messenger ﷺ, by His saying: they said ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once? Thus (it is) so that We may strengthen your heart with it﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]. It is understood from this that they did not remember. The pronoun in "lahum" (to them) refers to the polytheists (al-mushrikin).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 52–53:

Page 143
﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it—they believe in it.﴾ ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say: "We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were Muslims [submitting] before it."﴾

When His saying ﴿so that they may remember﴾ [al-Qasas: 43] made clear that they had not done so, and that they were not at the level of what the one who hopes had hoped for, He followed this with this resumptive sentence as a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because it is an answer to a questioner who asks: Did anyone else remember through the Qur'an, or were people equal in not remembering it? So it was answered that those who were given the Book before the revelation of the Qur'an believe in it with a firm faith.

The intended meaning of "those who were given the Book" is a known group among the People of the Book, whom God testified believe in the Qur'an and reflect upon it. They are some of the Christians who were in Mecca, such as Waraqa ibn Nawfal and Suhayb, and some of the Jews of Medina, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and Rifa'a ibn Rifa'a al-Qurazi, who had received the call of the Prophet ﷺ before the Prophet migrated to Medina; when he migrated, they displayed their Islam.

It was also said: what is meant is a delegation of twelve men of the Christians of Abyssinia, whom the Negus (al-Najashi) sent to ascertain the matter of the Prophet ﷺ in Mecca. They sat with the Prophet ﷺ and believed in him, while Abu Jahl and his companions were near them, listening to what they said. When they rose from the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Jahl and those with him followed them and said to them: "May God disappoint you as a caravan, and disgrace you as a delegation! You did not even delay before you affirmed him." They said: "Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant. For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds." By this it became apparent that when they returned, the Negus embraced Islam, and some of the Christians of Abyssinia had embraced Islam when the emigrants to Abyssinia came to them, recited the Qur'an to them, and explained the religion to them.

The pronoun in "from before it" refers to the word in "And We have certainly conveyed to them the word" [al-Qasas: 51], which is the Qur'an. Placing the subject before the verbal predicate in "they believe in it" serves to strengthen the predication. The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) restricts the statement to a relative restriction (al-qasr al-idafi), meaning: they are certain, unlike those to whom We conveyed the word.

Page 144
The predicate coming in the present tense indicates the continuity and renewal of their faith.

The narration of their faith in the past tense in His saying ﴿We believed in it﴾, although they say this at the first hearing of the Qur'an, is either because the past tense is used for the performance of faith (inshā' al-iman), like its use in formulas of contracts, or to indicate that they believed in it before its revelation, i.e., they believed that a messenger would come with a book confirming what is before him—meaning a general faith followed by detailed faith upon hearing its verses. To this meaning points His saying ﴿Indeed, we were Muslims before it﴾, i.e., confirming the coming of the messenger of Islam.

It is also permissible that "Muslims" means monotheists who confirm the messengers, for tawhid is Islam, as Abraham said ﴿So do not die except as Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132].

The sentence ﴿Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord﴾ is in the position of giving a reason for the sentence ﴿We believed in it﴾.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, we were Muslims before it﴾ is an explanation of the meaning of ﴿We believed in it﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 28, verses 54–55:**

﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they endured patiently, and they repel evil with good, and they spend from what We have provided them.﴾ ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say: "For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant."﴾

Referring to them here with the demonstrative (ism al-ishara, "those") serves to draw attention to the fact that they deserve what is mentioned after the demonstrative, because of the qualities mentioned before it, as occurred earlier in His words ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ (2:5) in Surah al-Baqarah.

Allah enumerated for them seven qualities of people of perfection:

The first is related to the Hereafter, and it is ﴿they will be given their reward twice﴾, meaning they will be given two rewards for their faith, that is, their reward will be doubled because they believed in their own Scripture first and then believed in the Qur'an. He expressed the doubling of the reward as two-fold by "twice", using the image of repeating the giving, although it is in fact one giving.

The benefit of this figurative usage (majaz) is to show special care, as if the one who rewards gives and then repeats his gift. Thus in ﴿they will be given their reward twice﴾ there is a representation (tamthil). In the Sahih (the authentic collection) it is related from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three will be given their reward twice: a man from the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and then encountered me, so he believed in me, followed me and affirmed me, for him are two rewards; a slave who fulfilled the right of Allah the Exalted and the right of his master, for him are two rewards; and a man who had a slave-girl, so he nourished her and nourished her well, then educated her and educated her well, then freed her and married her, for him are two rewards." This was narrated by al-Sha'bi, and he said to 'Ata' al-Khurasani: "Take it without any payment, for a man would travel far for less than this to Medina."

The second: patience (sabr). Patience is among the greatest qualities of righteousness and the most comprehensive of good deeds, and the most helpful in increasing them. By patience is meant their patience over the harm of the people of their religion, or their patience over the harm of Quraysh. This is realized in the case of the Abyssinian delegation. Perhaps they are the intended ones in this verse, and that is why it is followed by His words ﴿they repel evil with good﴾ and His words ﴿They said: "For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you."﴾

The third quality: their repelling evil with good, which is among the greatest of good qualities and the most conducive to good companionship. He the Exalted said: ﴿Good and evil are not equal. Repel [evil] with that which is better, and thereupon the one between whom and you is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend﴾ (41:34). Thereby the benefit is achieved of averting the harm of the one who does evil from oneself, and of conferring good upon another soul. They did not repay the coarseness of Abu Jahl with its like, but with turning away together with a good word, which is "Peace be upon you."

As for spending, perhaps they used to spend on the poor Muslims in Makkah. This is the fourth quality, and its place in righteousness is not hidden.

The fifth quality: turning away from idle talk (laghw), which is vain speech that has no benefit. This disposition is among the manifestations of wisdom, for it is not befitting for the intelligent person to occupy his hearing and his mind with what has no use. All the more so, he keeps himself far from such speech issuing from him.

The sixth quality: decisive speech (al-kalam al-fasl), which is their saying ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you.﴾ This is among the best ways of responding to the foolish, and it is closer to reforming them and safer from increasing their foolishness.

(Page 146)

Allah made them speak with a wisdom that He made worthy of being arranged in the thread of inimitability (i'jaz). So He inspired them with those words, then honoured them by having them related in the fabric of the Qur'an, just as He inspired 'Umar with his saying ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you﴾ (66:5), and so on in the verse.

The meaning of ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾ is that our deeds are due to us, as a metonymy (kinayah) for their constant attachment to them. As for their saying ﴿and for you are your deeds﴾, it is a completion, in the manner of ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ (109:6).

What is intended by the "peace" is the peace of departure (salam al-mutarakah), which is metonymically expressed as a farewell, meaning: we will not return to addressing you. Al-Hasan said: the phrase "Peace be upon you" is a greeting among believers, and a sign of disengagement from the ignorant. Perhaps the Qur'an altered their statement by putting it in a different order, so that it would contain the particularity suited to inimitability, because delaying the speech in which there is disengagement until the end of the address is more appropriate, so that it contains the excellence of a fine conclusion (bara'at al-maqta').

The Qur'an omitted their saying "We have not fallen short in seeking our own right guidance," for it is dispensed with by their saying ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾.

The seventh quality: what their saying ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾ makes clear, namely that this is their character: that they seek knowledge and noble morals. The clause is an explanation (ta'lil) for the disengagement, meaning: because we do not like to associate with those who are ignorant of Allah and of the religion of truth, and with people of the disposition of ignorance, which is the opposite of forbearance (hilm). Thus the word "ignorance" (jahl) is used in its two shared meanings. Perhaps this is an allusion to the kunyah of Abu Jahl, who insulted them with his tongue.

It is apparent that they said this word among themselves and did not declare it openly to Abu Jahl and his companions, as indicated by His saying "and they repel evil with good" and His saying "Peace be upon you." Accordingly, the reported speech becomes two statements: a statement directed at Abu Jahl and his companions, and a statement that passed among the members of the delegation.
