Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 56:

Page 147
﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills, and He knows best those who are guided.﴾

When He mentioned the excuses of the polytheists and their disbelief in the Qur'an, and informed His Messenger that they follow their desires and that they are stripped of the guidance of Allah, and then He praised a group of the People of the Book for believing in the Qur'an, and that caused the Prophet ﷺ grief that the Quraysh, who were the closest of people to him, turned away from his call, Allah addressed His Prophet ﷺ with what consoles his soul and removes his distress, by reminding him that guidance is in the hand of Allah. This is a metaphor (kinaya) for the command to entrust that matter to Allah, exalted is He.

The sentence is an independent new statement (isti'naf ibtida'i). Opening it with the particle of emphasis (harf al-ta'kid) signifies concern to draw the attention of the Prophet ﷺ, upon him be peace, to understanding what it contains, in the manner we established earlier in His saying ﴿So know that they only follow their desires﴾ [al-Qasas: 50]. The object of "ahbabta" (you loved) is omitted, indicated by "la tahdi" (you do not guide).

The implied meaning is: whom you love to be guided or to attain guidance. What the relative pronoun "man" (whom) refers to is everyone whom the Prophet calls to Islam, for he loves their guidance.

Narrations have converged that among the first intended by this is Abu Talib, the paternal uncle of the Prophet ﷺ, since the Prophet ﷺ had grieved over his death without Islam, as in the authentic hadiths. Al-Zajjaj said: The Muslims agreed that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib. Al-Tabari said: It is mentioned that this verse was revealed because of Abu Talib's refusal to answer his nephew when he called him to belief in Allah alone. Al-Qurtubi said: This is the text of the hadith of al-Bukhari and Muslim, and this has been mentioned previously in "Bara'a" (surah 9).

This is from the general (al-'amm) that was revealed concerning a specific cause (sabab khass), so it encompasses him and others. It implies that this surah was revealed immediately after the death of Abu Talib, and Abu Talib's death was in the third year before the Hijra; or the placement of this verse after the verses preceding it was by a specific divine directive (tawqif khass).

The meaning of ﴿but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ is that He creates whom He wills receptive to guidance within a determined scope and after limited calls, until his breast opens to faith. When he reflects upon what Allah has created him with and determined for him, and that increases in His knowledge and will, He makes guidance for him; so the intended meaning is guidance in actuality (al-hidaya bil-fi'l). As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52], that is guidance through calling and direction; thus the two usages differ.

The object of the verb of will is omitted, due to what precedes it, meaning: whom He wills to guide. Willing is known by the occurrence of guidance, and it depends on what has preceded from His knowledge and decree.

In His saying ﴿And He knows best those who are guided﴾ there is an indication of that, meaning: He is more knowing than anyone of those who are guided, regarding their states and the measures of their readiness, according to what their natural dispositions are prepared for: sound reflection, acceptance of good, fear of the consequence, and being affected by the call and its proofs. For each of these there is a state and a limit, and for both there are existential causes in the person and his ancestors, and causes of his growth or weakness, from his constitution, his environment, his era, and his reasoning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 57:

﴿They said: "If we were to follow the guidance with you, we would be snatched away from our land." Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of every thing are brought as provision from Us? But most of them do not know.﴾ "This is some of their excuses. It was said by a group of them, among those whom shyness overcame so that they did not persist in arrogance and openly deny, and whom habituation to their state of disbelief overcame so that they did not acknowledge the truth. So they offered this excuse. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that al-Harith ibn 'Uthman ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf and some people of Quraysh came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and al-Harith said: 'We certainly know that your words are true, but we fear that if we follow the guidance with you and believe in you, the Arabs will snatch us away from our land, and we have no power against them. We are merely "eaters of a head" (akalat ra's), meaning that our whole group is satisfied by a single head of camel.' This expression is a metaphor for scarcity. Thus these people, outwardly, acknowledged that the Prophet (ﷺ) calls to guidance.

Al-takhattuf (snatching away) is an intensive form of al-khatf, which is the seizing of something swiftly. It has already occurred in His saying ﴿You fear that people will snatch you away﴾ [al-Anfal: 26] in Surat al-Anfal. What is meant is that enemies will seize us along with them and take us to their lands. So God answered them: Quraysh, despite their small number and limited equipment, were granted by God a land that is a secure sanctuary, in which they are safe from enemies, despite the multitude of Arab tribes and their preoccupation with raiding their neighbours. Fruits were brought to them in abundance for long ages. So if they had reflected, they would have known that they have a divine protection, and that God who granted them security in the earlier centuries will grant them security if they respond to God and His Messenger.

Al-tamkin (establishment) means placing someone in a place. It has already occurred in His saying ﴿We established them in the land as We had not established you﴾ [al-An'am: 6] in Surat al-An'am, and in His saying at the beginning of this surah ﴿and We would establish for them in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 6]. Here it is used metaphorically for preparing and facilitating.

Al-jaby means gathering and bringing together, and from it comes jibayat al-kharaj (collection of land tax).

The interrogative is a denial that God did not establish a sanctuary for them. The basis of the denial is that they have placed themselves in the position of one who denies that this sanctuary is from God's establishment, so they used the interrogative to express denial of this negation.

This denial implies a rebuke for this state into which they have fallen, in which they have placed themselves in the position of one who denies that God established a sanctuary for them.

The waw conjoins the interrogative clause to the clause "and they said." The implied sense is: "and We did establish for them a sanctuary."

"Kulli shay'" is general in the sense of every bearer of fruit, and this is a customary generality, meaning the fruits of every one of the fruit-bearing things known in their land and in the neighbouring lands. Or "kull" is used to mean abundance.

"Rizqan" is a circumstantial accusative (hal) relating to "thamarat," and it is a verbal noun in the sense of a passive participle.

The meaning of "min ladunna" is "from Us." Nearness here is a metaphor for honour and blessing, meaning a provision that We decreed for them as an honour, so it is as if it were a special provision from a place most specifically attributed to God Most High.

In the course of refuting their statement there is an inserted reminder of God's favour upon them through this blessing, so that two restraints against ingratitude for blessings arise in them: the restraint of nullifying their excuse for disbelief, and the restraint of reminding them of the blessing of the One they disbelieve in.

The position of the exception in His saying ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ is that it is connected to the discourse that is directed as a response to their saying ﴿If we were to follow the guidance with you, we would be snatched away from our land﴾, since the sense is: that is a divine blessing, but most of them have no knowledge, so for this reason they did not perceive the reality of this blessing, and thought that Islam would lead to the Arabs' aggression against them, supposing that their sanctity among the Arabs is a distinction and a blessing that the Arab tribes had bestowed upon them.

The verb "they do not know" is treated as intransitive, so no object is to be supposed for it, meaning they are not people of knowledge and reflection, but are ignorant and do not contemplate circumstances. Knowledge is negated of most of them because some of them are people of opinion; had they looked and reflected, they would not have uttered that statement.

If an object were supposed for the verb "they know," indicated by the context, meaning "they do not know that the sanctuary was established for them and that the bringing of fruits to them is from Our bounty," then the attribution of the negation of knowledge to most of them would not be sound; rather it would be attributed to all of them, since their words were unanimous in the saying ﴿If we were to follow the guidance with you, we would be snatched away from our land﴾.

Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Ruways from Ya'qub read (tujba) with the feminine (ta') at the beginning. The rest read it with the masculine (ya') at the beginning, out of regard for the genitive noun it is attached to, which is (kulli shay'), thereby giving the attached noun a masculine form.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 58:

﴿And how many a town have We destroyed which exulted in its livelihood! Those are their dwellings, which have not been inhabited after them, except a little. And We were the inheritors.﴾ This is a conjunction with the clause ﴿Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary?﴾ [al-Qasas: 57], in terms of what it contains of reproach and rebuke, for that requires addressing retribution, the manner of the nations that disbelieved in the favours of God. So it is a warning to Quraysh of the evil outcome of peoples who were in a situation like theirs of security and provision, but who disregarded the blessing and met it with insolence (al-batar).

Al-batar: arrogance (al-takabbur). Its verb is intransitive, of the pattern fariha, so the accusative of "ma'ishatuha" after "batirat" is by way of implicit transitivity (tadmin), with "batirat" carrying the sense of (kafarat, "disbelieved"), because batar, which is arrogance, entails not acknowledging the good that is bestowed upon one.

The meaning is: she was insolent regarding the state of her livelihood, that is, the blessing of her living.

Al-ma'isha here is a verbal noun (ism masdar) meaning "living", and what is meant is its condition, so it is an elided construction (hadhf mudaf) indicated by the context. It is known that it is a good condition from his saying "batirat", and it is the condition of security and provision.

Page 151

The demonstrative "tilka" refers to "masakinuhum", which is specified by the demonstrative's own clarification, because it is in effect "tilka al-masakin". Thus the reference becomes to something present in the mind, treated as though it were present before the eyes of the listener. For this reason, his saying ﴿have not been inhabited after them﴾ is the predicate of the demonstrative. The estimated sense is: "so their dwellings have not been inhabited after them, except a little."

Al-sukna: dwelling in a house or the like at known times with the intention of continuing for a long time.

The meaning of ﴿have not been inhabited after them﴾ is that they left no successors in them. This is a metonymy for their complete extinction.

His saying "except a little" is a precaution (ihtiras), that is, except the stays of passers-by who take heed from the destruction of its people.

"Qalilan" is in the accusative by way of exception from the general sense of an elided set of times: "except for a few times", or by way of exception from an elided verbal noun: "they were not inhabited with any inhabiting except a little inhabiting." The little dwelling is mere alighting without intent of prolonged stay, so it is a passing by, not dwelling. Thus applying the term "dwelling" to that is a figurative correspondence (mushakala), so that the exception may be made: that is, they were not inhabited except by the alighting of travellers, or the halting of seekers of pasture, like the halting of the army of the expedition of Tabuk at al-Hijr, the dwelling of Thamud, and their drawing water from the well of the she-camel. The meaning is: "Those are their dwellings, desolate and empty, in which no inhabitant dwells," that is, God decreed that they remain empty so that they remain a lesson and an admonition of God's punishment in this world.

By this verse the interpretation becomes clear of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when he passed by al-Hijr of Thamud on his way to Tabuk, and said: "Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, lest there befall you what befell them, unless you are weeping." That is, fearful. This is limited to the necessity of passing through, lest they encounter the realisation of the true reality of dwelling, whose absence after their people God had decreed. For perhaps the destruction of whoever dwells there would be decreed, in fulfilment of His decree.

The clause ﴿And We were the inheritors﴾ is a conjunction with the clause ﴿have not been inhabited after them﴾, and it indicates that they were not inhabited after them, so no other people settle in them after them. He expressed the succession of dwelling by inheritance, in the manner of metaphor (isti'ara).

The restriction of the inheritance of those dwellings to God the Exalted is real, that is, no one else inherits them. It is a metonymy for the deprivation of those dwellings of an inhabitant.

Page 152

That metonymy is a symbol of the intensity of God the Exalted's anger against its former people, to the extent that His anger exceeded the inhabitants to the very dwellings themselves, so He punished them with deprivation of the delight of dwellings; for the delight of dwellings is their inhabitants, since the perfection of existing things is that by which the reality of their being is sustained.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 59:

﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities until He sends in their mother-town a messenger reciting to them Our verses. And We would never destroy the cities unless their people were wrongdoers.﴾ The reflection on the destroyed cities is followed by an explanation of the signs of their destruction and its cause, as a thorough establishment of the proof against the idolaters of the Arabs. He thus explains to them that it is not the custom of God Most High to destroy cities deserving of destruction until He sends a messenger to the greatest town among them, because the greatest town is the place where the people of the surrounding towns and deserts descend, so the call of the messenger there will not remain hidden; and because its people are an example to others in good and evil, so they are more prepared to grasp matters as they truly are. This is the explanation of the signs of destruction.

The "qura" (cities, i.e. settlements with permanent built dwellings of gatherings of people) was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿Enter this town﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58] in al-Baqarah.

It was singled out for mention because the lesson from it is more evident: when it is destroyed, its traces and ruins remain, and its news does not cease to reach the generations that come after it. It is understood that tents and encampments are like it by the implication of the meaning (dalalat al-fahwa).

The placing of the negation in the form of "ma kana" (it was not) followed by a doer and similar forms of denial indicates the firmness and consistency of this rule, as was mentioned previously in its parallels, among them His saying ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should give him the Book and wisdom﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 79] in Surat Ali 'Imran, and His saying ﴿And it was not [possible] that this Qur'an be fabricated other than by Allah﴾ [Yunus: 37] in Surat Yunus.

The cities of the land of the Arabs are many, such as Makkah, Jeddah, Mina, al-Ta'if, Yathrib and what surrounds it of towns, and likewise the towns of Yemen and the towns of Bahrain. Umm al-Qura (the mother of cities) is the great town among them. Makkah was the most famous of the lands of the Arabs, the most mentioned among them, and the most frequented by travellers and visitors because of the Ka'bah located in it and the Hajj to it.

The intended meaning of destroying the cities is the destruction of their people. The destruction was attached to the cities only to indicate that the severity of the destruction is such that it reaches the community and its people, namely destruction by calamities that leave no dwellings standing, in contrast to the destruction of a community, which may occur by plague or the like and so leaves no trace in the cities.

The attribution of the report to God under the title of His lordship (Rububiyyah) to the Prophet ﷺ indicates that the intended recipients of this warning are the community of Muhammad, those who denied. Thus the address is to the Prophet, peace be upon him, for this purpose. For this reason there is a shift from him to the first-person pronoun in His saying "Our verses", to indicate that the verses are from God and that the religion is the religion of God.

The pronoun in "upon them" refers to what is known from "the cities", namely their people, as in His saying ﴿And ask the town in which we were﴾ [Yusuf: 82], and from it His saying ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾ [al-'Alaq: 17].

In this sentence there is variety in styles, as it combines the explicit noun and pronouns of the third person, second person and first person.

Then He explained the cause by His saying ﴿And We would never destroy the cities unless their people were wrongdoers﴾, meaning: it was not Our custom with Our servants to destroy the people of the cities while they were in a state of wronging themselves through associating partners with God. So association (shirk) is the cause of destruction, and the sending of a messenger is its condition, so their wrongdoing is completed by their denial of the messenger.

The clause ﴿and its people are wrongdoers﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is a circumstance exempted from omitted circumstances required by the exceptive construction (al-istithna' al-mufarragh), meaning: We would not destroy the cities in any state except in the state of their people being wrongdoers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 60:

﴿And whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of the life of this world and its adornment; but what is with Allah is better and more lasting. Will you not then reason?﴾ When Allah reminded them of His favours upon them, a reminder inserted within the rebuttal of their saying ﴿If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land﴾ [al-Qasas: 57], with His saying "to which are brought the fruits of all things as a provision from Us," He followed it by stating that all the blessing they had been given, such as security and provision, is from the enjoyment of the life of this world, and from its adornments, such as clothing, livestock and wealth. As for what is with Allah of the bliss of the Hereafter, it is of that kind but more lasting, lest they suppose that what they are in, of security and provision, is the ultimate goal sought, so that they do not seek that by which the great and everlasting bliss is attained, and its attainment is through faith, and lest they do not make that a counterweight to following the guidance, even though following the guidance entails losing what they have of their land and its good things, were that to be preserved. This is the aspect of the connection of this verse to what precedes it.

"Min shay'" (from anything) is an explanation of "ma utitum" (what you have been given), and what is meant is things of benefit, as the context indicates, since "al-itaa'" (giving) is commonly used for giving what benefits.

The speech has shifted from the third person in His saying ﴿Have We not established for them a sanctuary?﴾ [al-Qasas: 57] to the second person in His saying "utitum" (you have been given), because what preceded required directing the rebuke at them face to face.

Al-mata' (enjoyment): that which is benefited from for a time and then passes away.

Al-zina (adornment): that which beautifies bodies.

What is meant by "what is with Allah is better" is that the kinds of the Hereafter are better than what they were given, in the perfection of their kinds. As for it being "more lasting," it means eternity (al-khulud).

Upon this statement there follows an interrogative of rebuke and affirmation regarding the lack of reason in those addressed; for when they did not use their intellects to reason towards the path of good, they were placed in the position of one whose intellect has been corrupted, so they were asked: "Are they like that?"

Al-Jumhur read (ta'qiluna) with the second-person ta' (of address). Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read (ya'qiluna) with the third-person ya' (of absence), by way of iltifat (shift) away from addressing them, expressing the wonder of the believers at their condition. It was also said: since they did not reason, they were placed in the position of the absent, due to their distance from the station of address.

[p. 155]

﴿Is he to whom We have promised a good promise, and who is going to meet it, like one whom We have given the enjoyment of the life of this world, and then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forth?﴾ I think the placement of the resultative *fa'* (*fa' al-tafri'*, the "fa'" that introduces a consequence) here is that it points to what is implied by His saying ﴿Whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Qasas: 60]. This refers to what the polytheists used to boast about against the Muslims, namely the abundance of wealth and the luxury of affluence, at a time when most of the Muslims were poor and weak. God the Exalted said: "And when they returned to their families, they returned jesting," meaning enjoying comfort. He also said ﴿Leave Me with the deniers, the people of luxury, and give them respite for a little while﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11]. It is thus evident from the verses of the Qur'an that the polytheists were accustomed to boasting of the blessings they enjoyed. God the Exalted said ﴿And those who did wrong followed what they had been given in luxury, and they were criminals﴾ [Hud: 116], and He said ﴿Return to what you were given in luxury and to your dwellings﴾ [al-Anbiya': 13]. So when God informed them that what they had of luxury was merely a little enjoyment, He set against it the surpassing and everlasting bliss prepared for the believers. This also serves to affirm the meaning of the sentence preceding it, because the second clause adds clarity to the first, showing that what they were given is passing away, and is replaced by the opposite of enjoyment and adornment. This is His saying ﴿then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forth﴾.

The one who is the referent of the first *man* (whoever) is those whom God has promised the good promise, namely the believers, and the referent of the second *man* is the group who are the disbelievers. The interrogative is used to deny the resemblance and equivalence indicated by the particle of comparison *ka* (the *kaf al-tashbih*), so the meaning is that the two groups are not equal, since those with fleeting, passing bliss and those with deferred, everlasting bliss are not alike.

The clause ﴿he is going to meet it﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*mu'tarida*) explaining that the promise is certain, and the *fa'* indicates causation.

The clause ﴿then he﴾ and so on is coordinated (*'atf*) upon the clause ﴿We have given him the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾, so it is part of the completion of the relative clause (*silat al-mawsul*). The *thumma* (then) here indicates rank-based sequence (*al-taraakhi al-rutbi*), to show that the rank of its content in loss is greater than the content of the preceding clause. That is, their loss was not limited to being deprived of the bliss of the Hereafter, but went beyond that to being recompensed with a painful punishment.

The meaning of ﴿among those brought forth﴾ is that he is among those brought forth for requital, based on what is indicated by the rebuke in ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾. The contrast in His saying ﴿Is he to whom We have promised a good promise﴾ requires that the specified group are promised the opposite of the good, so the complement of ﴿those brought forth﴾ has been omitted for brevity, as it is omitted in His saying ﴿Had it not been for the favour of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth﴾ [al-Saffat: 57], and His saying ﴿But they denied him, so they will surely be brought forth, except the sincere servants of God﴾ [al-Saffat: 127].

[Page 156]

﴿On the Day He calls to them, He will say: "Where are My associates whom you used to claim?" Those against whom the Word has been fulfilled will say: "Our Lord, these are the ones whom we misled; we misled them just as we ourselves went astray. We disown them before You; they did not worship us."﴾

This is a transition from establishing the sending of the Messengers and the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) to refuting the associates set up alongside God. The sentence is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the clause ﴿Is one to whom We have made a fair promise...﴾ [al-Qasas: 61], explaining the reason they are among those brought forth (al-muhdarin). That is, they took partners besides God and claimed that these would intercede for them, but on the Day they are brought forth for punishment, they will find none of them. You may make the beginning of the sentence His words "On the Day He calls to them," so that it is conjoined to the clause ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forth﴾ [al-Qasas: 61], meaning: they will be brought forth, and He will call to them, and He will say: ﴿Where are My associates?﴾, and so on. You may also make the beginning of the sentence His words "On the Day He calls to them." You may also take it as a conjunction of single words (ʿatf mufradat), so that "On the Day He calls to them" is conjoined to ﴿the Day of Resurrection, among those brought forth﴾ [al-Qasas: 61]; then "On the Day He calls to them" would be the very same as the Day of Resurrection. Its proper form would have been a substitute (badal) for "the Day of Resurrection," but He turned away from substitution to conjunction because the state of that day differs with the difference of the designation, so it is treated as a different day, to increase the awe of that day.

You may also make "On the Day He calls to them" an accusative (manṣub) governed by a verb understood after the conjunctive waw, with the estimate: "Remember," or with an estimated verb indicated by the meaning of the calling. The interrogation is one of reproach for the occurrence of a terrible matter; its estimate is: On the Day He calls to them, there will occur what cannot be described of terror.

The pronoun of "He calls to them" (yunadihim), the subject, refers to God, Exalted is He.

The pronoun of the plural object refers to those spoken of in the preceding verses, beginning from His words ﴿They said: If we follow the guidance with you, we shall be snatched from our land﴾ [al-Qasas: 57]. Thus those called are all the polytheists, as His words ﴿Where are My associates whom you used to claim?﴾ require.

The interrogation with the word "where" (ayna), apparently, is a question about the place where the associates are found, but it is used as a metonymy (kināya) for the non-existence of the alleged associates on that day; so the interrogation is used in the sense of negation.

The two objects of "you used to claim" (tazʿumūn) are omitted, indicated by ﴿my associates whom you used to claim﴾, meaning: you used to claim them to be My associates. This omission is an abbreviation and is permissible with the two objects of (ẓanna) [to think/suppose].

[Page 157]

The clause ﴿Those against whom the Word has been fulfilled said﴾ is detached from the conjunction particle, because it occurs in the position of a dialogue; it is an answer to His words ﴿Where are My associates whom you used to claim?﴾.

Those who undertook to answer are some of those called by ﴿Where are My associates whom you used to claim?﴾; they knew that they were the most deserving of the answer. These are the leaders (a'imma) of the polytheists of Mecca, such as Abu Jahl and Umayya ibn Khalaf, and the custodians (sadana) of their idols, such as the custodian of al-ʿUzzā. For this reason He described them as ﴿those against whom the Word has been fulfilled﴾ and did not describe them as "they said."

The meaning of ﴿the Word has been fulfilled against them﴾ may be that "haqqa" means "was realized and established," and "the Word" is a known word, namely what was known to the Muslims from His words ﴿The Word of your Lord has been fulfilled: I shall surely fill Hell with jinn and men together﴾ [Hud: 119], and His words ﴿Is one upon whom the Word of punishment has been fulfilled [...]﴾ [al-Zumar: 19]. So those against whom the Word has been fulfilled are those for whom the appointed time has arrived in which this word is due against them. The meaning: God compelled them to admit that they had misled those who went astray and led them astray.

It may also be that "haqqa" means "became obligatory and necessary," i.e., the answer became incumbent upon them, because they knew that His words ﴿then He will say: Where are My associates whom you used to claim?﴾ were directed at them, so they had no choice but to answer that question. The "word" would then mean the genus of speech, i.e., the speech spoken in that situation, which is the answer to the interrogation ﴿Where are My associates whom you used to claim?﴾. In both possibilities, those against whom the Word has been fulfilled are the leaders of disbelief, as His words ﴿These are the ones whom we misled...﴾ require.

The definite article in "the Word" (al-qawl) is most apparently the article of the genus, which is what "said" (qāla) indicates: "Those against whom it became incumbent to speak said." That is, those who were most deserving of answering, because they knew that the responsibility for what was asked falls upon them; for when the reproach was directed at the whole of them, it became necessary that the group who had kept the common people firm in polytheism and led the masses astray should take up the answer.

They began their answer by addressing a call to God under the title that He is their Lord, a call intended to solicit compassion, by recognizing that He is the One who created them, as an acknowledgment of servitude and a preparation for disowning being the originators of the religion of polytheism, since they only received it from others, from their predecessors. The indication by "these" (hā'ulā') refers to the rest of those called with them, intentionally, so that they may be distinguished from others among the people of the place of standing, and this is by inspiration from God, so that they may increase in terror, and so that they may have a hope of deliverance. And ﴿the ones whom we misled﴾ is the predicate of the demonstrative, and it is an acknowledgment that they misled them.

[Page 158]

The clause ﴿we misled them just as we went astray﴾ is an explanatory resumptive clause (istinaf bayani) to the clause ﴿the ones whom we misled﴾, because their admission that they misled them provokes the question of an astonished questioner: how do they admit to such a crime? So they intended to explain the motive for them to mislead their brethren, which is that they spread in the common mass of their followers the error that was settled in their souls, and they thought that this admission would lighten the punishment for them, by the indication of their words ﴿We disown them before You; they did not worship us.﴾

As for why they did not limit themselves to the clause "we misled them" by saying, "These are the ones whom we misled, just as we went astray," this is intended to give importance to the mention of this misleading by emphasizing it verbally, and by its being summarized the first time and detailed the second time. Thus the repetition of the verb "we misled" is not merely for emphasis. Ibn Jinni said in his book al-Tanbih ʿala i'rab al-Hamasa, regarding the saying of al-Ahwas:

So when he departs, he departs from a raging one, whose outbursts among his peers are feared.

"It is only permissible for him to say: 'So when he departs, he departs,' because the second verb was joined to the particle of the preposition, from which the benefit is derived; and similar to it is God's word: ﴿These are the ones whom we misled, we misled them just as we went astray.﴾ Had he said: 'These are the ones whom we misled, we misled them,' the speech would have conveyed nothing, because it would be like your saying: 'The one whom I struck, his striking,' and 'the one whom I honored, I honored her'; but when His words 'just as we went astray' were joined to the second 'we misled them,' the speech conveyed the meaning like your saying: 'The one whom I struck, his striking,' because he is ignorant." Abu ʿAli had refrained in this verse from what we have chosen, but the matter in it, in my view, is as I have made known to you. End of quote. Its explanation has already been given under His words ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves﴾ [al-Isra: 7] in Surat al-Isra, and His words ﴿When you strike, you strike as tyrants﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 130] in Surat al-Shuʿara, and His words ﴿When they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72] in Surat al-Furqan, for those verses correspond to the verse of al-Ahwas in containing "idha" (when).

The phrase ﴿just as we went astray﴾ is an adjunct (sifa) to a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., a misleading that produces in their souls an error like the error that is in our hearts. The point of similarity is that they received the misguidance from others, so the comparison indicates that those who answer were misled by misleaders before them, and they think that this answer repels responsibility from them, and they imagine that following the path of the misguided justifies the misguidance. This is like what He related of them in Surat al-Shuʿara: ﴿They will say, while they dispute therein: By God, we were indeed in manifest error when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds; and none misled us except the sinners﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 96–99].

The object of the first verb "we misled" has been omitted, which is the returning pronoun from the relative clause to the relative pronoun, because of the frequent omission of its like from every returning pronoun of a relative clause that is an attached object pronoun whose governing element is a verb or a verb-like adjective; since the relative noun is sufficient for it and indicates it, the omission of the returning pronoun is an abbreviation. The object of the second verb "we misled them" is mentioned out of concern to mention it, since it cannot be dispensed with in usage.

The clause ﴿We disown them before You﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf). Al-tabarru' is a reflexive form (tafa'ul) from al-bara'a, which is the negation of what defames; so al-tabarru' is the act of seeking to establish innocence and confirm it. It is transitive to the one for whose sake one seeks to establish innocence, by the preposition "ila" (to), which indicates figurative termination; one says: "I disown to God from such-and-such," i.e., I direct my innocence to God. It is also transitive to the thing that defames, by the preposition "min" (from), which is for figurative origin. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So God cleared him of what they said﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]. "Min" may also enter upon the name of an essence considering an estimated annexed noun, as in His words: ﴿And he said: I am disowned by you﴾ [al-Anfal: 48], i.e., from your disbelief. The estimate is: from your deeds and affairs, either from particular deeds indicated by the context, or from several deeds.

So the meaning here is the realization of disowning in your presence, and what is disowned is the content of the clause ﴿they did not worship us﴾; so it is an explanation of the general disowning.

The intended meaning is that they disown being those who were claimed to be associates; rather, the most they were is misleaders. This intention was a compulsion from God upon them, so that they would publicly announce their disavowal of the claim that they were associates before the assembly; or what they witnessed of the dreadfulness of the punishment of everyone whom the polytheists had falsely claimed to be divine led them to it, when they heard His words ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. This is what this verse contains of meanings.

The fronting of "us" (iyyana) before "they worship" rather than saying "they worship us" is for emphasis on this disowning, while observing the rhyme of the verse ending (fasila).

[Page 156]

﴿On the Day He calls to them, He will say: "Where are My associates whom you used to claim?" Those against whom the Word has been fulfilled will say: "Our Lord, these are the ones whom we misled; we misled them just as we ourselves went astray. We disown them before You; they did not worship us."﴾

This is a transition from establishing the sending of the Messengers and the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) to refuting the associates set up alongside God. The sentence is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the clause ﴿Is one to whom We have made a fair promise...﴾ [al-Qasas: 61], explaining the reason they are among those brought forth (al-muhdarin). That is, they took partners besides God and claimed that these would intercede for them, but on the Day they are brought forth for punishment, they will find none of them. You may make the beginning of the sentence His words "On the Day He calls to them," so that it is conjoined to the clause ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forth﴾ [al-Qasas: 61], meaning: they will be brought forth, and He will call to them, and He will say: ﴿Where are My associates?﴾, and so on. You may also make the beginning of the sentence His words "On the Day He calls to them." You may also take it as a conjunction of single words (ʿatf mufradat), so that "On the Day He calls to them" is conjoined to ﴿the Day of Resurrection, among those brought forth﴾ [al-Qasas: 61]; then "On the Day He calls to them" would be the very same as the Day of Resurrection. Its proper form would have been a substitute (badal) for "the Day of Resurrection," but He turned away from substitution to conjunction because the state of that day differs with the difference of the designation, so it is treated as a different day, to increase the awe of that day.

You may also make "On the Day He calls to them" an accusative (manṣub) governed by a verb understood after the conjunctive waw, with the estimate: "Remember," or with an estimated verb indicated by the meaning of the calling. The interrogation is one of reproach for the occurrence of a terrible matter; its estimate is: On the Day He calls to them, there will occur what cannot be described of terror.

The pronoun of "He calls to them" (yunadihim), the subject, refers to God, Exalted is He.

The pronoun of the plural object refers to those spoken of in the preceding verses, beginning from His words ﴿They said: If we follow the guidance with you, we shall be snatched from our land﴾ [al-Qasas: 57]. Thus those called are all the polytheists, as His words ﴿Where are My associates whom you used to claim?﴾ require.

The interrogation with the word "where" (ayna), apparently, is a question about the place where the associates are found, but it is used as a metonymy (kināya) for the non-existence of the alleged associates on that day; so the interrogation is used in the sense of negation.

The two objects of "you used to claim" (tazʿumūn) are omitted, indicated by ﴿my associates whom you used to claim﴾, meaning: you used to claim them to be My associates. This omission is an abbreviation and is permissible with the two objects of (ẓanna) [to think/suppose].

[Page 157]

The clause ﴿Those against whom the Word has been fulfilled said﴾ is detached from the conjunction particle, because it occurs in the position of a dialogue; it is an answer to His words ﴿Where are My associates whom you used to claim?﴾.

Those who undertook to answer are some of those called by ﴿Where are My associates whom you used to claim?﴾; they knew that they were the most deserving of the answer. These are the leaders (a'imma) of the polytheists of Mecca, such as Abu Jahl and Umayya ibn Khalaf, and the custodians (sadana) of their idols, such as the custodian of al-ʿUzzā. For this reason He described them as ﴿those against whom the Word has been fulfilled﴾ and did not describe them as "they said."

The meaning of ﴿the Word has been fulfilled against them﴾ may be that "haqqa" means "was realized and established," and "the Word" is a known word, namely what was known to the Muslims from His words ﴿The Word of your Lord has been fulfilled: I shall surely fill Hell with jinn and men together﴾ [Hud: 119], and His words ﴿Is one upon whom the Word of punishment has been fulfilled [...]﴾ [al-Zumar: 19]. So those against whom the Word has been fulfilled are those for whom the appointed time has arrived in which this word is due against them. The meaning: God compelled them to admit that they had misled those who went astray and led them astray.

It may also be that "haqqa" means "became obligatory and necessary," i.e., the answer became incumbent upon them, because they knew that His words ﴿then He will say: Where are My associates whom you used to claim?﴾ were directed at them, so they had no choice but to answer that question. The "word" would then mean the genus of speech, i.e., the speech spoken in that situation, which is the answer to the interrogation ﴿Where are My associates whom you used to claim?﴾. In both possibilities, those against whom the Word has been fulfilled are the leaders of disbelief, as His words ﴿These are the ones whom we misled...﴾ require.

The definite article in "the Word" (al-qawl) is most apparently the article of the genus, which is what "said" (qāla) indicates: "Those against whom it became incumbent to speak said." That is, those who were most deserving of answering, because they knew that the responsibility for what was asked falls upon them; for when the reproach was directed at the whole of them, it became necessary that the group who had kept the common people firm in polytheism and led the masses astray should take up the answer.

They began their answer by addressing a call to God under the title that He is their Lord, a call intended to solicit compassion, by recognizing that He is the One who created them, as an acknowledgment of servitude and a preparation for disowning being the originators of the religion of polytheism, since they only received it from others, from their predecessors. The indication by "these" (hā'ulā') refers to the rest of those called with them, intentionally, so that they may be distinguished from others among the people of the place of standing, and this is by inspiration from God, so that they may increase in terror, and so that they may have a hope of deliverance. And ﴿the ones whom we misled﴾ is the predicate of the demonstrative, and it is an acknowledgment that they misled them.

[Page 158]

The clause ﴿we misled them just as we went astray﴾ is an explanatory resumptive clause (istinaf bayani) to the clause ﴿the ones whom we misled﴾, because their admission that they misled them provokes the question of an astonished questioner: how do they admit to such a crime? So they intended to explain the motive for them to mislead their brethren, which is that they spread in the common mass of their followers the error that was settled in their souls, and they thought that this admission would lighten the punishment for them, by the indication of their words ﴿We disown them before You; they did not worship us.﴾

As for why they did not limit themselves to the clause "we misled them" by saying, "These are the ones whom we misled, just as we went astray," this is intended to give importance to the mention of this misleading by emphasizing it verbally, and by its being summarized the first time and detailed the second time. Thus the repetition of the verb "we misled" is not merely for emphasis. Ibn Jinni said in his book al-Tanbih ʿala i'rab al-Hamasa, regarding the saying of al-Ahwas:

So when he departs, he departs from a raging one, whose outbursts among his peers are feared.

"It is only permissible for him to say: 'So when he departs, he departs,' because the second verb was joined to the particle of the preposition, from which the benefit is derived; and similar to it is God's word: ﴿These are the ones whom we misled, we misled them just as we went astray.﴾ Had he said: 'These are the ones whom we misled, we misled them,' the speech would have conveyed nothing, because it would be like your saying: 'The one whom I struck, his striking,' and 'the one whom I honored, I honored her'; but when His words 'just as we went astray' were joined to the second 'we misled them,' the speech conveyed the meaning like your saying: 'The one whom I struck, his striking,' because he is ignorant." Abu ʿAli had refrained in this verse from what we have chosen, but the matter in it, in my view, is as I have made known to you. End of quote. Its explanation has already been given under His words ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves﴾ [al-Isra: 7] in Surat al-Isra, and His words ﴿When you strike, you strike as tyrants﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 130] in Surat al-Shuʿara, and His words ﴿When they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72] in Surat al-Furqan, for those verses correspond to the verse of al-Ahwas in containing "idha" (when).

The phrase ﴿just as we went astray﴾ is an adjunct (sifa) to a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., a misleading that produces in their souls an error like the error that is in our hearts. The point of similarity is that they received the misguidance from others, so the comparison indicates that those who answer were misled by misleaders before them, and they think that this answer repels responsibility from them, and they imagine that following the path of the misguided justifies the misguidance. This is like what He related of them in Surat al-Shuʿara: ﴿They will say, while they dispute therein: By God, we were indeed in manifest error when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds; and none misled us except the sinners﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 96–99].

The object of the first verb "we misled" has been omitted, which is the returning pronoun from the relative clause to the relative pronoun, because of the frequent omission of its like from every returning pronoun of a relative clause that is an attached object pronoun whose governing element is a verb or a verb-like adjective; since the relative noun is sufficient for it and indicates it, the omission of the returning pronoun is an abbreviation. The object of the second verb "we misled them" is mentioned out of concern to mention it, since it cannot be dispensed with in usage.

The clause ﴿We disown them before You﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf). Al-tabarru' is a reflexive form (tafa'ul) from al-bara'a, which is the negation of what defames; so al-tabarru' is the act of seeking to establish innocence and confirm it. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 64:

Page 160
﴿And it will be said, "Call upon your partners," so they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them; and they will see the punishment. If only they had been guided!﴾
This is addressed to all those who were called by His saying, ﴿Where are My partners, whom you used to claim?﴾ [al-Qasas: 62], for that call was a rebuke to them for taking gods as partners with Allah, the Exalted. When they perceived the purpose of their being called, and their leaders took up the task of making excuses for their taking them, He followed that with this statement.

The verb of saying is attributed to the passive voice, because the agent is known from what preceded it, i.e., "and Allah will say." The imperative is used to raise hopes, so that raising hopes is followed by despair.

The partners are attributed to the pronoun of the addressees because they are the ones who ascribed partnership to them, as in the verse of al-An'am: ﴿Those whom you claimed were partners among you﴾ [al-An'am: 94]. The call is a call for help, according to their assumption that they would be their intercessors with Allah in this world. His saying ﴿but they will not respond to them﴾ is the locus of the despair that is the intended purpose of the speech.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they will see the punishment. If only they had been guided!﴾, it admits of many meanings that the exegetes have proposed. The sum of their views on it, in acceptance and rejection, can be gathered into four aspects. The first: that it is a conjunction upon the clause "but they will not respond to them." The seeing is visual, and the punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter, i.e., He brought before them the instruments of punishment so that they would know that their partners would not avail them anything. On this basis, the clause ﴿If only they had been guided!﴾ is a fresh, independent, initial clause, separate from the clause "and they will see the punishment."

The second: that the waw is for the circumstantial (hal), the seeing is also visual, and the punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter, i.e., while they have seen the punishment, they become confused about finding the way to salvation. So it is said to them: "Call upon your partners for your deliverance." The clause ﴿If only they had been guided!﴾ is likewise a fresh, initial clause.

The third: that the seeing is cognitive, the second object has been omitted for brevity, and the punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter. The meaning is: "and they knew the punishment encompassing them," and the waw is for conjunction or circumstance. The clause ﴿If only they had been guided!﴾ is a fresh clause of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if a questioner asked: "What did they do when they became certain that they would be punished?" It is answered: "If only they had been guided to a way, they would have taken it, but there is no way for them to salvation."
On these three aspects, "law" is a conditional particle whose answer is omitted, indicated by the omission of the object of "yahtadun" (they would be guided), i.e., "they would be guided to deliverance or a way." The estimate is: "they would have been delivered from it." On all three aspects, the verb "kanu" (they were) is an expletive inserted into the speech to emphasize the predicate of "anna," i.e., "If only they were being guided with a guidance firmly established in their souls." This implies that at that time there is no settledness in their souls. The present form in "yahtadun" indicates renewal, so guidance is cut off from them, and this is a metonymy for not being guided at all.

The fourth aspect: that "law" is for wishing, used to express regret over them, and the intended meaning is their being guided during their worldly life so that they would not fall into this punishment. The verb "kanu" in this case is in its position indicating the attribution of the predicate in the past, and the present form in "yahtadun" is intended to express the renewal of the guidance whose loss they regret, for guidance does not benefit its possessor unless it persists until the end of his life.

A fifth aspect, in my own view: that the punishment means the punishment of this world, and the speech is by elision of a modifier, its estimate being: "and they saw the traces of the punishment." The seeing is visual, i.e., they saw the punishment in their lives, that is, they saw the traces of the punishment of the nations that denied the messengers. This is in the sense of His saying, exalted is He, in Surat Ibrahim: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, and it became clear to you how We dealt with them﴾ [Ibrahim: 45]. The clause ﴿If only they had been guided!﴾ is a conditional whose answer is omitted, indicated by ﴿If only they had been guided!﴾ — i.e., by taking admonition and by reasoning from the descent of punishment in this world to the conclusion that behind it lies a greater punishment — they would have been guided, abandoned shirk, and believed the Prophet (ﷺ). This is because it conveys a meaning additional to what the clause ﴿but they will not respond to them﴾ conveys. Thus these are several meanings that the wording of the verse conveys, and all of them are intended, so the verse is one of the comprehensive expressions (jawami' al-kalim).

He said: "The Day when He calls them and says, 'Where are My partners whom you used to claim?'" He repeated the account of it (of that Day) according to the multiplicity of what takes place in it, because the context of admonition calls for elaboration (*itnab*) in enumerating what deserves rebuke. The phrase "the Day when He calls them" is repeated, because repetition belongs to the requirements of the context of admonition. This is a rebuke for their denial of the Messengers after the rebuke for associating partners with God has ended.

The intended meaning of "What did you answer the Messengers?" is: what did you answer the Messengers when they called to the Oneness of God and the nullification of partners? The "Messengers" here refers to Muhammad ﷺ, as in His saying in Surat Saba': "But they denied My messengers" (34:45). The Qur'an has parallels to this, among them His saying: ﴿Then We shall save Our messengers and those who believed﴾ (10:103), meaning Muhammad ﷺ in Surat Yunus, and His saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ (26:105) and the verses after it in Surat al-Shu'ara'. Each group denied only one messenger. What required the plural form is that all the deniers denied their messengers on the ground that it is impossible for a human being to be sent as a messenger to humans. Thus they denied the category of messengers, and when the definite article of genus (*lam al-jins*) enters upon "jami'" (all), it removes from it the sense of collectivity.

The interrogation with "*madha*" (what) is rhetorical, intended to show their bewilderment. The "*dha*" after the interrogative "*ma*" is treated as a relative pronoun (*mawsul*), i.e., "what is it that you answered the Messengers," meaning "what was your response?"

"*Al-anba'*" is the plural of "*naba'*," which is news about an important matter. Here it refers to the answer to the question "What did you answer the Messengers?", because that answer is information about what took place between them and their messengers in the world.

The meaning is: the news became obscured to all those questioned, so they were all silent, and their leaders did not hasten to answer, unlike their behavior in responding to the earlier question: ﴿Where are My partners whom you used to claim?﴾ (28:62).

The meaning of "*ʿamiyat*" (became obscured) is: it was hidden from them. It is derived from blindness of sight, because it makes its possessor unable to discern things. Many similar meanings have been derived from blindness, distinguished by the verb's construction, as it is here construed with the preposition "*ʿala*" (upon), appropriate to concealment. One says "*ʿamiya ʿalayhi al-tariq*" (the road became obscure to him) when he does not know what leads him out of it. ʿAbdullah ibn Rawaha said:

"He showed us guidance after blindness, so our hearts are certain that what he said is coming to pass."

The meaning is: the news was hidden from them and they did not find the way to an answer, and that was from bewilderment and dread. When they were called with ﴿Where are My partners whom you used to claim?﴾ (28:62), their leaders stepped forward and fabricated an answer, turning away from the direct path of the question toward denying that they were the ones who had established the worship of idols for their people. But when they were asked about their response to the call of the Messenger ﷺ, they were unable to answer and found no sophistry, because they had not been preceded by their forefathers in denying the Messenger, since the Messenger was sent to them, to themselves.

For this reason, His saying ﴿So the news became obscured to them﴾ is followed by ﴿so they do not question one another﴾, meaning they do not ask one another to bring out opinions. This is due to the extreme confusion and sudden shock that affected all of them, since none of them had an escape from this question, so they were struck dumb.

Since the interrogation serves as a preparation for showing that they deserve punishment, it is understood from their inability to answer it that the punishment has indeed become due against them.
