Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 67:

﴿Then as for he who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds, it is hoped that he will be among the successful.﴾

The mention of the state of the other party, that of the believers, has come in between the description of the state of the polytheists, by way of parenthetical insertion (i'tiraq); for states become more distinct when their opposites are mentioned. The fa' (فاء) here is for consequence (al-tafri') upon what the statement ﴿Then the news will be obscured for them﴾ [al-Qasas: 66] conveyed, namely that the punishment has become due upon them.

Since "amma" (أمّا, "as for") serves to indicate detail (al-tafsil), which is the separation and distinction between two things or several things in a ruling, it here conveys that those who do not believe are losers in the Hereafter. This is what was alluded to by His saying ﴿so they will not question one another﴾ [al-Qasas: 66], for it suffices with the detailing of one of the two matters rather than mentioning its opposite. From this is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿As for those who believed in Allah and held fast to Him, He will admit them into mercy from Him and bounty﴾ [al-Nisa': 175], meaning: and as for those who disbelieved in Allah, it is by the opposite of that.

Repentance (al-tawbah) here is: abandoning polytheism (al-iqla' 'an al-shirk) and regret over having adopted it. Its being followed by faith (al-iman) is because the intended meaning is the occurrence of abandonment of the beliefs of polytheism and the establishment of the beliefs of Islam in their place. For this reason He followed it with ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾, because some of the people of polytheism were aware of the corruption of their religion, while there were enticing causes that prevented them from adopting the rites of Islam, namely the fleeting worldly goods with which they had been tempted.

"'Asa" (عسى, "it is hoped") is an expression of expectation (taraji), depicting their state by the state of one from whom success is hoped. And ﴿that he will be among the successful﴾ (أنْ يَكُونَ مِنَ المُفْلِحِينَ) is stronger in affirming success than "that he will succeed" (أنْ يُفْلِحَ), as has been previously mentioned more than once.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 68:

﴿And your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses. They do not have the choice.﴾

This is part of the continuation of the interjected statement, namely the sentence ﴿As for he who repents and believes and does righteousness﴾ [al-Qasas: 67]. The apparent meaning of its being conjoined to what precedes it is that its sense returns to entrusting matters to the wisdom of God Most High in creating hearts that are open to guidance, even if only after stages, and hearts that are not open to it, which are hard and deaf. And that He is the One who chose one group over another. In al-Wahidi's "Asbab al-Nuzul" it is said: The people of exegesis said: It was revealed in reply to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira when he said, as God related of him, ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31] End of quote. They meant by this al-Walid ibn al-Mughira from the people of Makkah and 'Urwah ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi from the people of al-Ta'if. These two are what is meant by "the two cities." Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya followed him. If its meaning is connected to His saying: ﴿What answer did you give the messengers?﴾ [al-Qasas: 65], then their saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31] is among what they answered the call of the Messenger (ﷺ) with. The meaning is: God creates whatever He wills of His creation, of humans and others, and chooses from among His creatures for what He wills whatever is suitable for the kind from which choosing is possible. Among that is His choosing for the prophethood whomever He wills to send. This is in the sense of His saying: "God knows best where to place His message," and that this is not by the choosing or desires of people. The two aspects do not conflict.

The intended point of the speech is His saying "and chooses," and He mentioned ﴿creates whatever He wills﴾ as an allusion to His being the most knowing of His creatures.

Placing the subject before its verbal predicate indicates restriction in this context if the occasion of revelation is taken into account, meaning: your Lord alone, not you choose who is sent to you.

It is permissible that "what" in His saying ﴿what they had no choice in﴾ be a relative pronoun, the object of the verb "chooses," with its returning pronoun being a genitive with "in," both elided. The estimate is: and He chooses what is good for them in it, that is, He chooses for them from among the messengers those whom He knows to be suitable for them, not those whom they desire from among their men.

The sentence ﴿They do not have the choice﴾ is a resumptive sentence that emphasizes the sense of restriction, lest it be supposed that the preceding sentence merely conveys reinforcement. The form "ma kana" indicates a negation of the state that conveys a stronger meaning than if it were said "ma lahum al-khiyara," as previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful﴾ [Maryam: 64] in Surat Maryam.

Beginning with His saying ﴿And your Lord creates whatever He wills﴾ is a preface to the intended matter, which is His saying ﴿and chooses what they had no choice in﴾, meaning: just as creation is among His distinctive attributes, so too is choosing.

Al-khiyara (with a kasra on the kha' and a fatha on the ya' with two dots beneath) is a noun of the verbal noun of ikhtiyar (choosing), like al-tiyara, a noun of the verbal noun of tatayyur (taking omens). Ibn al-Athir said: "There is no parallel to them both." In "al-Lisan" there is something that suggests their parallel: sabyun tiyabatun, when there is no treachery or breaking of a covenant in it. It is possible that he meant comparison in the pattern (wazn), not in meaning, since it is a rare pattern.

The lam in "lahum" indicates ownership, meaning they did not possess choice over creatures such that they could say: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. Negating ownership from them corresponds to His saying "whatever He wills," because "whatever He wills" conveys the meaning of possessing choice.

Mentioning God under the title of His being Lord of the Prophet (ﷺ) is an indication that He chose him because He is his Lord and Creator, so He knew his readiness to accept his message.

* * *

﴿Glory be to God, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾

This is an independent resumptive sentence to establish the glorification and exaltation of God in the manner of praising Him for His transcendence above every deficiency. It is interjected between the two conjoined elements. "Subhana" is a verbal noun standing in place of its verb, as previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿They said: Glory be to You, we have no knowledge﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32] in Surat al-Baqarah. "Subhana" was attached to His proper name rather than saying "wa subhanahu," after His saying "and your Lord knows," because the name of majesty (Allah) is exclusive to Him, and He deserves glorification by His essence; for the entitlement to all praises is what the name of majesty included in its original meaning before it was transferred to being a proper name.

The genitive phrase is governed by both verbs. The reason for restricting the glorification and exaltation with "what they associate" is that no one has dared to describe God Most High with what is unfitting for Him and impossible for Him except the people of polytheism, in their claim that what they attribute to God is perfection, such as taking a son, or that it is something informed to them by God: ﴿And when they commit an immorality they say: We found our fathers doing it, and God commanded us to it﴾ [al-A'raf: 28]. They also claimed that the gods are their intercessors with God. They said in the talbiyah: "Here I am, no partner is Yours, except a partner who is Yours; You own him and what he owns." As for the rest, they acknowledge the perfection of God, as He said: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: God﴾ [Luqman: 25]. The "ma" is a verbal (masdariyya) particle, meaning: Glory be to Him and exalted is He above their associating.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 69:

﴿And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose.﴾

It is an conjunction (ʿatf) upon ﴿And your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses﴾ [al-Qasas: 68]. That is, He is their Creator and the One who composes them according to the system from which actions and beliefs proceed, so that they are prepared to accept good and evil and to let one of them prevail over the other, in belief and in deed. And He knows what their breasts (ṣudūr, i.e. their souls) hide, and what they disclose of their statements and actions.

The pronoun in "their breasts" (ṣudūruhum) refers back to "mā" in His saying "He creates whatever He wills" with regard to its meaning, that is, what the breasts of the created beings conceal and what they disclose. And since the pronouns for rational beings have been applied to them, it is established that the intended meaning is humankind among the created beings, and they are the intended referents of the generality in "whatever He wills." Accordingly, He chooses them and recompenses them in accordance with what He knows of them, and thereby there is an allusion to the cause of choosing, and to promise and threat. This is the utmost in conciseness.

In mentioning the Divine Name in the form "your Lord" (Rabbuka) there is an allusion to the fact that among what their breasts conceal is hatred of Muhammad (ﷺ). The phrase "what their breasts conceal and what they disclose" has already occurred at the end of Surah al-Naml.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 70:

﴿He is Allah; there is no god except Him. To Him belongs praise in the first and the last [life], and to Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the sentence ﴿And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses﴾ [al-Qasas: 68], and so on. The intended point is His saying "and to Him belongs the judgment" (lahu al-ḥukm). He placed before it what is evidence that He is the sole possessor of judgment, together with the incorporation of the attributes of His essential greatness, which necessitate that all creation is in need of Him.

For this reason the sentence begins with the pronoun of absence (ḍamīr al-ghāʾib), so that it refers back to the One spoken of with everything mentioned earlier, from His saying ﴿And how many a town We destroyed, which had exulted in its livelihood﴾ [al-Qasas: 58] up to here; that is, the One described with those great attributes and the Doer of those sublime acts. The one mentioned under the title "your Lord" is the one named Allah, a name comprising all the meanings of perfection. So the pronoun of absence is the subject (mubtadaʾ) and the name of majesty (ism al-jalala) is its predicate; that is, do not be confused about Him and do not err by ascribing to Him what does not befit His name. Close to this is His saying ﴿That is Allah, your Lord, the Truth﴾ [Yunus: 32].

His saying "there is no god except Him" (lā ilāha illā huwa) is a second predicate of the pronoun referring to the name of majesty. In this second predicate there is an added affirmation of what the first predicate signifies. The name of majesty is specific in indicating the true God, but the polytheists distorted this or ascribed divinity to idols, while acknowledging that they possess a divinity other than the divinity of Allah the Exalted. Thus it was required that one should know that there is no god except Him. This was a refutation of polytheism after its refutation by the report of its vanishing from its adherents on the Day of Resurrection, through His saying: ﴿And it will be said, "Call upon your partners," and they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them﴾.

He gave a second predicate about the name of majesty in His saying ﴿To Him belongs praise in the first and the last [life]﴾. This is an argument for the negation of divinity of anything other than Him, on the ground that people, believers and disbelievers alike, do not praise anyone in this world except Allah. So you do not hear any of the polytheists saying, "Praise be to al-ʿUzzā," for example.

The lām in lahu indicates ownership (al-mulk); that is, no one other than Him possesses praise. The fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-majrūr) serves to indicate exclusivity (al-ikhtiṣāṣ), and this exclusivity is real.

The definiteness of al-ḥamd is the definiteness of genus (taʿrīf al-jins), which indicates comprehensiveness (al-istighrāq); that is, to Him belongs every praise.

"The first" (al-ūlā) is this world, and restricting praise to Him in this world is an exclusivity of the genus of praise to Him, because praising other than Him is figurative, as was mentioned at the beginning of al-Fatiha.

As for praise in the Hereafter, it is what is in His saying ﴿On the day when He calls you, you will respond with His praise﴾ [al-Isra: 52]. The exclusivity of the genus to Him in the Hereafter is a true (ḥaqīqa) one.

His saying "and to Him belongs the judgment" (wa lahu al-ḥukm): the lām here is likewise for ownership, and the fronting is likewise for exclusivity.

Al-ḥukm means judgment (al-qaḍāʾ), which is the determination of benefit or harm for another. The object of judgment is omitted because of the indication of His saying "in the first and the last," that is, to Him belongs judgment in both abodes. The exclusivity is used in both its literal and figurative senses, because judgment in this world is established for other than Allah in a figurative sense, whereas judgment in the Hereafter is restricted to Allah. In this there is a refutation of the dispositions the gods of the polytheists claim to exercise, and a refutation of their intercession which they claim, in their saying ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus: 18], that is, in the Hereafter, if what you claim of resurrection were true.

As for the sentence ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾, it is brought in the manner of specification after generalization: after establishing for Allah every praise and every judgment, the meaning is that you will return to Him in the Hereafter, where you will glorify Him and His judgment will be applied to you. The purpose of this is to bind them to affirming resurrection.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ is for the sake of rhyme (al-ri'āya ʿalā al-fāṣila), and for the emphasis on the ending toward Him, that is, toward His judgment.

﴿Say: Have you considered? If Allah were to make the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, who is a god other than Allah who could bring you light? Will you not then listen?﴾ ﴿Say: Have you considered? If Allah were to make the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, who is a god other than Allah who could bring you a night in which you find rest? Will you not then see?﴾

This is a transition from the argument for Allah's exclusive divinity based on His essential attributes to an argument for it based on His wondrous creation. Embedded within this argument is a reminder of the favours Allah bestows upon people, and an indirect rebuke of the polytheists for their ingratitude for His great blessings.

Among the most eloquent forms of argument is the choice of this marvellous phenomenon, which recurs twice every day, is perceived equally by every discerning person, and is the most evident manifestation of change in this world. It is therefore a proof of having been created (*hudūth*), and all existent things in this world are subject to it, including idols: they grow dark and their bodies blacken with the darkness of night, and they brighten and shine with the light of day. The argument from the alternation of light and darkness is stronger and clearer for people than an argument from the existence of only one of them if it were permanent, because the power of the Creator of the two opposites, who causes one to replace the other every day, is more manifest than it would be if He had created only the stronger and more beneficial of them. Moreover, the blessing of their perpetual alternation is greater than the bestowal of only the better and more beneficial of them, for if it were permanent it would be a calamity (*mash'ūman*), and the benefits of the one would be obtained while the benefits of its opposite would be lost. Thus, movement among blessings is desirable, even if it is a movement to something lesser.

This argument was directed at them through the Prophet ﷺ being instructed to say it to them, showing concern for this reminder and for this argument, and because it encompasses two successive opposites: even if their intellects were too limited to grasp the indication of one of the two opposites, the other opposite would serve as an alert to them; and even if they fell short of understanding the wisdom of each of them, their succession would suffice as an argument.

In the two conditional clauses the particle ﴿إن﴾ (*in*, "if") is used, because the condition is posited as a supposition contrary to reality. It is known that he intended the argument from the sign of the creation of light; hence he supposed the continuation of night, while the intended meaning is what follows it, namely His words: ﴿who is a god other than Allah who could bring you light?﴾

*Al-sarmad* means that which is lasting and does not cease. Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: it is derived from *al-sard*, meaning continuity, and from it comes the saying about the sacred months: "three in succession and one standing alone." The *mīm* is an augment, and its form is *fa'mal*, and its parallel is *dulāmiṣ*, from *al-dilāṣ* (lustre). *Dulāmiṣ*, with a *ḍamma* on the *dāl* and a *kasra* on the *mīm*, is an attribute of a coat of mail, and its origin is *dilāṣ*, with a *kasra* on the *dāl*, meaning shining. It is attributed to the author of *al-Qamūs* and some grammarians that the *mīm* of *sarmad* is original and its form is *fa'lal*. The meaning of making the night *sarmad* is that Allah did not create the sun, and that He created the earth, so the earth would be in darkness.

The seeing (*al-ru'ya*) here is of the heart (i.e., knowing, understanding).

The interrogative in ﴿Have you considered?﴾ is for affirmation (*taqrīrī*), and the interrogative in ﴿who is a god other than Allah who could bring you light?﴾ is for denial (*inkārī*), and they acknowledge this negation, and that the Creator of night and day is Allah, exalted is He, and no other.

The intended meaning of the limit in His words ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is the encompassing of the times of this world, and the intended meaning is not that the making of it *sarmad* ends.

The bringing (*ityān*) of light and of night is used metaphorically for bringing into existence (*ījād*): the bringing into existence of a thing that did not exist is likened to bringing something from one place to another, and the point of resemblance is becoming present and manifest.

*Al-diyā'* is light, and in this world it comes from the rays of the sun. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance﴾ [Yunus: 5]. This was discussed in Surat Yunus. He expressed it as *al-diyā'* rather than *al-nahār* (day) because the darkness of night may lighten slightly by the light of the moon, so mentioning *al-diyā'* alludes to that.

The use of the verb ﴿yatīkum﴾ (brings you) with a pronoun referring to the addressees in both places indicates that the bringing into existence of light and the bringing into existence of night is a blessing upon people. This is an embedding of the favour within the argument for exclusive divinity. Since the polytheists persisted in worshipping idols after this proof had become manifest, and they knew that idols cannot bring about light, they were treated as though they did not hear these verses which established the clear proof against the corruption of their belief. Therefore, upon that proof, he follows with the denying interrogative regarding their failure to hear, in His words: ﴿Will you not then listen?﴾, meaning: will you not listen to the speech containing the reminder that Allah is the Creator of night and light, and this verse is among it? His words ﴿Will you not then listen?﴾ are not a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*).

He repeated the command to speak in a context of affirmation (*taqrīr*), because repetition suits affirmation as it suits reproof and terrifying admonition.

The second argument is reversed by supposing that the day, which is the spreading of the sun's light, is *sarmad*, by supposing that Allah created the earth not spherical in shape, such that the sun's rays would be spread across the entire surface of the earth permanently.

The description of the night as ﴿in which you find rest﴾ is an embedding of the blessing within the argument, to remind of the blessing that encompasses many blessings, and these are the blessing of rest within it: for it includes the pleasure of repose, the pleasure of relief from heat, the pleasure of restoring the vigour of the nervous system by which thinking and action occur, and the pleasure of security from the enemy.

Light was not described by any attribute, because of the abundance of its benefits and the variety of its kinds.

Also branching from this argument is their being placed in the position of those who do not see the things that point to the great craftsmanship of Allah and His unique making of them, though those things are before their eyes.

The mention of hearing suited the supposition of the night being *sarmad*, because if night were permanent there would be no sight for people, since seeing things is conditioned on some light spreading over the surface of the visible body; pure darkness does not allow visible things to be seen. Therefore, in the case of supposing the permanence of night, the rebuke was for their failure to hear, and in the case of supposing the permanence of day, the rebuke was for their failure to see.

His words ﴿Will you not then see?﴾ are not a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 73:

﴿And of His mercy He has made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.﴾

This is an explicit statement of the blessing of the alternation of night and day upon people, by His saying: ﴿that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾. This is something the previous verse indicated by way of idmaj (incorporation), through His saying "it brings you" and His saying "you rest therein", as has been mentioned just above.

The clause ﴿He has made for you the night and the day﴾ etc. is conjoined (ma'tufah) to the clause ﴿Tell me, if Allah made the night perpetual over you﴾ [al-Qasas: 71].

The "min" (from) in ﴿ومِن رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ is partitive (tab'idiyyah), since the mercy of Allah toward people is a universal reality which has actualization in its kinds and its numerous individual instances. The prepositional phrase introduced by "min" is connected to the verb ﴿made for you the night﴾, and likewise "for you" (lakum) is connected to it. The intended meaning is to make clear that this is a mercy from Allah, and that it is a part of His mercy which encompassed everything, so that by means of these two [they] may remember other blessings.

He placed the prepositional phrase ﴿ومِن رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ before its governing verb for the sake of emphasizing the favor of mercy.

In His saying ﴿that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ he employed the figure of speech called al-laff wa al-nashr al-ma'kus (the reversed wrapping and unfolding): ﴿that you may rest therein﴾ refers to the night, and ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾ refers to the day. The estimated sense is: "and that you may seek of His bounty therein," so he omitted the pronoun and its preposition for brevity, relying on the correspondence (muqabalah).

Seeking of Allah's bounty is a metonymy (kinayah) for work and striving to obtain provision, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And others travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. And provision is a bounty from Allah.

It has been mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The lam in ﴿لِتَسْكُنُوا﴾ and the lam in ﴿ولِتَبْتَغُوا﴾ are lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), and what follows each of them constitutes two causes (illah) for the "making" derived from the verb ja'ala.

Upon these two causes is conjoined the hope of their gratitude for these two blessings, which are part of His mercy toward people. The proper course is that they should remember through these the manifestations of divine mercy and the great blessings, and thus thank Him by singling Him out in worship. This is an allusion (ta'ridh) that they disbelieved and therefore did not give thanks.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿أرَأيْتُمْ﴾ with an alif after the ra', as a lightening of the hamzah of ra'a. Al-Kisa'i read it with the hamzah deleted, as an additional lightening, and this is a dialect (lughah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verses 74–75:

﴿And on the Day He calls to them and says, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ ﴿And We will draw out from every nation a witness, and We will say, "Bring your proof." Then they will know that the truth belongs to Allah, and what they used to fabricate will have strayed from them.﴾

The phrase ﴿On the Day He calls to them﴾ [al-Qasas: 62] is repeated a second time, because repetition is among the requirements of the context of rebuke (al-tawbikh). For this reason it does not say "And on the Day We draw out from every nation a witness." Rather, the mention is renewed that Allah calls to them with this rebuking question, and draws out from every nation a witness. The apparent meaning of the verse is that this calling will be repeated on the Day of Resurrection. It is also possible that the repetition is only in the narration of it, and that it is a single call, followed by the answer of those against whom the Word has been fulfilled from among the polytheists of the Arabs, and the drawing out of a witness from every nation against them. Thus it includes the polytheists of the Arabs and others among the nations.

The past tense is used in "We drew out" (nazana), either to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, as if it has already happened, or because the waw is a waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), which is followed by the past tense with or without "qad." The meaning is: on the day that call takes place, We will have already brought out from every nation a witness against them, and We will have brought out from these a witness, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And on the Day We raise up in every nation a witness against them from among themselves, and We bring you as a witness against these﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]. The witness of every nation is its messenger.

Al-naza' (drawing out) is pulling something out from among what is mixed with it. It is used here metaphorically for taking out a part from a group, as in His saying: ﴿Then We will surely draw out from every faction whichever of them was most insolent toward the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam: 69], in the surah of Maryam. This is because the nations come to the place of assembly following their prophets. This is the first coming. Then the prophets come, each with those who believed in him, as has been reported in the hadith: "The prophet will come with a small group (rahT), and the prophet will come alone with no one with him."

The shift from the third person (ghaybah) to the first person (takallum) in "We drew out" serves to show the greatness of the Speaker. "Then We said" (fa-qulna) is conjoined to "We drew out," because it is the intended matter. The addressees of "Bring" (hatu) are the polytheists, meaning: bring your proof for the divinity of your idols.

"Hatu" is an ism al-fi'l (verb-noun), meaning "hand over" or "give." "Hat" is mabni (indeclinable) on kasra. This was discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿Say, "Bring your proof, if you are truthful."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], in surah al-Baqarah. Handing over (munawalah) has been borrowed here to mean producing (al-izhar).

The imperative is used in the sense of challenge (al-ta'jiz, showing their incapacity). It implies that they are in falsehood regarding what they claimed about the partners. When they knew their inability to produce a proof for their claim of partners with Allah, they were certain that the truth belongs to Allah the Exalted, meaning they knew with certainty of knowledge that they had no right to affirm partners, and that the truth belongs to Allah, since in the world He had forbidden them from polytheism through the tongue of the Messenger, and the truth belongs to Allah since He called them with the command of challenge in His saying: ﴿Bring your proof.﴾

And ﴿what they used to fabricate﴾ includes both the claims they lied about regarding the divinity of the idols and what they attributed to the idols of divinity. All of that is what they used to fabricate.

Al-dalal (straying) originally means failing to find the way. It is borrowed here for the thing not occurring to the mind, and for its absence from the place of assembly, by using the word in its metaphorical sense. "'Anhum" is connected to the verb "dalla" (strayed). The intended meaning is: it strayed from their intellects and their standing. They are depicted by the image of a traveler who wanders off the road and so does not reach the intended destination. The pronoun of their essences ("dhawatihim") is attached to the straying so as to include the straying of both matters, which conveys that they found no argument to promote their claim of the divinity of the idols, and they did not find the idols present to intercede for them. So they were struck dumb and could not answer, and they became certain of being held to account.

﴿And on the Day He calls to them and says, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ ﴿And We will draw out from every nation a witness, and We will say, "Bring your proof." Then they will know that the truth belongs to Allah, and what they used to fabricate will have strayed from them.﴾
