Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 76:

﴿Indeed, Qarun was from the people of Musa, but he oppressed them. We had given him of the treasures so much that its keys would burden a band of strong men.﴾

This was among the forms of harm that the leaders of disbelief inflicted upon the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims. Among the causes of their obstinacy in turning away from his call was their pride in their wealth. They said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two cities?" That is, to a man of wealth, for wealth was in their view the cause of greatness. They also used it to belittle the Muslims as the weak of the people. The Qur'an has repeatedly rebuked them for this, as in His saying: ﴿And they say, "We have more wealth and children"﴾ [Saba': 35], and His saying: ﴿And leave Me with the deniers, the people of luxury﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11], and so on. Al-Wahidi transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and others, through chains of narration: "The chiefs of Quraysh and their lords, among them 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi, and al-Harith ibn Nawfal, said: 'Does Muhammad want us to be followers of these people?' – meaning Khabbab, Bilal, 'Ammar, and Suhayb. 'If Muhammad were to drive away from himself our clients and slaves, it would be greater in our hearts, more inclining us toward him, more hopeful of our following him and believing in him.' So God Most High revealed: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 52], up to His saying: 'among the thankful.'"

Earlier, close to this passage, was His saying: ﴿And whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of this worldly life and its adornment﴾ [al-Qasas: 60], up to His saying: ﴿among those brought forth﴾ [al-Qasas: 61], as has already been mentioned.

God has struck examples for the polytheists in all their circumstances through the examples of their counterparts among the earlier nations. In this surah, He struck for the state of their pride in their wealth an example through the state of Qarun with Musa. The example of Qarun is fitting to be an example for Abu Lahab and Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib (before his conversion), regarding their kinship with the Prophet ﷺ and their harm to him; for al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi regarding his harm to Khabbab ibn al-Aratt and others; and for al-Walid ibn al-Mughira regarding his arrogance with his wealth and his offspring. God Most High said: ﴿Leave Me with the one I created alone, and to whom I gave abundant wealth﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11], for the one meant is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

So His saying: "Indeed, Qarun was from the people of Musa" is a fresh, initiating resumption introducing a story struck as an example for the state of some of the disbelievers of Makkah, namely their leaders such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. It has a particular connection with the sentence ﴿And whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of this worldly life and its adornment﴾ [al-Qasas: 60], up to His saying: ﴿then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forth﴾ [al-Qasas: 61].

This story is connected with the conclusion of the story of Pharaoh's army, which ends at His saying: ﴿And you were not on the side of the mountain when We called﴾ [al-Qasas: 46], and so on.

"Qarun" is an Arabized name. Its origin in Hebrew is "Qorah" with a long damma on the qaf and a fatha on the ra'. In its Arabization some of its letters were changed for ease, and its form was made to conform to familiar Arabic patterns, like Talut and Jalut. Therefore its letters are not letters of derivation from the root q-r-n.

This Qorah is the cousin of Musa, peace be upon him, according to what is said [dinya]. He is Qorah ibn Yishhar ibn Qahat ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub. Musa is the son of 'Imram – called 'Imran in Arabic – son of Qahit, so he would be a relative by marriage of 'Imram's brother.

It is recorded in the sixteenth chapter of the Book of Numbers that this Qorah conspired with some leaders of the Children of Israel, two hundred and fifty men, against Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, when God placed the priesthood among the sons of Harun from the tribe of Lawi. Qorah envied them, since he was their cousin, and said to Musa and Harun: "Why do you exalt yourselves above the congregation of the Lord? Indeed the congregation is holy and the Lord is with it." God was angered at Qorah and his followers, and the earth swallowed them, and all of Qorah's wealth was lost. That was when the Children of Israel were at the gates of Jericho, before its conquest. The exegetes mention that Pharaoh had made Qorah chief over the Children of Israel in Egypt, and that he amassed a great fortune.

What the Qur'an relates clarifies the cause of the arising of envy in his soul toward Musa: when Musa brought the message and departed with the Children of Israel, Qarun's domination over his people ended, so he harbored resentment toward Musa. The storytellers have greatly exaggerated the description of Qarun's luxury and grandeur, beyond what is in the Qur'an, and they have no proof for it. The exegetes have taken this up, except Ibn 'Atiyya.

Beginning the sentence with the emphatic particle may serve to affirm the predicate of "inna" and what is conjoined to it and connected with it from what the story contains, namely the evil end of those whom their wealth deceives and makes proud, so that they pay no heed to the gratitude due for blessings, make light of religion, and disbelieve in God's laws. This is because it is evident that informing about Qarun that he was from the people of Musa is not something about which a listener would doubt so as to require emphasis. So the focus of the emphasis is what follows His saying: ﴿When his people said to him, "Do not exult"﴾ up to the end of the story, which concludes with the sinking into the earth.

The particle "inna" may also be merely for the sake of drawing attention to the report, and the focus of attention is the whole of what the story contains of lessons, among which is that he was from the people of Musa, and yet he became an enemy to him and to his followers; so his affair is stranger than the affair of Pharaoh.

He avoided saying "he was from the Children of Israel" because the attribution of "people" to Musa carries an indication that Qarun had a special connection with Musa, namely the connection of kinship.

The clause ﴿so he oppressed them﴾ is parenthetical between the clause ﴿Indeed, Qarun was from the people of Musa﴾ and the clause ﴿We had given him of the treasures﴾. The "fa" in it indicates sequence and immediacy: that is, he soon became insolent with the blessing and overstepped against his own kin. It is for expressing wonder at one's oppression of his own people, as Tarafa said:

"And the wrong of close kin is more painful to a man than the blow of a keen Indian sword."

Oppression (al-baghy) is transgression, and transgressing against a community is treating its rights lightly, and the first of that is breaking its law. In describing him as from the people of Musa there is a preparation for an allusive indication, through this report, of the intention to draw a parallel with what befell the Messenger of God ﷺ from the oppression of some of his kin among the polytheists.

In His saying: "Indeed, Qarun was from the people of Musa" there is a rhetorical embellishment called "prose in measure" (al-nathr al-mutazin), that is, prose that comes in the meter of some of the poetic meters, for this sentence came in the measure of a hemistich of the al-Khafif meter. The reason such a thing occurs in the Qur'an is that the rhetorical situation calls for expression with words and structure whose whole falls into the measure of a hemistich of one of the poetic meters.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, its keys would burden a band of men﴾ is the relative clause of "ma" according to the grammarians of Basra, who do not prohibit "inna" from beginning a relative clause. The Kufans forbade this, and in their defense it is said that this is not heard in Arabic speech; therefore they interpreted "ma" here as an indefinite qualifying noun, and the clause after it as in the position of an attribute.

"Al-mafatih" is the plural of "miftah" – with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the taa' – which is an instrument of opening; the key is also called "miftah," and its plural is "mafatih." This was already discussed at His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ [al-An'am: 59] in Surah al-An'am.

"Al-kunuz" is the plural of "kanz," which is stored wealth in a chest or a storehouse. It was mentioned at His saying: ﴿Why has a treasure not been sent down to him?﴾ [Hud: 12] in Surah Hud, and that it was measured in a quantity of wealth, like what they call a "badra" of wealth, and that for that quantity a storehouse or chest was made to contain it, and each chest or storehouse had its key. On the authority of Abu Razin Laqit ibn 'Amir al-'Uqayli, one of the Companions, who said: "A single key suffices for Kufa" – that is, one key – meaning one treasure of wealth has one key. So the multiplicity of keys is a metonymy for the multiplicity of storehouses, and that is a metonymy for abundance of wealth; it is a metonymy at two levels, like the saying:

"Cowardly of dog, lean of foal."

"Tanu'" means "to be heavy." It appears that the "ba'" in His saying "bil-'usbah" is the "ba'" of accompaniment: the keys themselves are heavy together with the band who carry them; so due to their great weight they are heavy even though those carrying them are a band of strong men. This "ba'" is not the causal "ba'" as in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And he followed buttocks and leaned on a chest."

Nor is it like the example of the author of al-Kashshaf: "The load weighed him down," when the load made him bend until it tilted him. As for Abu 'Ubayda's claim that the structure of the verse contains an inversion, it is not accepted by anyone who has a heart.

"Al-'usbah" means the group. It was mentioned in Surah Yusuf. The closest of the opinions on its size is Mujahid's statement that it is from ten to fifteen. Qarun had acquired wealth in Egypt and departed with it.

* * *

﴿When his people said to him, "Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not love the exultant."﴾ ﴿But seek, through what Allah has given you, the Hereafter abode﴾ [al-Qasas: 77]

"Idh" is a temporal adverb in the accusative governed by the verb "baghā 'alayhim," and the purpose of this adverb is the story, not the dating of the oppression; therefore some exegetes regarded it as connected to an omitted "udhkur" (mention), which is what is meant in its parallels in the stories.

By "the people" is meant some of them, either a group among them, who were the people of admonition, or Musa, peace be upon him, who was called by the name "the people" because his sayings were an example for the people, so it is as if they said his saying.

"Al-farah" is applied to happiness, as in His saying: ﴿And they rejoiced in it﴾ [Yunus: 22] in Surah Yunus, and it is applied to insolence and vain self-admiration, which is excessive, blameworthy joy. It was mentioned at His saying: ﴿And they rejoiced in the life of this world﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26] in Surah al-Ra'd, and it is the total devotion to joy. The joy that is forbidden is the excessive kind of it, that is, the joy that is wholly devoted to attachment to the enjoyments and pleasures of the self; for absorption in that deadens in the soul concern for righteous deeds and rivalry for acquiring them, so that the persistent pursuit of the enjoyments drops it down to the bottom of turning away from spiritual perfection and concern for religious virtues. Therefore the object of the verb is omitted, the context indicating that the meaning is: do not exult in the pleasures of this world while turning away from religion and work for the Hereafter, as His saying clarifies: "And seek, through what Allah has given you, the Hereafter abode." I think that when joy is not attached to anything, it indicates that it has become a disposition of the one described, so it comes to mean conceit and insolence. The intended meaning is indicated, reinforcing the indication of the context, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the exultant﴾, that is, those excessive in joy, for the form "fa'il" is a form of intensity, along with an indication of the reason for the prohibition. So the clause is the cause of the preceding one, and excess in joy requires intense devotion to what one rejoices in, and this entails turning away from anything else; so the prohibition against intense joy became a symbol for turning away from seriousness and duty in that matter.

"Ibtighā' al-dār al-ākhirah" means seeking it, that is, seeking its bliss and reward. The phrase "fīmā ātākā Allāh" is connected to the verb of seeking by the particle of location, that is, seek with most of it and its greater part. The locative sense is figurative, to indicate the permeation of the seeking of the Hereafter abode into what God has given, and what God has given is the treasures of wealth; so the locative here is like that in His saying: ﴿And provide for them therein and clothe them﴾ [al-Nisa': 5], that is, from it and most of it, and like the saying of Sabra ibn 'Amr al-Faqa'si:

"We favor our equals with them and humiliate them, and drink with their price and gamble."

That is, seek by your treasures the means of obtaining reward by spending from them in the way of God, and in what He has obligated and encouraged of acts of nearness and ways of righteousness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 77:

﴿And do not forget your share of the world.﴾

This is a parenthetical clause placed between the two clauses it is flanked by, and the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah).

[p. 179]
The prohibition in ﴿and do not forget your share﴾ is used to express permission. "Forgetting" (al-nisyan) is a metaphor (kinayah) for abandoning, as in his words in the hadith about horses: "and he did not forget the right of God concerning their necks," meaning: We do not blame you for taking your share of the world, that which does not encroach upon the share of the Hereafter. This is a precaution (ihtiras) in exhortation, out of fear that the one being admonished would recoil from the preacher's admonition. For when they said to Qarun, ﴿And seek, through what God has given you, the abode of the Hereafter﴾, they gave the impression that he should abandon the portions of this world, so that he would use his wealth only for acts of devotion. Therefore it was made clear that he may use part of it for that which is purely for the delights of this world, provided he gives God His right from his wealth. It was said: They meant that you may take what God has made lawful for you.

The nasib (share) means portion and lot, and it is a form (fa'il) derived from naṣb (setting up), because what is given to someone is set up for him and distinguished. The attribution of "share" to his pronoun indicates that it is his right, and that a person has the benefit of his wealth in what suits him in this world specifically, from what is not among acts of devotion and was not forbidden. Malik said: In my opinion, the meaning of ﴿and do not forget your share of the world﴾ is: you live, eat and drink, without being restricted. Qatadah said: The share of the world is all that is lawful. Accordingly, this verse is an example of using the form of the prohibition to mean permission. The "min" (from) is partitive (lil-tab'id), and what is meant by "the world" is its delights, so the meaning is: your share, which is part of the delights of the world.

* * *

﴿And do good as God has done good to you, and do not seek corruption in the land. Indeed, God does not love the corrupters.﴾

Doing good is included in the general scope of seeking the Hereafter, but it is mentioned here so that the argument may be built upon it with His words: ﴿as God has done good to you﴾. The kaf is for comparison, and "ma" is verbal-masdariyyah, meaning: like God's goodness to you. The compared item is the goodness derived from "ahsin", i.e., goodness resembling God's goodness to you. The sense of similarity is that gratitude be for every blessing of its kind. It has become common among grammarians to call this kaf the kaf of causation (kaf al-ta'lil), and similar to it is His saying: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198]. The verification is that causation arises from the meaning of comparison, and is not an independent meaning among the meanings of the kaf.

The object of the goodness is omitted to generalize what one does good to, so that it includes himself, his people, his animals, and the creatures of God that fall within the scope of his ability to do good to them. In the hadith: "Indeed God has prescribed excellence (ihsan) in everything" [p. 180]. So excellence is in everything according to its nature, and doing good to each thing is according to what suits it, even harm that is permitted is according to its measure, and it is by good speech, a cheerful face, and good meeting.

The conjunction of "do not seek corruption in the land" is for warning against mixing goodness with corruption, for corruption is the opposite of goodness, so the command to goodness entails the prohibition of corruption. He stated it explicitly because, since the occasions of goodness and harm are many, it may escape the mind that harming something alongside doing good to other things is not considered goodness.

By "the land" is meant their land in which they dwell, and since it was a part of the terrestrial globe, corrupting it is corruption contained within the generality of the earth. Its parallels have already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿Indeed, God does not love the corrupters﴾ is the reason for the prohibition of corruption, because a deed that God does not love is not permissible for His servants to perform. Qarun was a monotheist according to the religion of Israel, but he was doubtful about the truthfulness of Musa's promises and about his legislation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 78:

﴿He said, "I have only been given it on account of knowledge I possess. Did he not know that Allah had already destroyed before him generations that were greater than him in strength and more abundant in accumulation? And the criminals will not be questioned about their sins."﴾

This is a response to the admonition of those among his people who advised him. It is related in the style of recounting dialogues, so it is not introduced by a conjunction. It is an arrogant reply by which he sought to silence them and to make them stop their admonition, because it stirred up his insolence and self-conceit.

The "innama" here is the restrictive particle (adat al-hasr) composed of "inna" and the attached "ma," made into a single word. It is the one which ought to be written with the nun joined to the mim of "ma." The meaning is: "I was not given this wealth except on account of knowledge that I acquired."

The pronoun in "utītuhu" refers back to the relative "ma" in their words: ﴿And seek, through what Allah has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Qasas: 77]. The verb is put in the passive voice because the agent is known from the speech of his admonishers.

Page 181
﴿On knowledge﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to the nominative pronoun.
"ʿAla" (on) is used for figurative elevation, in the sense of firm establishment and certainty. That is: "I was not given the wealth you mentioned in any state except in a state of my firm establishment in a sound knowledge." It is permissible that the intended knowledge is the knowledge of the rules of producing wealth from the Torah, that is: "I know better than you what you admonish me with." He means by this their saying to him: ﴿Do not exult﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], ﴿And seek, through what Allah has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Qasas: 77], ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you, and do not seek corruption in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 77]. Qarun was well known for his knowledge of the Torah, but Allah misled him despite (his) knowledge. By this reply he intended to cut off their admonition, similar to the reply of ʿAmr ibn Saʿid ibn al-ʿAs, known as al-Ashdaq, to Abu Shurayh al-Kaʿbi when he came to Medina as governor on behalf of Yazid ibn Muʿawiya in the year sixty, and began to equip armies and dispatch expeditions to Mecca to fight ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who had rebelled against Yazid. Abu Shurayh said to him: "Permit me, O Amir, to relate to you a saying which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ uttered on the day after the Conquest. My ears heard it, my heart retained it, and my eyes saw him when he spoke it. He praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: 'Indeed Mecca was made sacred by Allah and was not made sacred by people. So it is not lawful for a person who believes in Allah and the Last Day to shed blood therein or to cut down a tree. If anyone takes permission for fighting in it on account of the Messenger of Allah, say: Indeed Allah permitted His Messenger, but He did not permit you. He permitted me only for an hour of a day. Its sanctity has returned today as it was sanctified yesterday. Let the one present convey it to the absent.'" ʿAmr ibn Saʿid said: "I know that better than you, O Abu Shurayh. Indeed the sanctuary does not protect a disobedient person, nor a fugitive with blood guilt, nor a fugitive with a crime."

It is also permissible that the intended knowledge is the knowledge of acquiring wealth through trade and the like. By his reply he intended to deny their saying "Allah has given you," out of arrogance and rebellion.

His saying "ʿindī" (with me) is a qualifier of "ʿilm" (knowledge), to emphasize his firm establishment in knowledge and his fame for it. This is the correct interpretation of this clause of the verse, and it is the one that agrees with the following words of the Exalted: ﴿Did he not know that Allah had already destroyed before him generations﴾ and so on, as you will come to know. The exegetes mentioned other interpretations which bring out different structures for the composition of the verse concerning the meaning of "ʿalā," the meaning of the intended "ʿilm," and the meaning of "ʿindī." We will not lengthen by mentioning them, for they are of little worth.

His saying: ﴿Did he not know?﴾ and so on, is a turning to address the Muslims.

Page 182
The hamza in ﴿Did he not know?﴾ is an interrogative of reproach and wonder, wondering at his failure to act according to the requirement of his knowledge that Allah destroyed nations for their insolence toward blessing and their pride in their strength, and at his forgetting until it is as if he did not know it, wondering at the loss of heeding that on his part despite the breadth of his knowledge of other things, after the manner of "you memorised something and other things escaped you."

This interrogation is conjoined to the clause ﴿He said, "I have only been given it"﴾. This clause is an interjection between the parts of the story.

"Al-quwwa" (strength) is that by which one is aided in difficult tasks, likening it to bodily strength which enables its possessor to carry heavy loads and the like. The Exalted said: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of strength﴾ [al-Anfal: 60].

"Al-jam'" (accumulation) is the group of people. It is said: Qarun's followers were two hundred and fifty men from the Children of Israel, leaders of groups.

The clause ﴿And the criminals will not be questioned about their sins﴾ is a concluding appendage to the speech. It is a resumption and not a coordination with "that Allah had already destroyed those before him." The negated questioning is questioning in this world, not questioning in the Hereafter. The meaning admits that the questioning is a metonymy for the lack of need to inquire about their sins; so it is a metonymy for Allah's knowledge of their sins, and it is a metonymy for their punishment for their crimes, so it is a metonymy through intermediaries. The statement is a warning to the criminals so that they may be on guard lest they be seized suddenly. It may also be that the questioning is in its literal meaning, i.e., the criminal is not questioned about his crime before his punishment, because Allah has already made clear to people, through the tongues of the Messengers, the two boundaries of good and evil, and gave the criminal respite; so when He seizes him, He seizes him suddenly. This is like the Exalted's saying: ﴿Until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair﴾ [al-An'am: 44], and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed Allah gives respite to the wrongdoer until, when He seizes him, He does not let him go."

﴿So he went out to his people in his adornment. Those who desired the worldly life said, "Oh, would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given. Indeed, he is one of great fortune."﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿And We gave him of the treasures﴾ [al-Qasas: 76] to its end, together with what is conjoined to it and connected to it. The particle الفاء (fa) indicates that his going out among his people in his adornment, after all of that, was because he had not refrained from any part of his conduct, had not heeded those admonitions, nor even for a short time. Rather, he followed them with this outing, full of arrogance and self-admiration. The implied sense is: he said, "I was given it only on knowledge that is with me," then he went out, meaning he rejected the admonition by his words and deeds. The verb خرج (kharaja, "to go out") is construed with the preposition على (ʿala, "upon") to imply the meaning of descending (al-nuzul), indicating that it was an exalted, self-elevating outing. ﴿في زينته﴾ (in his adornment) is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in خرج.

The زينة (zīna, "adornment") is that by which a thing is beautiful and by which one shows off, such as garments, perfume, mounts, weapons, and servants. Its usage was previously mentioned in the words of the Exalted: ﴿and not display their adornment﴾ [al-Nur: 31] in Surat al-Nur. The clause ﴿Those who desired the worldly life said﴾ is detached (fuṣila) and not conjoined, because it functions in the position of an inclusive apposition (badal al-ishtimal, "apposition of inclusion"), since adornment includes what those who desire worldly life wish for. That comprises all conditions of luxury in the most concise manner. Those who desire the worldly life have various inclinations and differing desires, so each one wishes for a particular aspect of the adornment that Qarun was clothed in. Thus this meaning is achieved together with the report that his people were divided into those deceived by the transient ornaments without knowledge, and scholars who prefer the enduring over the transient. Had the clause ﴿said those who desire﴾ been conjoined with the particles و (wa) and ف (fa), this eloquent specificity would have been lost, and the clause would become either a report within the reports about the condition of his people, or part of a report within his story.

As for those who desire the worldly life: when they are contrasted with those who were given knowledge, the intended meaning is the general populace and those whose certainty is weak, whom the adornments of the world distract from what lies within them of evil consequences. Their insight falls short of reflection when they see the adornment of the world, so they yearn for it and wish for nothing but its attainment. These people, although they are believers, their faith is weak. Therefore, what Qarun had of ostentation greatly impressed them, so they said: ﴿Indeed, he is one of great fortune﴾, meaning, indeed he is one of luck and happiness.

The original meaning of حظ (ḥaẓẓ, "share/portion") is the portion that is given to the one allotted it at the time of distribution, and it is intended here as what was allotted to him of the delights of this world.

The emphasis in His words ﴿Indeed, he is one of great fortune﴾ is a kināya (implicature, indirect expression) of amazement, to the point that it is as if the listener denies his fortune, so the speaker affirms it.

[Page 184]

﴿Those who had been given knowledge said, "Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for those who believe and do righteous deeds."﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the clause ﴿Those who desire the worldly life said﴾ (28:79), so it shares its meaning. What the story of Qarun contains, which his splendor and finery show, is a temptation that indicates little regard for Allah's reward and a total devotion to pursuing the pleasures of this world and its vain glories. In the words of those given knowledge there is therefore a warning about this and a removal of what Qarun's condition stirs in the souls of those tested by the adornments of this world.

"Woe" (wayl) is a name for destruction and evil condition. Its discussion was already covered at the words of the Exalted, ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands﴾ (2:79), in Surat al-Baqara. The word "woe" is also used to express wonder mixed with rebuke. Yet those given knowledge are not calling down woe upon those who desire the worldly life, because gentle address suits the context of admonition, so that it is more helpful for being admonished. Rather, they marvel at those people's attachment to the adornment of the worldly life and their envy of Qarun's condition, without concern for Allah's reward, which they could attain by devoting themselves to religious practice and beneficial action. They know that Qarun was not characterized by religious virtues.

The fronting of the subject in the words ﴿The reward of Allah is better﴾ serves to firmly establish the predicate in the minds of the listeners, because beginning with what denotes a reward ascribed to the most generous of the generous is something the soul looks up to with eagerness.

He shifted from the pronoun to the relative construction in the words ﴿for those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, rather than "better for you." This is because explicit mention indicates that Allah's reward is attained only by the believers who do righteous deeds, and that it is in proportion to the soundness of faith and the abundance of action. Moreover, the relative construction includes those among them who are like this, as well as others who were not present at that scene.

* * *

﴿But none will receive it except the patient.﴾

The conjunction "wa" may be a coordinating one, so the sentence is part of the speech of those given knowledge, who commanded those whom Qarun's condition had tempted to endure patiently their deprivation of what Qarun possessed.

[Page 185]

The "wa" may also be parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya), with the sentence being a parenthetical insertion from Allah the Exalted, by which He taught His servants the virtue of patience.

The pronoun in "yulaqqāhā" refers to something understood from the discourse that is feminine in grammatical gender, namely the quality, which is the reward of Allah, or the upright conduct, which is the conduct of faith and righteous action.

The verb "talqiya" means making a thing encounter something, that is, to be joined with another thing. Its discussion was already covered at the words of the Exalted, ﴿and they will be greeted therein with greeting and peace﴾ (25:75), in Surat al-Furqan. It is used here in the sense of giving, by way of metaphor. That is, none gives that quality or conduct except the patient, because patience is the means to attaining great matters, since the effort toward them requires steadfastness in the face of the difficulties and arduous obstacles that arise along the way. If a person is not characterized by patience, his resolve weakens and he abandons the one for the other.

The Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 28, verse 81:

﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. He had no company to help him against God, nor was he among those who could defend themselves.﴾

The particle *fa* (so/then) indicates that the sinking came immediately after Qarun's emerging in his finery, and after what took place at that time: the wish of some people to be like him, and the rebuke their scholars gave them for their heedlessness about competing for the reward of the Hereafter, since his punishment was hastened in this world before the eyes of those who had wished to be like him.

*Khasf* (sinking into the earth, the earth swallowing) is the collapse of part of the surface of the earth into its interior, or the reverse. It is said: "the earth sank" (*khasafat al-ard*) and "God sank the earth" (*khasafa Allah al-ard*), so that the verb is used both intransitively and transitively. Such sinking occurs only through the force of an earthquake. As for the saying "the sun was eclipsed" (*khasafat al-shams*), it is used figuratively.

The *ba'* in God's words ﴿fakhasafna bihi﴾ ("So We caused the earth to swallow him") is the *ba'* of accompaniment. That is, We caused the earth to swallow him together with his home, so that he and his house were swallowed along with the earth in which he was. God's words ﴿an yakhsifa Allah bihimu al-ard﴾ ("that God might cause the earth to swallow them") have already been mentioned in Surat al-Nahl (16:45).

This sinking was a departure from the normal course of events, because it did not touch anyone other than Qarun, the two men who supported him from the tribe of Reuben, and Qarun's house alone. Therefore it is a miracle for Musa, peace be upon him.

[Page 186]

The sixteenth chapter of the Book of Numbers states that Qorah, who is Qarun, and those with him, when they harmed Musa as mentioned earlier, were reminded by Musa that God had given them the privilege of serving His tabernacle, but He had given the priesthood to the sons of Aaron, and admonition did not benefit them. Musa became angry with them and prayed against them. Then he commanded the people to move away from around the dwellings of Qorah, that is Qarun, and the tents of his company. Musa said: "If these men die as all people die, then know that God has not sent me to you. But if God creates something new, and the earth opens its mouth and swallows them and all that they have, so that they descend alive into the pit, then you will know that these men have shown contempt for the Lord." When Musa finished speaking, the ground beneath them split open and swallowed them, their households, and all that belonged to Qorah with all his wealth. Fire came out from the earth and consumed the two hundred and fifty men. Qarun had been boasting against Musa because of the group that had supported him against Musa, who were many of the leaders of the Levite community and others. Therefore God said: ﴿So he had no company to help him against God﴾, since he had prepared them to help him against Musa, the Messenger of God. So he was swallowed with them while he was watching them, ﴿nor was he among those who could defend themselves﴾, as he had supposed. It is said: "So-and-so defended himself" (*intasara fulan*) when he obtained victory. That is, his helpers did not help him, and he did not obtain victory by himself.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 82:

﴿And those who had wished to be in his position the day before began to say, "Woe! It is as if Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it. Had Allah not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us. Woe! It is as if the disbelievers will never prosper."﴾

"Asbaḥa" here means "ṣāra" (became).

"Al-ams" (yesterday) is used, by way of metonymy (al-majāz al-mursal), for any time that has recently passed. "Makān" (position) is used metaphorically for the state in which its possessor is settled, and the state may also be expressed by "manzilah" (rank).

The meaning of "yaqūlūna" is that they openly declared this out of regret for what they had wished for, and a return to entrusting the matter to the wisdom of Allah in what He chooses for whom He wills of His servants. The substance of their statements is related in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Woe! It is as if Allah extends provision to whom He wills﴾, to the end of the verse.

The word "wayka'anna" (ويْكَأنَّ), according to al-Akhfash and Qutrub, is composed of three words: "wayk" (وَيْ), the particle of address "ka" (كَ), and "anna" (أنَّ). "Wayk" is a verb-noun (ism fi'l) meaning "I wonder!" (a'jabu); the "ka" is the particle of addressing, drawing attention to the one addressed, like the "ka" attached to demonstrative nouns; and "anna", with a fatḥa on the hamza, is a sister of "inna" (with a kasra on the hamza). What follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar), which is the object of the wonder. A preposition is therefore presumed for it, whose deletion is obligatory because of its frequent use; its deletion with "anna" was permissible, but in this construction it became obligatory. This preposition is either "lām" or "min". The sense is: "I wonder, O you, at Allah's extending provision to whom He wills."

Each of these three words is used without the others: one says "wayy" meaning "I wonder," and one says "wayka" with the same meaning. 'Antarah said:

And indeed he has healed my soul and cured its sickness, when the horsemen said: "Woe to you, 'Antar, advance!"

One also says "wayka'anna," as in this verse, and in the line of Sa'id ibn Zayd or Nabih ibn al-Hajjaj al-Sahmi:

Woe! It is as if whoever has wealth is being made to lose it, and whoever is poor lives a life of hardship.

They lightened "anna" and wrote it joined, because it had become so on people's tongues in much speech, and they did not verify the original structure of its composition. The analogy would have been to write "wayk" separately from "an", and indeed they found it written separately in the line of Sa'id ibn Zayd. Al-Khalil, Yunus, Sibawayh, al-Jawhari and al-Zamakhshari held that it is composed of two words, "wayk" and "ka'anna" (as if) which is used for comparison. The meaning: wonder at the matter, and that it resembles being such-and-such; comparison is used for both supposition and certainty. The meaning: "Do you not wonder? It is as if Allah extends provision."

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', al-Kisa'i, al-Layth and Tha'lab, and al-Zamakhshari attributed it in al-Kashshaf to the Kufans (while Abu 'Amr was from Basra), held that it is composed of four words: the word "wayl" (woe), the particle of address "ka", the verb "i'lam" (know), and "anna". Its origin is: "Woe to you, know that it is such-and-such," so the "lam" of "wayl" was deleted and the verb "i'lam" was deleted, becoming "wayka'anna". Writing it joined in this view is necessary, because it became a symbol for the whole of its words, and so it was like a compound coinage (naht).

Because these assessments differ, they differed over where to pause: the majority pause on "wayka'annahu" in full, some pause on "wayk", and some pause on "wayka".

The meaning of the verse, on all the opinions, is that those who had wished for Qarun's rank regretted their wish when they saw the evil outcome of his fate, and wonder seized them at that story and at the hidden workings of Allah's governance over His creation. They knew the obligation to be content with what Allah has decreed as provision for people, so some of them addressed one another with this and declared it.

"Al-bast" (extension) is used metaphorically for abundance and plenty.

"Wayaqdiru" is the present tense of the transitive "qadara", which in the sense of "a'da bi-miqdar" (to cause to measure out). It is metaphorical for scarcity, because measuring out entails the smallness of what is measured, since it is hard to measure out a great quantity. The Exalted said: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what Allah has given him. Allah does not burden a soul beyond what He has given it﴾ [al-Talaq: 7].

The benefit of the explanation by the phrase "of His servants" is an allusion to the fact that in the extension and measure of provisions He acts as an owner disposes of his property, since those to whom provision is extended and those upon whom it is restricted are all His servants, so their duty is to be content with what their Master has apportioned to them.

The meaning of ﴿Had Allah not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us﴾: Had Allah not been gracious to us and protected us from a provision like Qarun's, He would have caused the earth to swallow us; that is, we would have transgressed like Qarun's transgression and He would have caused the earth to swallow us as He caused it to swallow him. Or: Had Allah not been gracious to us by our not being among Qarun's faction, He would have caused the earth to swallow us as He did to him and to his two companions. Or: Had Allah not been gracious to us by the steadfastness of faith.

Al-Jumhur read "lakhusifa bina" with the verb "khusifa" in the passive, because the agent is known from their words: ﴿Had Allah not been gracious to us﴾. Ya'qub read it with a fatḥa on the kha and the sin, meaning: "the Allah caused the earth to swallow us."

The clause ﴿Woe! It is as if the disbelievers will never prosper﴾ is a repetition of the wonder, meaning: it has become clear that the cause of Qarun's destruction was his disbelief in the Messenger of Allah.

صفحة ١٨٩
﴿That is the Last Abode. We assign it to those who do not seek haughtiness in the earth or corruption, and the good end is for the God-fearing.﴾

Qarun's story has ended, with the lessons it contains of good and evil. It is followed by resuming speech about the recompense for good and its opposite in the everlasting life, and that it is prepared for those whose state is the opposite of Qarun's state. There is also a connection between mentioning Paradise under the title "the abode" and mentioning the sinking of Qarun's abode, for the contrast between a perishable abode and an enduring one.

The speech begins with an arresting opening, namely a demonstrative pronoun referring to something not previously mentioned, so that the listener becomes eager to know what is pointed to. It is then followed by its explanation through the definite noun with *al-lam* (the definite article), which stands either as an explanatory apposition or as a substitute for the demonstrative, as in the saying of ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras:

"That is my wife, angry, wanting to leave me. Is it because of separation that she wants, or because of coquetry?"
...the verses.

The clause ﴿najʿaluhā﴾ (We assign it) is the predicate of the subject. The second-person particle in the demonstrative is not intended to address a specific listener; it is directed to every hearer among the readers of the Qur'an. It may also be an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), with the intention that it be conveyed to the community, as is the case with all the verses of the Qur'an.

*Al-dār* (the abode) is the place of dwelling, as in His saying: ﴿For them is the abode of peace with their Lord﴾ [al-Anʿam: 127] in al-Anʿam. As for applying *al-dār* to Hell in His saying: ﴿And they made their people dwell in the abode of ruin﴾ [Ibrahim: 28], it is mockery, like the saying of Abu al-Ghul al-Tuhawi:

"They do not tend the banks of Huwayna when they alight, nor the meadow of Hudun."

The use of "meadow" for "Hudun" is mockery, because the context is one of implicit reproach.

*Al-akhirah* (the Last) is intended to mean the everlasting, that is, the one after which there is no abode. The word is therefore used both in its explicit meaning and in its figurative sense.

The meaning of "We assign it to them" is that it is made present for their sake, and they have nothing other than it. As for others, they have states with degrees, which other verses and prophetic reports have clarified, for the rulings of the religion are not confined, in deriving them, to chewing on a single word.

صفحة ١٩٠
It is related from al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad that he recited this verse and then said: "The wishful thinking has vanished here," meaning the wishful thinking of those who claim that nothing harms along with faith, and that all believers are saved from punishment. This is the view of the Murji'ah (a sect holding that faith is not affected by sin), whose speaker said:

"Be a Muslim, and do not fear sins,
far be it from the Guardian to inflict torment.

Had He willed to make you burn in the fire of Hell,
He would not have inspired your heart with monotheism."

The meaning of "they do not seek" is a metonymy for "they do not do," because one who does not intend an act does not perform it except under compulsion. This is of the same type as ﴿And We wished to bestow favor upon those who were oppressed in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 5], as has preceded at the beginning of this surah.

*Al-ʿuluww* (haughtiness) is arrogance toward the truth and over creation, and tyranny in deeds. *Al-fasad* (corruption) is the opposite of righteousness, and it is every deed blameworthy in the Sharia or according to people of sound intellect.

His saying ﴿wa-l-ʿaqibatu lil-muttaqin﴾ (and the good end is for the God-fearing) is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*), coordinated with the clause "That is the abode." By it the whole clause "That is the abode" becomes a concluding statement, because it includes establishing the ruling for the general category through the relative pronoun in His saying ﴿for those who do not seek haughtiness in the earth﴾ and through the definite noun with the *lam* of comprehensiveness.

*Al-ʿaqibah* (the end) is a descriptive term treated as a noun, because it is so frequently used as a description. It means the final state after a previous state, and its use has become predominantly applied to a good end. It was discussed previously at His saying: ﴿So see how was the end of the deniers﴾ [al-Anʿam: 11] at the beginning of al-Anʿam.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 84:

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and whoever comes with an evil deed—those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except according to what they used to do.﴾

The clause ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾ stands in the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal, a substitute that is connected to the thing it replaces by way of inclusion) for the clause ﴿And the good outcome is for the righteous﴾ [al-Qasas: 83]; this is because the good outcome has states of goodness and degrees of bliss, and it is in accordance with what the righteous bring of good deeds, so their degrees vary according to the variation of those deeds.

The choice of the verb "jaa'a" (came) in both places here indicates that what is meant is: whoever is present (hadara) with a good deed, and whoever is present with an evil deed on the day of presentation before the reckoning. In this there is an indication that what matters is the final outcome of the matter, which is the question of the concluding state (al-muwafah, the state in which one meets one's end). As for the choice of the verb "'amilu" (did) in His saying ﴿those who did evil deeds﴾, it is because of what it contains of alerting to the fact that their deed is the cause of their recompense, further emphasizing the justice of God the Exalted.

The meaning of ﴿then he will have better than it﴾ is that every good deed necessarily contains a good that reaches the doer himself or others; so the one who comes with a good deed has a good better than what is in his good deed, or, He gives him, in addition to it, a benefaction from God better than the benefaction that is in the good deed. God the Exalted said in other verses ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160], meaning he will have, as recompense, good deeds like it; and this is a measure known to God.

When the recompense for good deeds was mentioned, it was followed by its opposite, the contrast of God's favour toward the doer of good with His justice toward the evildoer, according to the Qur'an's custom of pairing encouragement with warning.

﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾: its referent is ﴿those who did evil deeds﴾; and the second ﴿those who did evil deeds﴾ is the very same as ﴿whoever comes with an evil deed﴾. So the context called for the pronoun, such that it would be said: "and whoever comes with an evil deed, they will not be recompensed," etc. But it departed from what the apparent structure requires, because stating their description as ﴿did evil deeds﴾ repeats the attribution of the doing of evil deeds to them, for the purpose of denouncing this blameworthy action and making evil deeds hateful to the hearts of the believing listeners.

In His saying ﴿except according to what they used to do﴾ there is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh, an exception in which the excluded element is left unstated) drawn from the verb "yujza" (is recompensed) in the negated form, which, through negation, conveys the generality of all kinds of recompense. The excepted element is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), meaning: the recompense of the likeness of what they used to do. What is meant by likeness and equivalence is in the usage of the religion: a recompense commensurate with what they used to do, proceeding according to its measure without injustice; and this is entrusted to divine knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verse 85:

﴿Indeed, He who ordained the Qur'an for you will surely bring you back to a place of return. Say: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance and who is in manifest error.﴾

This is the opening of a statement that highlights the status of Muhammad (ﷺ), strengthens his heart, and promises him a good outcome in this world and the Hereafter. The denial of the people of misguidance regarding his prophethood does not harm him, because God knows that he is upon guidance and that they are upon error. This follows the presentation, earlier, of aspects of the mission of Musa (peace be upon him), which contains a lesson through comparing the situations of the two Messengers and what each of them encountered from those who turned away.

The opening of the speech with the emphatic particle (inna) is for the sake of giving it importance.

The predicate is introduced by the relative noun "alladhi" rather than by God's proper name, because of what the relative clause implies concerning the basis of the statement, and that it is a report of honour and support. That is, the One who gave you the Qur'an only did so decreeing your victory and your honour, because giving the Qur'an is something without equal, and so it is a proof of the completeness of God's care for the one given it. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

"Gently, may He who gave you the surplus of the Qur'an guide you, wherein are admonitions and detailed explanation."

In it is also an allusion to the magnification of the status of the Messenger (ﷺ).

The meaning of "faradha 'alayka al-Qur'an" (ordained the Qur'an for you) is: He chose it for you, from the expression "faradha lahu kadha" (he assigned to him such-and-such), when one assigns to him a portion (fard), that is, a share. Since "faradha" is here construed with the sense of "anzala" (sent down)—because the ordaining of the Qur'an is its sending down—it is construed with "'ala" (upon).

Al-radd means returning a thing to its state or place. Al-ma'ad is the noun of place of return, that is, the original one, as the particle of ending (ila) requires. The indefiniteness in "ma'ad" is for magnification, as the context of promise and good tidings requires, and its placement after His saying: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160], that is, to a return—what a return!

Al-ma'ad may be used in the sense of the final state of a thing and its settled condition from which there is no moving on, by analogy with the place to which one returns after having departed from it; or as a metonymy for the Hereafter, in which case the Hereafter is what is meant. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The Day of Resurrection has become known as al-ma'ad, because it is the return of all." That is, so rejoice in what you will meet on your return of honour that no honour equals, and which is given to no one other than you. Thus the indefiniteness of "ma'ad" indicates that it is of great status, and its following the relative clause indicates that no one else is given the like of it, just as the Qur'an was not ordained upon anyone like it.

It is also possible that al-ma'ad is meant in its apparent, near-to-literal sense: that to which a person returns if he is absent from it. Here, then, his land where he was would be meant, which is Mecca. This reading implies that it is a metonymy for his departure from it and then his return to it, since "radd" entails separation. Since the surah is Meccan and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was in Mecca, the promise of return is a metonymy for his departure from it before he is returned to it. The Prophet (ﷺ) had been shown in a dream that he would emigrate to a land of palm trees, as in the hadith of al-Bukhari, and Waraqa ibn Nawfal had said to him: "Would that I were with you when your people expel you; and if your day reaches me, I would support you with a strong support." All this could not be hidden from the knowledge of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Moreover, it has been said that this verse was revealed to him at al-Juhfa on his way to the Hijra, as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah, so he was promised a return to it, which is his entry into it as a conqueror and one empowered over it. Indeed, it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he explained al-ma'ad by this. Both interpretations may be intended, as established in the ninth introduction.

Then the sentence ﴿My Lord knows best who has come with guidance﴾, in relation to the first interpretation, stands as a consequence of the sentence ﴿will surely bring you back﴾, that is: He who brings you back to the Day of Return will make manifest the guided and the misguided. The knowledge of God regarding the guided and the astray is thus a metonymy for the clarity of the matter beyond doubt, because God's knowledge is not subject to confusion. This metonymy is also an oblique reference to the polytheists being the misguided, and to the Prophet (ﷺ) being the guided one.

For this subtlety, he expressed the side of the guided with the verb "man jaa'" (who has come), to indicate that the guided one is the one who came with a guidance not previously known, as the phrase "jaa bi-kadha" (he came with such-and-such) requires. He expressed the side of the misguided with a nominal sentence, which implies the permanence of error, indicating that error is their old and firmly rooted matter, together with what the adverbial particle (fi) conveys of their immersion in error and its encompassing them. The meaning then is in the manner of His saying: ﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in manifest error﴾ [Saba': 24], since it is evident that the one conveying this speech cannot be assumed to be the misguided side; so it is determined that the misguided is the one who opposes him.

In relation to the second interpretation, it stands as a form of farewell, disengagement, and ending of debate. The meaning is: Turn away from asserting your guidance and their error, and leave them to the Day of your return to your return-place, the day when it becomes clear that God has given you victory and humbled them. On both meanings, the sentence ﴿Say: My Lord knows best﴾ is resumed as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) relating to the sentence ﴿Indeed, He who ordained the Qur'an for you﴾, as an answer to a question raised by one of the two meanings.

Placing the sentence ﴿Indeed, He who ordained the Qur'an for you will surely bring you back to a place of return﴾ before the sentence ﴿Say: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance﴾ prepares the second sentence to be suitable for the two mentioned meanings. This is among the indications of the meanings of speech through its placement and the arrangement of its order, and the advancing of sentences from their places of delay in order to gather meanings.

﴿You did not hope that the Book would be delivered to you, except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Qasas: 86].

This is a conjunction with the sentence ﴿Indeed, He who ordained the Qur'an for you﴾ etc., in view of what it includes of the promise of great reward or of manifest victory. That is: just as He entrusted you with conveying the Qur'an, and that was a sign that He had prepared for you the recompense of victory in this world and the Hereafter, so too His giving you the Book without your expecting it, but purely by the mercy of your Lord, is likewise a sign for you that God will not abandon your victory over your enemies, for He chose you for this only because He prepared for you manifest victory and abundant reward.

This too is part of the sentence's indication of a meaning not expressly stated, but rather an allusive meaning by the indication of the sentence's placement.

The "casting" of the Book to him means the revelation of it to him. It is called "casting" by way of metaphor, as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Then they will cast to them the word: "You are indeed liars." And they will offer submission to God on that day﴾ [al-Nahl: 86], in Surat al-Nahl.

The exception in ﴿except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Qasas: 86] is a discontinuous exception (istithna' munqati'), because the Prophet (ﷺ) had not entertained in his soul the hope that God would send him with a Book from Himself; rather, that was purely a mercy from God the Exalted toward him and His choosing of him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 28, verses 86–87:

﴿So never be a supporter of the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And let them not turn you away from the verses of Allah after they have been sent down to you. And invite (people) to your Lord, and never be among the polytheists.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the statement ﴿Indeed, He who has imposed upon you the Qur'an will surely bring you back to a destination﴾ [al-Qasas: 85], and of what is conjoined to it, and of what intervenes between them, all of which necessitate the promise of His support, the manifestation of His command, and his success in this world and the Hereafter; and that it has come from Allah to a people who are in manifest error; and that He who has shown him mercy and given him the Book, without his expecting it, does not leave his affair without purpose. Thus He follows that with a warning against even the slightest support for the polytheists. For when the verb "to be" (al-kawn) occurs in the context of a prohibition, and the context of a prohibition is like the context of a negation, since the prohibition is the brother of the negation in all the varieties of speech, the occurrence of the verb "to be" in its context conveys the generalisation of the prohibition over every form of supporting the polytheists.

Al-zahir means the helper, and al-muzahara means assistance. Its degrees range from the highest, which is victory (al-nusra), to the lowest, which is flattery and leniency (al-musana'a wa al-tasamuh), because in flattery toward what is desired there is assistance to the one who desires it. Thus, when the prohibition encompasses all forms of supporting them, it requires the prohibition of flattering them and being lenient toward them, and this entails the command to the opposite of supporting them. So it is a metonymy (kinaya) for the command to be harsh toward them, like the explicit words of His, exalted is He: ﴿And be harsh with them﴾ [al-Tawba: 73]. This meaning is consistent with these verses being the last to be revealed before the Hijra, after he had abandoned the polytheists and departed from the city that they inhabited.

It has been said: the prohibition is for stirring up (al-tahyij), to arouse the anger of the Prophet ﷺ against them and to strengthen the motive for his severity toward them. The way of interpreting the prohibition by diverting it from its apparent meaning, or from part of its apparent meaning, is that the forbidden act cannot be presumed to occur from the Messenger ﷺ so as to be prohibited to him; so this is an indication that it is to be interpreted figuratively.

The directing of the prohibition to him, in His saying ﴿And let them not turn you away from the verses of Allah﴾, is a metonymy for forbidding him from accepting from them anything that involves turning away from the verses of Allah, just as the Arabs say: "I will not see you doing such-and-such," meaning that he will not do it, so the speaker forbids him from doing the act. The intended meaning is to warn the Muslims against inclining toward the disbelievers in any matter of the affairs of Islam, for the polytheists seek to divert the Muslims from listening to the Qur'an: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during its recitation, that perhaps you may prevail﴾ [Fussilat: 26].

It has also been said: it too is for stirring up, and the interpretation of this prohibition is more emphatic than the interpretation of His saying: ﴿So never be a supporter of the disbelievers.﴾

It is possible that the prohibition in ﴿let them not turn you away﴾ is a prohibition of pure turning away (nahy sarfa), just as the command in His saying ﴿Then Allah said to them: Die﴾ [al-Baqara: 243] was a command of creation (amr takwin). The meaning is: Allah has guaranteed to His Messenger that He will turn the polytheists away from turning him away from the verses of Allah, and this occurred when He placed a barrier between him and them by commanding him to emigrate and facilitating it for him and for the Muslims with him.

The restriction by posteriority in His saying ﴿after they have been sent down to you﴾ serves to give the reason for the prohibition, whatever its intended meaning: that is, it is not permissible for them to turn you away from the verses of Allah after He has sent them down to you, for He sent them down to you only so that you would act upon them and continue to recite them. Were it supposed that they could turn you away from them, the sending down of them to you would become void and vain, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾ [al-Baqara: 213].

The command in His saying ﴿And invite (people) to your Lord﴾ is used to mean a command to persist in calling to Allah, not to bring about the initiation of the call, because that is already accomplished; that is, the opposition of the polytheists should not divert you from renewing your call to them, as an excuse for them.

It is also possible that the call (al-du'a') is used in its most complete form among its kinds; that is, after your departure from Makkah you are more firmly established in calling to Allah than you were before, because the polytheists' clamour against him used to cloud the clarity of his leisure for the call.

All these prohibitions and commands fall within the scope of the consequence introduced by the particle "fa" (so) in His saying ﴿So never be a supporter of the disbelievers.﴾

As for His saying ﴿and never be among the polytheists﴾: if "min" in it is taken to mean partitive (al-tab'id), then the prohibition is interpreted, like the two prohibitions before it, as being for stirring up, or as the intended addressees being the Muslims.

[صفحة ١٩٧]

This prohibition is, outwardly, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, but its real purpose is to nullify polytheism (shirk) and to expose the error of its adherents. They claimed to acknowledge the divinity of God, Exalted, and said that they had only taken partners and intercessors besides Him. So He made clear to them that there is no god but Him, and that His being the sole God, in reality, requires the invalidity of associating anyone with Him in belief, even the slightest association. Thus the clause ﴿There is no god but He﴾ serves as the reason (ʿillah) for the prohibition in the clause before it.

The clause ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾ is a second reason for the prohibition, because the perishing of things, among them the idols and everything that is worshipped alongside God and associated with Him, is evidence that divinity is negated from them, since divinity is incompatible with perishing, which is non-existence.

"The Face" is used here in the sense of the Essence (dhat). The meaning is: every existent thing perishes except God, Exalted. Perishing means cessation and annihilation.

The clause ﴿To Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned﴾ is a concluding summary (tadhyil), and that is why it is separated from what precedes it. The fronting of the prepositional phrase with lam (lahu, "to Him") serves to restrict (hasr), and what is restricted is the complete judgment, that is, the judgment that no one can reverse.

The word "return" (rujuʿ) is used figuratively to mean the end of existence. Its literal meaning is turning back to a place one has left. It is used here for the destiny of creation, which is resurrection after death. It is likened to the return of a householder to his home, and the point of comparison is settling and abiding, so what is meant is the long duration of stay.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase with ilā ("to") serves to emphasize the news, because the polytheists denied return altogether and did not claim that anyone shares in it, so the fronting would not be for exclusivity.

The purpose of the repetition of these clauses is to establish that God is singular in divinity in His essence, which is the meaning of the clause ﴿There is no god but He﴾. This also indicates the attribute of eternal pre-existence (qidam), because when divinity in its genus has been negated from anything other than Him, Exalted, it follows that nothing else brought Him into existence. Thus eternal pre-existence is established for Him, and God, Exalted, is everlasting and cannot be subject to non-existence, since the eternal (qadim) cannot cease to exist. This is the meaning of ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾. And He, Exalted, is singular in His acts, with absolute disposal that no other can reverse, which entails the affirmation of will and power. In all of this there is a refutation of the polytheists who permitted His having partners in divinity and who associated their gods with Him in disposal through intercession and aid.

Then he nullified their denial of resurrection with His words: ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾.

[صفحة ١٩٨]

[صفحة ١٩٩]
In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
Surat al-ʿAnkabut (The Spider)

This surah has been known as "Surat al-ʿAnkabut" since the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, on the basis of what ʿIkrimah reported: he said, "When the polytheists heard the name 'Surat al-ʿAnkabut' they would mock both of them," that is, mock this designation, "so God revealed His words: ﴿Indeed, We suffice you against the mockers﴾ (Al-Hijr 15:95)," meaning the mockers at this and the like of it. The allusion to this was already made in connection with His words: ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to present an example, [even of] a mosquito or what is above it﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:26) in Surat al-Baqarah.

The reason for applying this name to this surah is that it singles out the mention of the example of the spider in His words: ﴿The example of those who take other than God as protectors is like the spider that takes a house﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabut 29:41).

It is entirely Meccan according to the majority of scholars, and entirely Medinan according to one of the two opinions attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah. It was also said that some of it is Medinan. Al-Tabari and al-Wahidi in "Asbab al-Nuzul" report from al-Shaʿbi that the first two verses of it, up to His words: ﴿and He will surely make evident the liars﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabut 29:3), were revealed after the Hijrah concerning some people of Mecca who had embraced Islam. The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ in Medina wrote to them that no Islam would be accepted from them until they migrated to Medina. So they set out as emigrants, and the polytheists pursued them and turned them back.

Al-Tabari reported from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that His words: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in God"﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabut 29:10), up to His words "and He will surely make evident the hypocrites," were revealed concerning a people in Mecca, and he mentioned something close to what was reported from al-Shaʿbi.

In "Asbab al-Nuzul" by al-Wahidi, from Muqatil: the first two verses were revealed concerning Mihjaʿ, the freed slave of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who went out with the Muslim army to Badr. ʿAmir ibn al-Hadrami of the polytheists shot him with an arrow and killed him, so his father and his wife grieved over him, and God revealed these two verses. It is also reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib that the whole surah was revealed between Mecca and Medina. It was also said that the verse ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in God"﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabut 29:10) was revealed concerning some weak Muslims in Mecca, who, when they were harmed by the disbelievers, would agree with them inwardly and would show the Muslims that they had remained upon their Islam, as will come when its interpretation is discussed.

In "al-Itqan" he said: To what has been excepted from the Meccan portions of it is added His words: ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabut 29:60), because of what Ibn Abi Hatim reported: that the Prophet ﷺ "ordered the believers who were in Mecca to migrate to Medina, and they said, 'How can we go to a land in which we have no livelihood?' So God revealed: ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabut 29:60)."

It was also said: this surah is the last thing revealed in Mecca. Its apparent meaning conflicts with their making this surah to have been revealed before Surat al-Mutaffifin, and Surat al-Mutaffifin is the last of the Meccan surahs. It is possible to reconcile this by saying that the beginning of the revelation of Surat al-ʿAnkabut came before the beginning of the revelation of Surat al-Mutaffifin, and then Surat al-Mutaffifin was revealed in its entirety during the period in which Surat al-ʿAnkabut was being revealed, and after that all of this surah was completed.

This surah is the eighty-fifth in the order of revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an. It was revealed after Surat al-Rum and before Surat al-Mutaffifin. What will come when Surat al-Rum is mentioned implies that al-ʿAnkabut was revealed at the end of the eleventh year before the Hijrah, so it is among the last of the Meccan surahs, such that after it nothing was revealed in Mecca except Surat al-Mutaffifin.

Its verses number sixty-nine, by the agreement of the scholars of counting among the people of the major cities.

* * *

The aims of this surah

The opening of this surah with the disjointed letters indicates that among its aims is the challenge to the polytheists to produce something like a surah of it, as we explained in Surat al-Baqarah. The disputation of the polytheists over whether the Qur'an came down from God is the root of the events that occurred between the Muslims and the polytheists, which are expressed as "trial" (fitnah) in His words here: ﴿that they will say, "We believe," and they will not be tried?﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabut 29:2). So it is established that the first of the aims of

[صفحة ٢٠١]
this surah is to strengthen the Muslims whom the polytheists tried and prevented from Islam or from emigration along with those who had emigrated.

God's promise of victory to the believers and of humiliation to the people of polytheism, their helpers, and those who instructed them from among the People of the Book.

The command to keep away from the polytheists and to distance oneself from them, even if they were the nearest of kin.

The obligation for the believers to endure the harm of the polytheists, and that for them there is spaciousness in the earth by which they may escape the harm of the people of polytheism.

Disputing with the People of the Book in the best manner, except for those among them who are wrongdoers.

The command to the Prophet ﷺ to persist in conveying the Qur'an and the laws of Islam.

Taking consolation in this from the circumstances of the nations to which messengers came, and that Muhammad ﷺ came with the like of what they brought.

And the lessons contained within the accounts of the messengers mentioned in it.

Proof that the Qur'an is sent down from God, by the evidence of the unlettered state of the one to whom it was revealed ﷺ.

Reminding the polytheists of God's blessings upon them, so that they may desist from worshipping other than Him.

Holding them to account for affirming His oneness, by the fact that they acknowledge that He is the Creator of whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth.

Proof of resurrection by contemplating the beginning of creation, which is more wondrous than its repetition.

Affirmation of recompense for deeds.

The threat to the polytheists of a punishment that will come upon them suddenly while they mock its hastening.

And the striking of a parable for the polytheists' taking of protectors besides God, by a parable: the house of the spider.
